g.c: G G (jē) 1. G is the seventh letter of the English alphabet, and a vocal consonant. It has two sounds; one simple, as in gave, go, gull; the other compound (like that of j), as in gem, gin, dingy. See Guide to Pronunciation, §§ 231-6, 155, 176, 178, 179, 196, 211, 246.

gab.c: Gab Gab (găb), n. [Cf. Gaff.] (Steam Engine) The hook on the end of an eccentric rod opposite the strap. See. Illust. of Eccentric.

Gab Gab, n. [OE. gabbe gabble, mocking, fr. Icel. gabb mocking, mockery, or OF. gab, gabe; perh. akin to E. gape, or gob. Cf. Gab, v. i., Gibber.] The mouth; hence, idle prate; chatter; unmeaning talk; loquaciousness. [Colloq.]
Gab Gab, v. i. [OE. gabben to jest, lie, mock, deceive, fr. Icel. gabba to mock, or OF. gaber. See 2d Gab, and cf. Gabble.] 1. To deceive; to lie. [Obs.] Chaucer.

gabarage.c: Gabarage Gab"ar*age (?), n. A kind of coarse cloth for packing goods. [Obs.]

gaberdine.c: Gaberdine Gabardine Gab`ar*dine", Gab`er*dine" (?), n. [Sp. gabardina; cf. It. gavardina, OF. galvardine, calvardine, gavardine, galeverdine; perh. akin to Sp. & OF. gaban a sort of cloak or coat for rainy weather, F. caban great coat with a hood and sleeves, It. gabbano and perh. to E. cabin.] A coarse frock or loose upper garment formerly worn by Jews; a mean dress. Shak.

gabber.c: Gabber Gab"ber (?), n. 1. A liar; a deceiver. [Obs.]

gabble.c: Gabble Gab"ble (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gabbled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gabbling (?).] [Freq. of gab. See Gab, v. i.] 1. To talk fast, or to talk without meaning; to prate; to jabber. Shak.
Gabble Gab"ble, n. 1. Loud or rapid talk without meaning.

gabbler.c: Gabbler Gab"bler (?), n. One who gabbles; a prater.

gabbro.c: Gabbro Gab"bro (?), n. [It.] (Geol.) A name originally given by the Italians to a kind of serpentine, later to the rock called euphotide, and now generally used for a coarsely crystalline, igneous rock consisting of lamellar pyroxene (diallage) and labradorite, with sometimes chrysolite (olivine gabbro).

gabel.c: Gabel Ga"bel (?), n. [F. gabelle, LL. gabella, gabulum, gablum; of uncertain origin. Cf.Gavel tribute.] (O. Eng. Law) A rent, service, tribute, custom, tax, impost, or duty; an excise. Burrill.

gabeler.c: Gabeler Ga"bel*er (?), n. (O. Eng. Law) A collector of gabels or taxes.

gabelle.c: Gabelle ‖Ga`belle" (?), n. [F. See Gabel.] A tax, especially on salt. [France] Brande & C.

gaberlunzie.c: Gaber-lunzie Gab"er-lun`zie (?), n. [Gael. gabair talker + lunndair idler.] A beggar with a wallet; a licensed beggar. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.

gabert.c: Gabert Gab"ert (?), n. [Cf.F.gabare, Arm. kobar, gobar.] A lighter, or vessel for inland navigation. [Scot.] Jamieson.

gabion.c: Gabion Ga"bi*on (?), n.[F., from It. gabbione a large cage, gabion, from gabbia cage, L. cavea. See Cage.] 1. (Fort.) A hollow cylinder of wickerwork, like a basket without a bottom. Gabions are made of various sizes, and filled with earth in building fieldworks to shelter men from an enemy's fire.

gabionade.c: Gabionade Ga`bi*on*ade" (?), n. [F. gabionnade.] 1. (Fort.) A traverse made with gabions between guns or on their flanks, protecting them from enfilading fire.

gabionage.c: Gabionage Ga"bi*on*age (?), n. [F. gabionnage.] (Mil.) The part of a fortification built of gabions.

gabioned.c: Gabioned Ga"bi*oned (?), p. a. Furnished with gabions.

gable.c: Gable Ga"ble, n. [OE. gable, gabil, F. gable, fr. LL. gabalum front of a building, prob. of German or Scand. origin; cf. OHG. gibil, G. giebel gable, Icel. gafl, Goth. gibla pinnacle; perh. akin to Gr.? head, and E. cephalic, or to G. gabel fork, AS. geafl, E. gaffle, L. gabalus a kind of gallows.] (Arch.) (a) The vertical triangular portion of the end of a building, from the level of the cornice or eaves to the ridge of the roof. Also, a similar end when not triangular in shape, as of a gambrel roof and the like. Hence: (b) The end wall of a building, as distinguished from the front or rear side. (c) A decorative member having the shape of a triangular gable, such as that above a Gothic arch in a doorway.

gablet.c: Gablet Ga"blet (?), n. (Arch.) A small gable, or gable-shaped canopy, formed over a tabernacle, niche, etc.

gablock.c: Gablock Gab"lock (?), n. [See Gavelock.] A false spur or gaff, fitted on the heel of a gamecock. Wright.

gaby.c: Gaby Ga"by (?), n. [Icel. gapi a rash, reckless man. Cf. Gafe.] A simpleton; a dunce; a lout. [Colloq.]

gad.c: Gad Gad (?), n. [OE. gad, Icel. gaddr goad, sting; akin to Sw. gadd sting, Goth. gazds, G. gerte switch. See Yard a measure.] 1. The point of a spear, or an arrowhead.

Gad Gad, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gadded; p. pr. & vb. n. Gadding.] [Prob. fr. gad, n., and orig. meaning to drive about.] To walk about; to rove or go about, without purpose; hence, to run wild; to be uncontrolled. “The gadding vine.” Milton.

gadder.c: Gadder Gad"der (?), n. One who roves about idly, a rambling gossip.

gadding.c: Gadding Gad"ding, a. & n. Going about much, needlessly or without purpose.

gaddingly.c: Gaddingly Gad"ding*ly (?), adv. In a roving, idle manner.

gaddish.c: Gaddish Gad"dish (?), a. Disposed to gad. -- Gad"dish*nes, n. “Gaddishness and folly.” Abp. Leighton.

gade.c: Gade Gade (?), n. [Cf. Cod the fish.] (Zool.) (a) A small British fish (Motella argenteola) of the Cod family. (b) A pike, so called at Moray Firth; -- called also gead. [Prov. Eng.]

gadre.c: Gadre Gadere Gad"er*e (?), Gad"re (?), v. t. & i. To gather. [Obs.] Chaucer.

gadfly.c: Gadfly Gad"fly` (găd"flī`), n.; pl. Gadflies (#). [Gad + fly.] (Zool.) Any dipterous insect of the genus Oestrus, and allied genera of botflies.

gadhelic.c: Gadhelic Ga*dhel"ic (gȧ*dĕl"ĭk; găd"eil*ĭk), a. [See Gael.] Of, belonging to, or designating, that division of the Celtic languages which includes the Irish, Gaelic, and Manx.

gadic.c: Gadic Gad"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or derived from, the cod (Gadus); -- applied to an acid obtained from cod-liver oil, viz., gadic acid.

gaditanian.c: Gaditanian Gad`i*ta`ni*an (?), a. [L. Gaditanus, fr. Gades Cadiz.] Of or relating to Cadiz, in Spain. -- n. A native or inhabitant of Cadiz.

gadling.c: Gadling Gad"ling (?), n. [Gad, n. + -ling.] (Mediæval Armor) [R.] See Gad, n., 4.
Gadling Gad"ling, a. [See Gad, v. i.] Gadding about. [Obs.]
Gadling Gad"ling, n. A roving vagabond. [Obs.] Rom. of R.

gadoid.c: Gadoid Ga"doid (?; 277), a. [NL. gadus cod + -oid: cf. F. gadoïde gadoid, Gr.? a sort of fish, F. gade.] (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the family of fishes (Gadidæ) which includes the cod, haddock, and hake. -- n. One of the Gadidæ. [Written also gadid.]

gadolinia.c: Gadolinia Gad`o*lin"i*a (?), n. [NL. See Gadolinite.] (Chem.) A rare earth associated with yttria and regarded as the oxide (Gd2O3) of a metallic element, gadolinium.

gadolinic.c: Gadolinic Gad`o*lin"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to or containing gadolinium.

gadolinite.c: Gadolinite Gad"o*lin*ite (?), n. [Named after Gadolin, a Russian chemist.] (Min.) A mineral of a nearly black color and vitreous luster, and consisting principally of the silicates of yttrium, cerium, and iron.

gadolinium.c: Gadolinium Gad`o*lin"i*um (?), n. [NL. See Gadolinite.] (Chem.) A rare earth metallic element of the Lanthanide series, with a characteristic spectrum, found associated with yttrium and other rare earth elements. Symbol, Gd; it has an atomic number of 64, an atomic weight of 157.25 (C=12.011), and a valence of +3.

gadsman.c: Gadsman Gads"man (?), n. One who uses a gad or goad in driving.

gaduin.c: Gaduin Gad"u*in (?), n.[NL. gadus codfish.] (Chem.) A yellow or brown amorphous substance, of indifferent nature, found in cod-liver oil.

gadwall.c: Gadwall Gad"wall (?), n. [Gad to walk about + well.] (Zool.) A large duck (Anas strepera), valued as a game bird, found in the northern parts of Europe and America; -- called also gray duck. [Written also gaddwell.]

gaekwar.c: Gaekwar Gaek"war (?), n. [Also Gaikwar, Guicowar.] [Marathi gāekwār, prop., a cowherd.] The title of the ruling Prince of Baroda, in Gujarat, in Bombay, India.

gael.c: Gael Gael (?), n.sing. & pl. [See Gaelic.] (Ethnol.) A Celt or the Celts of the Scotch Highlands or of Ireland; now esp., a Scotch Highlander of Celtic origin.

gaelic.c: Gaelic Gael"ic (?; 277), a. [Gael. Gàidhealach, Gaelach, from Gàidheal, Gael, a Scotch Highlander.] (Ethnol.) Of or pertaining to the Gael, esp. to the Celtic Highlanders of Scotland; as, the Gaelic language.
Gaelic Gael"ic (?), n. [Gael. Gaelig, Gàilig.] The language of the Gaels, esp. of the Highlanders of Scotland. It is a branch of the Celtic.

gaff.c: Gaff Gaff (găf), n. [OE. gaffe, F. gaffe an iron hook with which seamen pull great fishes into their ships; cf. Ir. gaf, gafa hook; perh. akin to G. gabel fork, Skr. gabhasti. Cf. Gaffle, Gable.] 1. A barbed spear or a hook with a handle, used by fishermen in securing heavy fish.
Gaff Gaff, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gaffed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gaffing.] To strike with a gaff or barbed spear; to secure by means of a gaff; as, to gaff a salmon.

gaffer.c: Gaffer Gaf"fer (găf"fẽr), n. [Possibly contr. fr. godfather; but prob. fr. gramfer for grandfather. Cf. Gammer.] 1. An old fellow; an aged rustic.

gaffle.c: Gaffle Gaf"fle (?), n. [Cf. AS. geafl fork, LG., D., Sw., & Dan. gaffel, G. gabel, W. gafl, Ir. & Gael. gabhal. Cf. Gaff.] 1. An artificial spur or gaff for gamecocks.

gafftopsail.c: Gaff-topsail Gaff`-top"sail (?), n. (Naut.) A small triangular sail having its foot extended upon the gaff and its luff upon the topmast.

gag.c: Gag Gag (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gagged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gagging (?).] [Prob. fr. W. cegio to choke or strangle, fr. ceg mouth, opening, entrance.] 1. To stop the mouth of, by thrusting sometimes in, so as to hinder speaking; hence, to silence by authority or by violence; not to allow freedom of speech to. Marvell.
Gag Gag, v. i. 1. To heave with nausea; to retch.
Gag Gag, n. 1. Something thrust into the mouth or throat to hinder speaking.
Gag law Gag law. (Parliamentary Law) A law or ruling prohibiting proper or free debate, as in closure. [Colloq. or Cant]

gagate.c: Gagate Gag"ate (?; 48), n. [L. gagates. See Jet a black mineral.] Agate. [Obs.] Fuller.

gage.c: Gage Gage (gāj), n. [F. gage, LL. gadium, wadium; of German origin; cf. Goth. wadi, OHG. wetti, weti, akin to E. wed. See Wed, and cf. Wage, n.] 1. A pledge or pawn; something laid down or given as a security for the performance of some act by the person depositing it, and forfeited by nonperformance; security.

Gage Gage (gāj), n. [So called because an English family named Gage imported the greengage from France, in the last century.] A variety of plum; as, the greengage; also, the blue gage, frost gage, golden gage, etc., having more or less likeness to the greengage. See Greengage.

Gage Gage, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gaged (gājd); p. pr & vb. n. Gaging (gā"jĭng).] [Cf. F. gager. See Gage, n., a pledge.] 1. To give or deposit as a pledge or security for some act; to wage or wager; to pawn or pledge. [Obs.]
Gage Gage, n. A measure or standard. See Gauge, n.
Gage Gage, v. t. To measure. See Gauge, v. t.

gager.c: Gager Ga"ger (gā"jẽr), n. A measurer. See Gauger.

gaggle.c: Gaggle Gag"gle (găg"g'l), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gaggled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gaggling (?).] [Of imitative origin; cf. D. gaggelen, gagelen, G. gackeln, gackern, MHG. gāgen, E. giggle, cackle.] To make a noise like a goose; to cackle. Bacon.
Gaggle Gag"gle, n. [Cf. Gaggle v. i.] 1. (Zool.) A flock of wild geese, especially when on the ground. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.

gagtooth.c: gagtooth gag"tooth` (găg"tōoth`), n.; pl. Gagteeth (găg"tēth`). A projecting tooth. [Obs.]

gahnite.c: gahnite gahn"ite (gän"īt), n. [Named after Gahn, a Swedish chemist.] (Min.) Zinc spinel; automolite.

gaidic.c: gaidic ga*id"ic (?), a. [Gr. gai^a earth.] (Chem.) Pertaining to hypogeic acid; -- applied to an acid obtained from hypogeic acid.

gaillard.c: Gaillard ‖Gail`lard" (?), a. [F. See Galliard.] Gay; brisk; merry; galliard. Chaucer.

gailliarde.c: Gailliarde ‖Gail*liarde" (?), n. [See Galliard a dance.] A lively French and Italian dance.

gaily.c: Gaily Gai"ly (?), adv. [From Gay.] Merrily; showily. See gaily.

gain.c: Gain Gain (?), n. [Cf. W. gan a mortise.] (Arch.) A square or beveled notch cut out of a girder, binding joist, or other timber which supports a floor beam, so as to receive the end of the floor beam.

Gain Gain, a. [OE. gein, gain, good, near, quick; cf. Icel. gegn ready, serviceable, and gegn, adv., against, opposite. Cf. Again.] Convenient; suitable; direct; near; handy; dexterous; easy; profitable; cheap; respectable. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]

Gain Gain (gān), n. [OE. gain, gein, gaȝhen, gain, advantage, Icel. gagn; akin to Sw. gagn, Dan. gavn, cf. Goth. gageigan to gain. The word was prob. influenced by F. gain gain, OF. gaain. Cf. Gain, v. t.] 1. That which is gained, obtained, or acquired, as increase, profit, advantage, or benefit; -- opposed to loss.

Gain Gain, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gained (gānd); p. pr. & vb. n. Gaining.] [From gain, n. but. prob. influenced by F. gagner to earn, gain, OF. gaaignier to cultivate, OHG. weidinōn, weidinen to pasture, hunt, fr. weida pasturage, G. weide, akin to Icel. veiðr hunting, AS. wāðu, cf. L. venari to hunt, E. venison. See Gain, n., profit.]
Gain Gain (?), v. i. To have or receive advantage or profit; to acquire gain; to grow rich; to advance in interest, health, or happiness; to make progress; as, the sick man gains daily.

gainable.c: Gainable Gain"a*ble (?), a. [CF. F. gagnable. See Gain, v. t.] Capable of being obtained or reached. Sherwood.

gainage.c: Gainage Gain"age (?, 48), n. [OF. gaignage pasturage, crop, F. gaignage pasturage. See Gain, v. t.] (O. Eng. Law) (a) The horses, oxen, plows, wains or wagons and implements for carrying on tillage. (b) The profit made by tillage; also, the land itself. Bouvier.

gainer.c: Gainer Gain"er (?), n. One who gains. Shak.

gainful.c: Gainful Gain"ful (?), a. Profitable; advantageous; lucrative. “A gainful speculation.” Macaulay. -- Gain"ful*ly, adv. -- Gain"ful*ness, n.

gaingiving.c: Gaingiving Gain"giv`ing (?), n. [See Again, and Give.] A misgiving. [Obs.]

gainless.c: Gainless Gain"less, a. Not producing gain; unprofitable. Hammond. -- Gain"less/ness, n.

gainly.c: Gainly Gain"ly, adv. [See Gain, a.] Handily; readily; dexterously; advantageously. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

gainpain.c: Gainpain Gain"pain` (?), n.[F. gagner to gain + pain bread.] Bread-gainer; -- a term applied in the Middle Ages to the sword of a hired soldier.

gainsay.c: Gainsay Gain`say" (? or?; 277), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gainsaid (? or?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gainsaying.] [OE. geinseien, ageinseien. See Again, and Say to utter.] To contradict; to deny; to controvert; to dispute; to forbid.

gainsayer.c: Gainsayer Gain`say"er (?), n. One who gainsays, contradicts, or denies. “To convince the gainsayers.” Tit. i. 9.

gainsborough.c: Gainsborough hat Gains"borough hat (?). A woman's broad-brimmed hat of a form thought to resemble those shown in portraits by Thomas Gainsborough, the English artist (1727-88).

gainstand.c: Gainstand Gain"stand` (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gainstood; p. pr. & vb. n. gainstanding.] [See Again, and Stand.] To withstand; to resist. [Obs.]

gainstrive.c: Gainstrive Gain"strive` (?), v. t. & i. [See Again, and Strive.] To strive or struggle against; to withstand. [Obs.] Spenser.

gairishness.c: Gairish/ness Gairishly Gairish Gair"ish (?), a., Gair"ish*ly, adv., Gair"ish/ness, n. Same as Garish, Garishly, Garishness.

gait.c: Gait Gait (?), n. [See Gate a way.] 1. A going; a walk; a march; a way.

gaited.c: Gaited Gait"ed (?), a. Having (such) a gait; -- used in composition; as, slow-gaited; heavy-gaited.

gaiter.c: Gaiter Gait"er (?), n. [F. guêtre, cf. Armor. gweltren; or perh. of German origin, and akin to E. wear, v.] 1. A covering of cloth or leather for the ankle and instep, or for the whole leg from the knee to the instep, fitting down upon the shoe.
Gaiter Gai"ter (?), v. t. To dress with gaiters.

gaytre.c: Gaytre Gaitre Gai"tre, Gay"tre (gā"tẽr), n. [OE. Cf. Gatten tree.] The dogwood tree. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Gaytre Gay"tre (?), n. [See Gaitre.] The dogwood tree. [Obs.] Chaucer.

gala.c: Gala Ga"la (?), n. [F. gala show, pomp, fr. It. gala finery, gala; of German origin. See Gallant.] Pomp, show, or festivity. Macaulay.

galactagogue.c: Galacta-gogue Ga*lac"ta-gogue (?), n. [Gr.?,?, milk +? to lead.] (Med.) An agent exciting secretion of milk.

galactic.c: Galactic Ga*lac"tic (?), a. [Gr.? milky, fr.?,?, milk. See Galaxy, and cf. Lactic.] 1. Of or pertaining to milk; got from milk; as, galactic acid.

galactin.c: Galactin Ga*lac"tin (?), n. [Gr.?,?, milk. Cf. Lactin.] (Chem.) (a) An amorphous, gelatinous substance containing nitrogen, found in milk and other animal fluids. It resembles peptone, and is variously regarded as a coagulating or emulsifying agent. (b) A white waxy substance found in the sap of the South American cow tree (Galactodendron). (c) An amorphous, gummy carbohydrate resembling gelose, found in the seeds of leguminous plants, and yielding on decomposition several sugars, including galactose.

galactodensimeter.c: Galactodensimeter Ga*lac`to*den*sim"e*ter (?), n. [Gr.?,? + E. densimeter.] Same as Galactometer.

galactometer.c: Galactometer Gal`ac*tom"e*ter (?), n. [Gr.?,?, milk + -meter: cf. F. galactomètre. Cf. Lactometer.] An instrument for ascertaining the quality of milk (i.e., its richness in cream) by determining its specific gravity; a lactometer.

galactophagist.c: Galactophagist Gal`ac*toph"a*gist (?), n. [Gr.?,?, milk +? to eat: cf.? to live on milk.] One who eats, or subsists on, milk.

galactophagous.c: Galactophagous Gal`ac*toph"a*gous (?), a. [Gr.?: cf. F. galactophade.] Feeding on milk.

galactophorous.c: Galactophorous Gal`ac*toph"o*rous (?), a. [Gr.?;?,?, milk + fe`rein to bear: cf. F. galactophore. Cf. Lactiferous.] (Anat.) Milk-carrying; lactiferous; -- applied to the ducts of mammary glands.

galactopoietic.c: Galactopoietic Ga*lac`to*poi*et"ic (?), a. [Gr.?,?, milk +? capable of making; fr.? to make.] (Med.) Increasing the flow of milk; milk-producing. -- n. A galactopoietic substance.

galactose.c: Galactose Ga*lac"tose (?), n. (Chem.) A white, crystalline sugar, C6H12O6, isomeric with dextrose, obtained by the decomposition of milk sugar, and also from certain gums. When oxidized it forms mucic acid. Called also lactose (though it is not lactose proper).

galago.c: Galago Ga*la"go (?), n.; pl. Galagos (#). [Native name.] (Zool.) A genus of African lemurs, including numerous species.

galangal.c: Galangal Galanga { Ga*lan"ga (?), Ga*lan"gal (?) }, n.[OE. galingale, OF. galingal, garingal, F. galanga (cf. Sp. galanga), prob. fr. Ar. khalanjān. ] The pungent aromatic rhizome or tuber of certain East Indian or Chinese species of Alpinia (Alpinia Galanga and Alpinia officinarum) and of the Kæmpferia Galanga), -- all of the Ginger family.

galatea.c: Galatea Gal`a*te"a (?), n. [After Galatea, a British man-of-war, the material being used for children's sailor suits.] A kind of striped cotton fabric, usually of superior quality and striped with blue or red on white.

galantine.c: Galantine Gal"an*tine (? or?), n. [F. galantine.] A dish of veal, chickens, or other white meat, freed from bones, tied up, boiled, and served cold. Smart.

galapee.c: Galapee tree Gal"a*pee` tree" (?), (Bot.) The West Indian Sciadophyllum Brownei, a tree with very large digitate leaves.

galatian.c: Galatian Ga*la"tian (?), prop. a. Of or pertaining to Galatia or its inhabitants. -- A native or inhabitant of Galatia, in Asia Minor; a descendant of the Gauls who settled in Asia Minor.

galaxy.c: Galaxy Gal"ax*y (?), n.; pl. Galaxies (#). [F. galaxie, L. galaxias, fr. Gr.? (sc.? circle), fr.?,?, milk; akin to L. lac. Cf. Lacteal.]

galbanum.c: Galbanum Galban { Gal"ban, Gal"ba*num (?), } n. [L. galbanum, Gr.?, prob. from Heb. klekb'n?h: cf. F. galbanum.] A gum resin exuding from the stems of certain Asiatic umbelliferous plants, mostly species of Ferula. The Bubon Galbanum of South Africa furnishes an inferior kind of galbanum. It has an acrid, bitter taste, a strong, unpleasant smell, and is used for medical purposes, also in the arts, as in the manufacture of varnish.

galbe.c: Galbe ‖Galbe (?), n. [F.; OF. garbe, fr. It. garbo grace, gracefulness. See Garb dress.] (Art) The general outward form of any solid object, as of a column or a vase.

gale.c: Gale Gale (gāl), n. [Prob. of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. gal furious, Icel. galinn, cf. Icel. gala to sing, AS. galan to sing, Icel. galdr song, witchcraft, AS. galdor charm, sorcery, E. nightingale; also, Icel. gjōla gust of wind, gola breeze. Cf. Yell.] 1. A strong current of air; a wind between a stiff breeze and a hurricane. The most violent gales are called tempests.
Gale Gale (?), v. i. (Naut.) To sale, or sail fast.
Gale Gale, n. [OE. gal. See Gale wind.] A song or story. [Obs.] Toone.
Gale Gale, v. i. [AS. galan. See 1st Gale.] To sing. [Obs.] “Can he cry and gale.” Court of Love.

Gale Gale, n. [AS. gagel, akin to D. gagel.] (Bot.) A plant of the genus Myrica, growing in wet places, and strongly resembling the bayberry. The sweet gale (Myrica Gale) is found both in Europe and in America.
Gale Gale, n. [Cf. Gabel.] The payment of a rent or annuity. [Eng.] Mozley & W.

galea.c: Galea ‖Ga"le*a (?), n. [L., a helmet.] 1. (Bot.) The upper lip or helmet-shaped part of a labiate flower.

galeated.c: Galeated Galeate { Ga"le*ate (?), Ga"le*a`ted (?), } a. [L. galeatus, p. p. of galeare helmet.] 1. Wearing a helmet; protected by a helmet; covered, as with a helmet.

galei.c: Galei ‖Ga"le*i (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Galeus, name of one genus, fr. Gr.? a kind of shark.] (Zool.) That division of elasmobranch fishes which includes the sharks.

galena.c: Galena Ga*le"na (?), n.[L. galena lead ore, dross that remains after melting lead: cf. F. galène sulphide of lead ore, antidote to poison, stillness of the sea, calm, tranquility.]

galenical.c: Galenical Galenic Ga*len"ic (?), Ga*len"ic*al (?), a. Pertaining to, or containing, galena.
Galenical Galenic Ga*len"ic, Ga*len"ic*al, a. [From Galen, the physician.] Relating to Galen or to his principles and method of treating diseases. Dunglison.

galenism.c: Galenism Ga"len*ism (?), n. The doctrines of Galen.

galenist.c: Galenist Ga*len*ist, n. A follower of Galen.

galeopithecus.c: Galeopithecus ‖Ga`le*o*pi*the"cus (gā`le*o*pĭ*thē"kŭs), n. [NL., fr. Gr. gale`h a weasel + pi`qhkos an ape.] (Zool.) A genus of flying Insectivora, formerly called flying lemurs. See Colugo.

galericulate.c: Galericulate Gal`er*ic"u*late (?), a. [L. galericulum, dim. of galerum a hat or cap, fr. galea helmet.] Covered as with a hat or cap. Smart.

galerite.c: Galerite Gal"er*ite (?), n. [L. galerum a hat, cap: cf. F. galérite.] (Paleon.) A cretaceous fossil sea urchin of the genus Galerites.

galician.c: Galician Ga*li"cian (?), a. [Cf. Sp. Galiciano, Gallego, fr. L. Gallaecus, Gallaicus, fr. Gallaeci a people in Western Spain.] Of or pertaining to Galicia, in Spain, or to Galicia, the kingdom of Austrian Poland. -- n. A native of Galicia in Spain; -- called also Gallegan.

galilean.c: Galilean Gal`i*le"an (?), a. Of or pertaining to Galileo; as, the Galilean telescope. See Telescope.
Galilean Gal`i*le"an (?), a. [L. Galilaeus, fr. Galilaea Galilee, Gr.?: cf. F. galiléen.] Of or relating to Galilee.
Galilean Gal`i*le"an, n. 1. A native or inhabitant of Galilee, the northern province of Palestine under the Romans.

galilee.c: Galilee Gal"i*lee (?), n. [Supposed to have been so termed in allusion to the scriptural “Galilee of the Gentiles.” cf. OF. galilée.] (Arch.) A porch or waiting room, usually at the west end of an abbey church, where the monks collected on returning from processions, where bodies were laid previous to interment, and where women were allowed to see the monks to whom they were related, or to hear divine service. Also, frequently applied to the porch of a church, as at Ely and Durham cathedrals. Gwilt.

galimatias.c: Galimatias Gal`i*ma"tias (?), n. [F.] Nonsense; gibberish; confused and unmeaning talk; confused mixture.

galingale.c: Galingale Gal"in*gale (?), n. [See Galangal.] (Bot.) A plant of the Sedge family (Cyperus longus) having aromatic roots; also, any plant of the same genus. Chaucer.

galiot.c: Galiot Gal"i*ot (?), n. [OE. galiote, F. galiote. See Galley.] (Naut.) (a) A small galley, formerly used in the Mediterranean, built mainly for speed. It was moved both by sails and oars, having one mast, and sixteen or twenty seats for rowers. (b) A strong, light-draft, Dutch merchant vessel, carrying a mainmast and a mizzenmast, and a large gaff mainsail.

galipot.c: Galipot Gal"i*pot (?), n. [F. galipot; cf. OF. garipot the wild pine or pitch tree.] An impure resin of turpentine, hardened on the outside of pine trees by the spontaneous evaporation of its essential oil. When purified, it is called yellow pitch, white pitch, or Burgundy pitch.

gall.c: Gall Gall (gäl), n.[OE. galle, gal, AS. gealla; akin to D. gal, OS. & OHG. galla, Icel. gall, SW. galla, Dan. galde, L. fel, Gr.?, and prob. to E. yellow. √49. See Yellow, and cf. Choler] 1. (Physiol.) The bitter, alkaline, viscid fluid found in the gall bladder, beneath the liver. It consists of the secretion of the liver, or bile, mixed with that of the mucous membrane of the gall bladder.

Gall Gall (gäl), n. [F. galle, noix de galle, fr. L. galla.] (Zool.) An excrescence of any form produced on any part of a plant by insects or their larvae. They are most commonly caused by small Hymenoptera and Diptera which puncture the bark and lay their eggs in the wounds. The larvae live within the galls. Some galls are due to aphids, mites, etc. See Gallnut.
Gall Gall, v. t. (Dyeing) To impregnate with a decoction of gallnuts. Ure.

Gall Gall, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Galled (gäld); p. pr. & vb. n. Galling.] [OE. gallen; cf. F. galer to scratch, rub, gale scurf, scab, G. galle a disease in horses' feet, an excrescence under the tongue of horses; of uncertain origin. Cf. Gall gallnut.] 1. To fret and wear away by friction; to hurt or break the skin of by rubbing; to chafe; to injure the surface of by attrition; as, a saddle galls the back of a horse; to gall a mast or a cable.
Gall Gall, v. i. To scoff; to jeer. [R.] Shak.
Gall Gall, n. A wound in the skin made by rubbing.

gallant.c: Gallant Gal"lant (găl"laint), a. [F. gallant, prop. p. pr. of OF. galer to rejoice, akin to OF. gale amusement, It. gala ornament; of German origin; cf. OHG. geil merry, luxuriant, wanton, G. geil lascivious, akin to AS. gāl wanton, wicked, OS. gēl merry, Goth. gailjan to make to rejoice, or perh. akin to E. weal. See Gala, Galloon.]
Gallant Gal*lant" (?; 277), a. Polite and attentive to ladies; courteous to women; chivalrous.
Gallant Gal*lant" (?; 277), n. 1. A man of mettle or spirit; a gay, fashionable man; a young blood. Shak.
Gallant Gal*lant" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gallanted; p. pr. & vb. n. Gallanting.] 1. To attend or wait on, as a lady; as, to gallant ladies to the play.

gallantly.c: Gallantly Gal*lant"ly (?), adv. In a polite or courtly manner; like a gallant or wooer.
Gallantly Gal"lant*ly (?), adv. In a gallant manner.

gallantness.c: Gallantness Gal"lant*ness (?), n. The quality of being gallant.

gallantry.c: Gallantry Gal"lant*ry (?), n.; pl. Gallantries (#). [F. galanterie.] 1. Splendor of appearance; ostentatious finery. [Archaic]

gallate.c: Gallate Gal"late (?; 277), n. [Cf. F. gallate. See Gall gallnut.] (Chem.) A salt of gallic acid.

gallature.c: Gallature Gal"la*ture (?; 135), n. [From L. gallus a cock.] (Zool.) The tread, treadle, or chalasa of an egg.

galleass.c: Galleass Gal"le*ass (?; 135), n. [F. galéasse, galéace; cf. It. galeazza, Sp. galeaza; LL. galea a galley. See Galley.] (Naut.) A large galley, having some features of the galleon, as broadside guns; esp., such a vessel used by the southern nations of Europe in the 16th and 17th centuries. See Galleon, and Galley. [Written variously galeas, gallias, etc.]

gallego.c: Gallego Gallegan { Gal*le"gan (găl*lē"gain), Gal*le"go (găl*lē"go or gȧ*lyā"go), } n. [Sp. Gallego.] A native or inhabitant of Galicia, in Spain; a Galician.

gallein.c: Gallein Gal"le*ïn (?), n. [Pyrogallol + phthaleïn.] (Chem.) A red crystalline dyestuff, obtained by heating together pyrogallic and phthalic acids.

galleon.c: Galleon Gal"le*on (?), n. [Sp. galeon, cf. F. galion; fr. LL. galeo, galio. See Galley.] (Naut.) A sailing vessel of the 15th and following centuries, often having three or four decks, and used for war or commerce. The term is often rather indiscriminately applied to any large sailing vessel.

gallery.c: Gallery Gal"ler*y (?), n.; pl. Galleries (#). [F. galerie, It. galleria, fr. LL. galeria gallery, perh. orig., a festal hall, banquetting hall; cf. OF. galerie a rejoicing, fr. galer to rejoice. Cf. Gallant, a.] 1. A long and narrow corridor, or place for walking; a connecting passageway, as between one room and another; also, a long hole or passage excavated by a boring or burrowing animal.

galletyle.c: Galletyle Gal"le*tyle (?), n. [OE. gallytile. Cf. Gallipot.] A little tile of glazed earthenware. [Obs.] “The substance of galletyle.” Bacon.

galley.c: Galley Gal"ley (?), n.; pl. Galleys (#). [OE. gale, galeie (cf. OF. galie, galée, LL. galea, LGr.?; of unknown origin.] 1. (Naut.) A vessel propelled by oars, whether having masts and sails or not; as: (a) A large vessel for war and national purposes; -- common in the Middle Ages, and down to the 17th century. (b) A name given by analogy to the Greek, Roman, and other ancient vessels propelled by oars. (c) A light, open boat used on the Thames by customhouse officers, press gangs, and also for pleasure. (d) One of the small boats carried by a man-of-war.

galleybird.c: Galley-bird Gal"ley-bird` (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] (Zool.) The European green woodpecker, called also the yaffle; also, the spotted woodpecker. [Prov. Eng.]

galleyworm.c: Galley-worm Gal"ley-worm` (?), n. [Prob. so called because the numerous legs along the sides move rhythmically like the oars of a galley.] (Zool.) A chilognath myriapod of the genus Iulus, and allied genera, having numerous short legs along the sides; a milliped or “thousand legs.” See Chilognatha.

gallfly.c: Gallfly Gall"fly` (?), n.; pl. Gallflies (?). (Zool.) An insect that deposits its eggs in plants, and occasions galls, esp. any small hymenopteran of the genus Cynips and allied genera. See Illust. of Gall.

galliambic.c: Galliambic Gal`li*am"bic (?), a. [L. galliambus a song used by the priests of Cybele; Gallus (a name applied to these priests) + iambus] (Pros.) Consisting of two iambic dimeters catalectic, the last of which lacks the final syllable; -- said of a kind of verse.

gallian.c: Gallian Gal"li*an (?), a. [See Gallic.] Gallic; French. [Obs.] Shak.

galliard.c: Galliard Gal"liard (?), a. [OE., fr. F. gaillard, perh. of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. & Gael. galach valiant, or AS. gagol, geagl, wanton, lascivious.] Gay; brisk; active. [Obs.]
Galliard Gal"liard, n. A brisk, gay man. [Obs.]
Galliard Gal"liard, n. [F. gaillarde, cf. Sp. gallarda. See Galliard, a.] A gay, lively dance. Cf. Gailliarde.

galliardise.c: Galliardise Gal`liard*ise (?), n. [F. gaillardise. See Galliard, a.] Excessive gayety; merriment. [Obs.]

gallic.c: Gallic Gal"lic (?), a. [From Gallium.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or containing, gallium.
Gallic Gal"lic (277), a. [From Gall the excrescence.] Pertaining to, or derived from, galls, nutgalls, and the like.
Gallic Gal"lic (?), a. [L. Gallicus belonging to the Gauls, fr. Galli the Gauls, Gallia Gaul, now France: cf. F. gallique.] Pertaining to Gaul or France; Gallican.

gallican.c: Gallican Gal"li*can (?), a. [L. Gallicanus: cf. F. gallican.] Of or pertaining to Gaul or France; Gallic; French; as, the Gallican church or clergy.
Gallican Gal"li*can, n. An adherent to, and supporter of, Gallicanism. Shipley.

gallicanism.c: Gallicanism Gal"li*can*ism (?), n. The principles, tendencies, or action of those, within the Roman Catholic Church in France, who (esp. in 1682) sought to restrict the papal authority in that country and increase the power of the national church. Schaff-Herzog Encyc.

gallicism.c: Gallicism Gal"li*cism (?), n. [F. gallicisme.] A mode of speech peculiar to the French; a French idiom; also, in general, a French mode or custom.

gallicize.c: Gallicize Gal"li*cize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gallicized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gallicizing (?).] To conform to the French mode or idiom.

gallied.c: Gallied Gal"lied (?), p. p. & a. (Naut.) Worried; flurried; frightened. Ham. Nav. Encyc.

galliform.c: Galliform Gal"li*form (?), a. (Zool.) Like the Gallinae (or Galliformes) in structure.

galligaskins.c: Galligaskins Gal`li*gas"kins (?), n. pl. [Prob. corrupted fr. It. Grechesco Grecian, a name which seems to have been given in Venice, and to have been afterwards confused with Gascony, as if they came from Gascony.] Loose hose or breeches; leather leg quards. The word is used loosely and often in a jocose sense.

gallimatia.c: Gallimatia ‖Gal`li*ma"ti*a (? or?), n. Senseless talk. [Obs. or R.] See Galimatias.

gallimaufry.c: Gallimaufry Gal`li*mau"fry (?), n.; pl. Gallimaufries (#). [F. galimafrée a sort of ragout or mixed hash of different meats.] 1. A hash of various kinds of meats, a ragout.

gallin.c: Gallin Gal"lin (?), n. (Chem.) A substance obtained by the reduction of gallein.

gallinaceae.c: Gallinaceae ‖Gal"li*nace*ae (?), n. pl. [NL. See Gallinaceous.] (Zool.) Same as Gallinae.

gallinacean.c: Gallinacean Gal`li*na"cean (?), n. (Zool.) One of the Gallinae or gallinaceous birds.

gallinaceous.c: Gallinaceous Gal`li*na"ceous (?), a.[L. gallinaceus, fr. gallina hen, fr. gallus cock.] (Zool.) Resembling the domestic fowls and pheasants; of or pertaining to the Gallinae.

gallinae.c: Gallinae ‖Gal*li"nae (?), n.; pl. [NL., fr. L. gallina a hen, gallus a cock.] (Zool.) An order of birds, including the common domestic fowls, pheasants, grouse, quails, and allied forms; -- sometimes called Rasores.

galling.c: Galling Gall"ing (?), a. Fitted to gall or chafe; vexing; harassing; irritating. -- Gall"ing*ly, adv.

gallinule.c: Gallinule Gal"li*nule (?), n. [L. gallinula chicken, dim. of gallina hen: cf. F. gallinule.] (Zool.) One of several wading birds, having long, webless toes, and a frontal shield, belonging to the family Rallidae. They are remarkable for running rapidly over marshes and on floating plants. The purple gallinule of America is Ionornis Martinica, that of the Old World is Porphyrio porphyrio. The common European gallinule (Gallinula chloropus) is also called moor hen, water hen, water rail, moor coot, night bird, and erroneously dabchick. Closely related to it is the Florida gallinule (Gallinula galeata).

gallipoli.c: Gallipoli oil Gal*lip"o*li oil` (?). An inferior kind of olive oil, brought from Gallipoli, in Italy.

gallipot.c: Gallipot Gal"li*pot (?), n. [Prob. fr. OD. gleypot, the first part of which is possibly akin to E. glad. See Glad, and Pot.] A glazed earthen pot or vessel, used by druggists and apothecaries for containing medicines, etc.

gallium.c: Gallium Gal"li*um (?), n. [NL.; perh. fr. L. Gallia France.] (Chem.) A rare metallic element, found combined in certain zinc ores. It is white, hard, and malleable, resembling aluminium, and remarkable for its low melting point (86° F., 30° C.). Symbol, Ga; at. wt., 69.9. Gallium is chiefly trivalent, resembling aluminium and indium. It was predicted with most of its properties, under the name eka-aluminium, by the Russian chemist Mendelyeev on the basis of the periodic law. This prediction was verified in its discovery (in 1875) by the French chemist Lecoq de Boisbaudran by its characteristic spectrum (two violet lines), in an examination of a zinc blende from the Pyrenees.

gallivant.c: Gallivant Gal"li*vant (?), v. i. [From Gallant.] To play the beau; to wait upon the ladies; also, to roam about for pleasure without any definite plan. [Slang] Dickens.

gallivat.c: Gallivat Gal"li*vat (?), n.[Prob. fr. Pg. galeota; cf. E. galiot, galley.] (Naut.) A small armed vessel, with sails and oars, -- used on the Malabar coast. A. Chalmers.

galliwasp.c: Galliwasp Gal"li*wasp` (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] (Zool.) A West Indian lizard (Celestus occiduus), about a foot long, imagined by the natives to be venomous.

gallize.c: Gallize Gal"lize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gallized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gallizing (?).] [After Dr. L. Gall, a French chemist, who invented the process.] In wine making, to add water and sugar to (unfermented grape juice) so as to increase the quantity of wine produced. -- Gal`li*za"tion (#), n.

gallnut.c: Gallnut Gall"nut` (?), n. (Zool.) A round gall produced on the leaves and shoots of various species of the oak tree. See Gall, and Nutgall.

gallomania.c: Gallomania Gal`lo*ma"ni*a (?), n. [L. Galli Gauls + mania madness.] An excessive admiration of what is French. -- Gal`lo*ma"ni*ac (#), n.

gallon.c: Gallon Gal"lon (?), n. [OF galon, jalon, LL. galo, galona, fr. galum a liquid measure; cf. F. jale large bowl. Cf. Gill a measure.] A measure of capacity, containing four quarts; -- used, for the most part, in liquid measure, but sometimes in dry measure.

galloon.c: Galloon Gal*loon" (?), n. [From F. or Sp. galon. See Gala. ] 1. A narrow tapelike fabric used for binding hats, shoes, etc., -- sometimes made ornamental.

gallooned.c: Gallooned Gal*looned` (?), a. Furnished or adorned with galloon.

gallop.c: Gallop Gal"lop (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Galloped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Galloping.] [OE. galopen, F. galoper, of German origin; cf. assumed Goth. ga-hlaupan to run, OHG. giloufen, AS. gehleápan to leap, dance, fr. root of E. leap, and a prefix; or cf. OFlem. walop a gallop. See Leap, and cf. 1st Wallop.] 1. To move or run in the mode called a gallop; as a horse; to go at a gallop; to run or move with speed.
Gallop Gal"lop (?), v. t. To cause to gallop.

Gallop Gal"lop, n. [Cf. F. galop. See Gallop, v. i., and cf. Galop.] A mode of running by a quadruped, particularly by a horse, by lifting alternately the fore feet and the hind feet, in successive leaps or bounds.

gallopade.c: Gallopade Gal"lo*pade` (?), n. [F. galopade. See Gallop, n.] 1. I horsemanship, a sidelong or curveting kind of gallop.
Gallopade Gal`lo*pade" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gallopaded; p. pr. & vb. n. Gallopading.] 1. To gallop, as on horseback.

galloper.c: Galloper Gal"lop*er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, gallops.

gallopin.c: Gallopin Gal"lo*pin (?), n.[F. galopin. See Gallop, v. i.] An under servant for the kitchen; a scullion; a cook's errand boy. [Obs.] Halliwell.

galloping.c: Galloping Gal"lop*ing (?), a. Going at a gallop; progressing rapidly; as, a galloping horse.

gallotannic.c: Gallotannic Gal`lo*tan"nic (?), a. [Gall nutgall + tannic.] (Chem.) Pertaining to the tannin or nutgalls.

gallow.c: Gallow Gal"low (?), v. t. [Cf. AS. āgelwan to stupefy.] To fright or terrify. See Gally, v. t. [Obs.] Shak.

galloway.c: Galloway Gal"lo*way (?), n. (Zool.) A small horse of a breed raised at Galloway, Scotland; -- called also garran, and garron.

gallowglass.c: Gallowglass Gal"low*glass` (?), n. [Ir. galloglach. Cf. Gillie.] A heavy-armed foot soldier from Ireland and the Western Isles in the time of Edward? Shak.

gallows.c: Gallows Gal"lows (?), n. sing.; pl. Gallowses (#) or Gallows. [OE. galwes, pl., AS. galga, gealga, gallows, cross; akin to D. galg gallows, OS. & OHG. galgo, G. galgen, Icel. gālgi, Sw. & Dan. galge, Goth. galga a cross. Etymologically and historically considered, gallows is a noun in the plural number, but it is used as a singular, and hence is preceded by a; as, a gallows.] 1. A frame from which is suspended the rope with which criminals are executed by hanging, usually consisting of two upright posts and a crossbeam on the top; also, a like frame for suspending anything.

gallstone.c: Gallstone Gall"stone` (?), n. A concretion, or calculus, formed in the gall bladder or biliary passages. See Calculus, n., 1.

gally.c: Gally Gal"ly (?), v. t. [See Gallow, v. t.] To frighten; to worry. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.] T. Brown.
Gally Gall"y (?), a. Like gall; bitter as gall. Cranmer.

galoshe.c: Galoshe Galoche Ga*loche", Ga*loshe" (?), [OE. galoche, galache, galage, shoe, F. galoche galoche, perh. altered fr. L. gallica a Gallic shoe, or fr. LL. calopedia wooden shoe, or shoe with a wooden sole, Gr.?, dim. of?,?, a shoemaker's last;? wood +? foot.] 1. A clog or patten. [Obs.]

galoot.c: Galoot Ga*loot" (?), n. A noisy, swaggering, or worthless fellow; a rowdy. [Slang, U. S.]

galop.c: Galop Gal"op (?), n. [F.] (Mus.) A kind of lively dance, in 2-4 time; also, the music to the dance.

galore.c: Galore Ga*lore" (?), n. & a. [Scot. gelore, gilore, galore, fr. Gael. gu leòr, enough; gu- to, also an adverbial prefix + leòr, leòir, enough; or fr. Ir. goleor, the same word.] Plenty; abundance; in abundance.

galosh.c: Galosh Ga*losh" (?), n. 1. Same as Galoche, Galoshe.

galpe.c: Galpe Galpe (?), v. i. To gape,; to yawn. [Obs.] Chaucer.

galsome.c: Galsome Gal"some (?), a. [Gall bitterness + some.] Angry; malignant. [Obs.] Bp. Morton.

galt.c: Galt Galt (?), n. [See Gault.] Same as Gault.

galvanic.c: Galvanic Gal*van"ic (?), a. [From Galvani, a professor of physiology at Bologna, on account of his connection (about 1780) with the discovery of dynamical or current electricity: cf. F. galvanique.] Of or pertaining to, or exhibiting the phenomena of, galvanism; employing or producing electrical currents.

galvanism.c: Galvanism Gal"va*nism (?), n. [From Galvani: cf. F. galvanisme. See Galvanic.] (Physics) (a) Electricity excited by the mutual action of certain liquids and metals; dynamical electricity. (b) The branch of physical science which treats of dynamical elecricity, or the properties and effects of electrical currents.

galvanist.c: Galvanist Gal"va*nist (?), n. One versed in galvanism.

galvanization.c: Galvanization Gal"va*niza`tion (?), n. The act of process of galvanizing.

galvanize.c: Galvanize Gal"va*nize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Galvanized (?); p pr. & vb. n. Galvanizing (?).] [Cf. F. galvaniser.] 1. To affect with galvanism; to subject to the action of electrical currents.

galvanizer.c: Galvanizer Gal"va*ni`zer (?), n. One who, or that which, galvanize.

galvanocaustic.c: Galvanocaustic Gal*van`o*caus"tic (?), a. [Galvanic + caustic.] Relating to the use of galvanic heat as a caustic, especially in medicine.

galvanocautery.c: Galvanocautery Gal*van`o*cau"ter*y (?), n. (Med.) Cautery effected by a knife or needle heated by the passage of a galvanic current.

galvanoglyphy.c: Galvanoglyphy Gal`va*nog"ly*phy (?), n. [Galvanic + Gr.? to engrave.] Same as Glyphography.

galvanograph.c: Galvanograph Gal*van"o*graph (?), n. [Galvanic + -graph.] (Engraving) A copperplate produced by the method of galvanography; also, a picture printed from such a plate.

galvanographic.c: Galvanographic Gal*van`o*graph"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to galvanography.

galvanography.c: Galvanography Gal`va*nog"ra*phy (?), n. [Galvanic + -graphy.] 1. The art or process of depositing metals by electricity; electrotypy.

galvanologist.c: Galvanologist Gal`va*nol"o*gist (?), n. One who describes the phenomena of galvanism; a writer on galvanism.

galvanology.c: Galvanology Gal`va*nol"o*gy (?) n. [Galvanic + -logy.] A treatise on galvanism, or a description of its phenomena.

galvanometer.c: Galvanometer Gal`va*nom"e*ter (?), n. [Galvanic + -meter: cf. F. galvanomètre.] (Elec.) An instrument or apparatus for measuring the intensity of an electric current, usually by the deflection of a magnetic needle.

galvanometric.c: Galvanometric Gal*van`o*met"ric (?), a. Of, pertaining to, or measured by, a galvanometer.

galvanometry.c: Galvanometry Gal`va*nom"e*try (?), n. The art or process of measuring the force of electric currents.

galvanoplastic.c: Galvanoplastic Gal*van`o*plas"tic (?), a. [Galvanic + -plastic.] Of or pertaining to the art or process of electrotyping; employing, or produced by, the process of electolytic deposition; as, a galvano-plastic copy of a medal or the like.

galvanoplasty.c: Galvanoplasty Gal*van"o*plas`ty (?), n. [Cf. F. galanoplastie.] The art or process of electrotypy.

galvanoscope.c: Galvanoscope Gal*van`o*scope (?), n. [Galvanic + -scope: cf. F. galvanoscope.] (Elec.) An instrument or apparatus for detecting the presence of electrical currents, especially such as are of feeble intensity.

galvanoscopic.c: Galvanoscopic Gal*van`o*scop"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to a galvanoscope.

galvanoscopy.c: Galvanoscopy Gal`va*nos"co*py (?), n. (Physiol.) The use of galvanism in physiological experiments.

galvanotonus.c: Galvanotonus ‖Gal`va*not"o*nus (?), n. [NL., fr. E. galvanic + Gr.? to tone.] (Physiol.) Same as Electrotonus.

galvanotropism.c: Galvanotropism Gal`va*not"ro*pism (?), n. [Galvanic + Gr.? to turn.] (Bot.) The tendency of a root to place its axis in the line of a galvanic current.

gam.c: Gam Gam (găm), n. [Orig. uncert., perh. from gammon, talk.] 1. (Naut.) A herd, or school, of whales.
Gam Gam (găm), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gammed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gam"ming.] (Naut.) (a) To gather in a gam; -- said of whales. (b) To engage in a gam, or (Local, U. S.) in social intercourse anywhere.
Gam Gam (găm), v. t. (Naut.) To have a gam with; to pay a visit to, esp. among whalers at sea.

gama.c: Gama grass Ga"ma grass` (?). [From Gama, a cluster of the Maldive Islands.] (Bot.) A species of grass (Tripsacum dactyloides) tall, stout, and exceedingly productive; cultivated in the West Indies, Mexico, and the Southern States of North America as a forage grass; -- called also sesame grass.

gamashes.c: Gamashes Ga*mash"es (?), n. pl. [F. gamaches.] High boots or buskins; in Scotland, short spatterdashes or riding trousers, worn over the other clothing.

gambadoes.c: Gambadoes Gam*ba"does (?), n. pl. [I. or Sp. gamba leg. See Gambol, n.] Same as Gamashes.

gambeer.c: Gambeer Gam*beer" (?), v. t. [Cf. F. gambier a kind of hook.] (Fishing) To gaff, as mackerel.

gambet.c: Gambet Gam"bet (?), n. [Fr. gambette, or It. gambetta.] (Zool.) Any bird of the genuis Totanus. See Tattler.

gambier.c: Gambier Gam"bier (?), n. [Malayan.] (a) The inspissated juice of a plant (Uncaria Gambir) growing in Malacca. It is a powerful astringent, and, under the name of Terra Japonica, is used for chewing with the Areca nut, and is exported for tanning and dyeing. (b) Catechu. [Written also gambeer and gambir.]

gambison.c: Gambison Gam"bi*son (?), n. [OF. gambeson, gambaison, fr. gambais, wambais, of German origin: cf. MHG. wambeis, G. wams doublet, fr. OHG. wamba, stomach. See Womb.] A defensive garment formerly in use for the body, made of cloth stuffed and quilted.

gambist.c: Gambist Gam"bist (?), n. [It. gamba leg.] (Mus.) A performer upon the viola di gamba. See under Viola.

gambit.c: Gambit Gam"bit (?), n. [F. gambit, cf. It. gambitto gambit, a tripping up. See Gambol, n.] (Chess Playing) A mode of opening the game, in which a pawn is sacrificed to gain an attacking position.

gamble.c: Gamble Gam"ble (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gambled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gambling (?).] [Dim. of game. See 2d Game.] To play or game for money or other stake.
Gamble Gamble, v. t. To lose or squander by gaming; -- usually with away. “Bankrupts or sots who have gambled or slept away their estates.” Ames.
Gamble Gam"ble (?), n. An act of gambling; a transaction or proceeding involving gambling; hence, anything involving similar risk or uncertainty. [Colloq.]

gamboge.c: Gamboge Gam*boge" (?), n. A concrete juice, or gum resin, produced by several species of trees in Siam, Ceylon, and Malabar. It is brought in masses, or cylindrical rolls, from Cambodia, or Cambogia, -- whence its name. The best kind is of a dense, compact texture, and of a beatiful reddish yellow. Taken internally, it is a strong and harsh cathartic and emetic. [Written also camboge.]

gambogic.c: Gambogic Gambogian { Gam*bo"gi*an (?), Gambogic (?), } a. Pertaining to, resembling, or containing, gamboge.

gambol.c: Gambol Gam"bol (?), n. [OE. gambolde, gambaulde, F. gambade, gambol, fr. It. gambata kick, fr. L. gamba leg, akin to F. jambe, OF. also, gambe, fr. L. gamba, hoof or perh. joint: cf. Gr.? a binding, winding, W., Ir. & Gael. cam crooked; perhaps akin to E. chamber: cf.F. gambiller to kick about. Cf. Jamb, n., Gammon ham, Gambadoes.] A skipping or leaping about in frolic; a hop; a sportive prank. Dryden.
Gambol Gam"bol v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gamboled (?), or Gambolled; p. pr. & vb. n. Gamboling or Gambolling.] To dance and skip about in sport; to frisk; to skip; to play in frolic, like boys or lambs.

gambrel.c: Gambrel Gam"brel (?), n. [OF. gambe, jambe leg, F. jambe. Cf. Cambrel, Chambrel, and see Gambol. n.] 1. The hind leg of a horse.
Gambrel Gam"brel v. t. To truss or hang up by means of a gambrel. Beau. & Fl.

gambroon.c: Gambroon Gam*broon" (?), n. A kind of twilled linen cloth for lining. Simmonds.

game.c: Game Game (?), a. [Cf. W. cam crooked, and E. gambol, n.] Crooked; lame; as, a game leg. [Colloq.]

Game Game, n. [OE. game, gamen, AS. gamen, gomen, play, sport; akin to OS., OHG., & Icel. gaman, Dan. gammen mirth, merriment, OSw. gamman joy. Cf. Gammon a game, Backgammon, Gamble v. i.] 1. Sport of any kind; jest, frolic.
Game Game, a. 1. Having a resolute, unyielding spirit, like the gamecock; ready to fight to the last; plucky.

Game Game (gām), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gamed (gāmd); p. pr. & vb. n. Gaming.] [OE. gamen, game?en, to rejoice, AS. gamenian to play. See Game, n.] 1. To rejoice; to be pleased; -- often used, in Old English, impersonally with dative. [Obs.]
Game fowl Game" fowl` (gām"foul`). (Zool.) A handsome breed of the common fowl, remarkable for the great courage and pugnacity of the males.

gamecock.c: Gamecock Game"cock` (gām"kŏk`), n. (Zool.) The male game fowl.

gameful.c: Gameful Game"ful (gām"fụl), a. Full of game or games.

gamekeeper.c: Gamekeeper Game"keep`er (gām"kēp`ẽr), n. One who has the care of game, especially in a park or preserve. Blackstone.

gamely.c: Gamely Game"ly, adv. In a plucky manner; spiritedly.

gamesome.c: Gamesome Game"some (gām"sŭm), a. Gay; sportive; playful; frolicsome; merry. Shak.

gamester.c: Gamester Game"ster (gām"stẽr), n. [Game + -ster.] 1. A merry, frolicsome person. [Obs.] Shak.

gamete.c: Gamete Gam"ete (găm"ēt; gȧ*mēt"; the latter usually in compounds), n. [Gr. gameth` wife, or game`ths husband, fr. gamei^n to marry.] (Biol.) A sexual cell or germ cell having a single set of unpaired chromosomes; a conjugating cell which unites with another of like or unlike character to form a new individual. In Bot., gamete designates esp. the similar sex cells of the lower thallophytes which unite by conjugation, forming a zygospore. The gametes of higher plants are of two sorts, sperm (male) and egg (female); their union is called fertilization, and the resulting zygote an oospore. In Zool., gamete is most commonly used of the sexual cells of certain Protozoa, though also extended to the germ cells of higher forms.

gametophyte.c: Gametophyte Ga*me"to*phyte (?), n. [Gamete + Gr. fyto`n plant.] (Bot.) In the alternation of generations in plants, that generation or phase which bears sex organs and produces gametes. In the lower plants, as the algæ, the gametophyte is the conspicuous part of the plant body; in mosses it is the so-called moss plant; in ferns it is reduced to a small, early perishing body; and in seed plants it is usually microscopic or rudimentary.

gamic.c: Gamic Gam"ic (?), a. [Gr.? marriage.] (Biol.) Pertaining to, or resulting from, sexual connection; formed by the union of the male and female elements.

gamin.c: Gamin ‖Gam"in (?), n. [F.] A neglected and untrained city boy; a young street Arab.

gaming.c: gaming gam"ing (gām"ĭng), n. The act or practice of playing games for stakes or wagers; gambling.

gamma.c: gamma gam"ma (găm"mȧ), n. The third letter (Γ, γ = Eng. G) of the Greek alphabet.

Gamma ray Gam"ma ray. n. (Physics) A very penetrating electromagnetic ray not appreciably deflected by a magnetic or electric field, emitted by radioactive substances. Gamma rays are photons of electromagnetic radiation having a wavelength shorter than that of X-rays, (i. e. shorter than 0.1 nanometer) and are correspondingly more penetrating than X-rays. In addition to being given off in certain types of radioactive decay, they may be found in cosmic radiation, though they are largely absorbed by the earth's atmosphere. Gamma-ray detectors orbited above the atmosphere have found bursts of gamma radiation, in some cases associated with visually observed supernova explosions, but in most cases from unidentified sources.

gammadion.c: Gammadion Gam*ma"di*on (?), n. A cross formed of four capital gammas, formerly used as a mysterious ornament on ecclesiastical vestments, etc. See Fylfot.

gammer.c: Gammer Gam"mer (găm"mẽr), n. [Possibly contr. fr. godmother; but prob. fr. grammer for grandmother. Cf. Gaffer.] An old wife; an old woman; -- correlative of gaffer, an old man.

gammon.c: Gammon Gam"mon (găm"mŭn), n. [OF. gambon, F. jambon, fr. OF. gambe leg, F. jambe. See Gambol, n., and cf. Ham.] The buttock or thigh of a hog, salted and smoked or dried; the lower end of a flitch. Goldsmith.
Gammon Gam"mon (găm"mŭn), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gammoned (găm"mŭnd); p. pr. & vb. n. Gammoning.] To make bacon of; to salt and dry in smoke.

Gammon Gam"mon, v. t. 1. To beat in the game of backgammon, before an antagonist has been able to get his “men” or counters home and withdraw any of them from the board; as, to gammon a person. In certain variants of the game one who gammons an opponent scores twice the normal value of the game.
Gammon Gam"mon, v. t. [Etymol. unknown.] (Naut.) To fasten (a bowsprit) to the stem of a vessel by lashings of rope or chain, or by a band of iron. Totten.

gammoning.c: Gammoning Gam"mon*ing, n. [From 5th Gammon.] (Naut.) The lashing or iron band by which the bowsprit of a vessel is secured to the stem to opposite the lifting action of the forestays.
Gammoning Gam"mon*ing, n. [From 4th Gammon.] The act of imposing upon or hoaxing a person. [Colloq.]

gamogenesis.c: Gamogenesis ‖Gam`o*gen"e*sis (?), n. [Gr.? marriage + E. genesis.] (Biol.) The production of offspring by the union of parents of different sexes; sexual reproduction; -- the opposite of agamogenesis.

gamogenetic.c: Gamogenetic Gam`o*ge*net"ic (?), a. (Biol.) Relating to gamogenesis. -- Gam`o*ge*net"ic*al*ly, adv.

gamomorphism.c: Gamomorphism Gam`o*mor"phism (?), n. [Gr.? marriage + morfh` form, shape.] (Biol.) That stage of growth or development in an organism, in which the reproductive elements are generated and matured in preparation for propagating the species.

gamopetalous.c: Gamopetalous Gam`o*pet"al*ous (?), a. [Gr.? marriage + E. petalous: cf. F. gamopétale.] (Bot.) Having the petals united or joined so as to form a tube or cup; monopetalous.

gamophyllous.c: Gamophyllous Ga*moph"yl*lous (?), a. [Gr.? marriage +? leaf.] (Bot.) Composed of leaves united by their edges (coalescent). Gray.

gamosepalous.c: Gamosepalous Gam`o*sep"al*ous (?), a. [Gr.? marriage + E. sepal.] (Bot.) Formed of united sepals; monosepalous.

gamp.c: Gamp Gamp (gămp), n. A large umbrella; -- said to allude to Mrs. Gamp's umbrella, in Dickens's “Martin Chuzzlewit.”

gamut.c: Gamut Gam"ut (?), n. [F. gamme + ut the name of a musical note. F. gamme is fr. the name of the Greek letter?, which was used by Guido d'Arezzo to represent the first note of his model scale. See Gamma, and Ut.] (Mus.) The scale.

gamy.c: gamy gam"y (?), a. 1. (Cookery) Having the flavor of game, esp. of game kept uncooked till near the condition of tainting; high-flavored.

gan.c: Gan Gan (?), imp. of Gin. [See Gin, v.] Began; commenced.

ganancial.c: Ganancial Ga*nan"cial (?), a. [Sp., pertaining to gain, held in common, fr. ganancia gain.] (Law) Designating, pertaining to, or held under, the Spanish system of law (called ganancial system) which controls the title and disposition of the property acquired during marriage by the husband or wife.

ganch.c: Ganch Ganch (?), v. t. [Cf. F. ganche, n., also Sp. & Pg. gancho hook, It. gancio.] To drop from a high place upon sharp stakes or hooks, as the Turks dropped malefactors, by way of punishment.

gander.c: Gander Gan"der (?), n. [AS. gandra, ganra, akin to Prov. G. gander, ganter, and E. goose, gannet. See Goose.] The male of any species of goose.

gane.c: Gane Gane (?), v. i. [See Yawn.] To yawn; to gape. [Obs.] Chaucer.

ganesha.c: Ganesha Ganesh Ganesa Ga*ne"sa, Ganesh, Ganesha (?), prop. n. (Hindu Myth.) The Hindu god of wisdom, prudence and prophesy; the remover of obstacles.

gang.c: Gang Gang (găng), v. i. [AS. gangan, akin to OS. & OHG. gangan, Icel. ganga, Goth. gaggan; cf. Lith. żengti to walk, Skr. jaṅgha leg. √48. Cf. Go.] To go; to walk.
Gang Gang, n. [Icel. gangr a going, gang, akin to AS., D., G., & Dan. gang a going, Goth. gaggs street, way. See Gang, v. i.] 1. A going; a course. [Obs.]

gange.c: Gange Gange (gănj), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ganged (gănjd); p. pr. & vb. n. Ganging (găn"jĭng).] [Of uncertain origin.] 1. To protect (the part of a line next a fishhook, or the hook itself) by winding it with wire.

ganger.c: Ganger Gang"er (?), n. One who oversees a gang of workmen. [R.] Mayhew.

gangetic.c: Gangetic Gan*get"ic (?), a. Pertaining to, or inhabiting, the Ganges River; as, the Gangetic shark.

gangflower.c: Gang-flower Gang"-flow`er (?), n. (Bot.) The common English milkwort (Polygala vulgaris), so called from blossoming in gang week. Dr. Prior.

gangion.c: Gangion Gan"gion (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] A short line attached to a trawl. See Trawl, n.

ganglial.c: Ganglial Gangliac { Gan"gli*ac (?), Gan"gli*al (?), } a. (Anat.) Relating to a ganglion; ganglionic.

gangliated.c: Gangliated Gangliate { Gan"gli*ate (?), Gan"gli*a`ted (?), } a. (Anat.) Furnished with ganglia; as, the gangliated cords of the sympathetic nervous system.

ganglioform.c: Ganglioform Gangliform { Gan"gli*form` (?), Gan"gli*o*form` (?), } a. [Ganglion + -form.] (Anat.) Having the form of a ganglion.

ganglion.c: Ganglion Gan"gli*on (?), n.; pl. L. Ganglia (#), E. Ganglions (#). [L. ganglion a sort of swelling or excrescence, a tumor under the skin, Gr.?: cf. F. ganglion.] 1. (Anat.) (a) A mass or knot of nervous matter, including nerve cells, usually forming an enlargement in the course of a nerve. (b) A node, or gland in the lymphatic system; as, a lymphatic ganglion.

ganglionic.c: Ganglionic Gan`gli*on"ic (?), a. [Cf. F. ganglionique.] (Anat.) Pertaining to, containing, or consisting of, ganglia or ganglion cells; as, a ganglionic artery; the ganglionic columns of the spinal cord.

gangrel.c: Gangrel Gan"grel (?), a. [Cf. Gang, v. i.] Wandering; vagrant. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.

gangrene.c: Gangrene Gan"grene (?), n. [F. gangrène, L. gangraena, fr. Gr.?, fr.? to gnaw, eat; cf. Skr. gras, gar, to devour, and E. voracious, also canker, n., in sense 3.] (Med.) A term formerly restricted to mortification of the soft tissues which has not advanced so far as to produce complete loss of vitality; but now applied to mortification of the soft parts in any stage.
Gangrene Gan"grene, v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Gangrened (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gangrening.] [Cf. F. gangréner.] To produce gangrene in; to be affected with gangrene.

gangrenescent.c: Gangrenescent Gan`gre*nes"cent (?), a. Tending to mortification or gangrene.

gangrenous.c: Gangrenous Gan"gre*nous (?), a. [Cf. F. gangréneux.] Affected by, or produced by, gangrene; of the nature of gangrene.

gangue.c: Gangue Gangue (?), n. [F. gangue, fr. G. gang a metallic vein, a passage. See Gang, n.] (Mining) The mineral or earthy substance associated with metallic ore.

gangway.c: Gangway Gang"way` (?), n. [See Gang, v. i.] 1. A passage or way into or out of any inclosed place; esp., a temporary way of access formed of planks.

ganil.c: Ganil Gan"il (?), n. [F.] A kind of brittle limestone. [Prov. Eng.] Kirwan.

gannister.c: Gannister Ganister Gan"is*ter (?), Gan"nis*ter, n. (Mech.) A refractory material consisting of crushed or ground siliceous stone, mixed with fire clay; -- used for lining Bessemer converters; also used for macadamizing roads.

ganja.c: Ganja Gan"ja (?), n. [Hind. gānjhā.] The dried hemp plant, used in India for smoking. It is extremely narcotic and intoxicating.

gannet.c: Gannet Gan"net (?), n. [OE. gant, AS. ganet, ganot, a sea fowl, a fen duck; akin to D. gent gander, OHG. ganazzo. See Gander, Goose.] (Zool.) One of several species of sea birds of the genus Sula, allied to the pelicans.

ganocephala.c: Ganocephala ‖Gan`o*ceph"a*la (?), prop. n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? brightness +? head.] (Paleon.) A group of fossil amphibians allied to the labyrinthodonts, having the head defended by bony, sculptured plates, as in some ganoid fishes.

ganocephalous.c: Ganocephalous Gan`o*ceph"a*lous (?), a. (Paleon.) Of or pertaining to the Ganocephala.

ganoid.c: Ganoid Ga"noid (?), a. [Gr.? brightness + -oid.] (Zool.) Of or pertaining to Ganoidei. -- n. One of the Ganoidei.

ganoidei.c: Ganoidei ‖Ga*noi"de*i (?), n. pl. [NL. See Ganoid.] (Zool.) One of the subclasses of fishes. They have an arterial cone and bulb, spiral intestinal valve, and the optic nerves united by a chiasma. Many of the species are covered with bony plates, or with ganoid scales; others have cycloid scales.

ganoine.c: Ganoine Ga"no*ine (?), n. (Zool.) A peculiar bony tissue beneath the enamel of a ganoid scale.

gansa.c: Gansa Gan"sa (?), n. Same as Ganza. Bp. Hall.

gantlet.c: Gantlet Gant"let (?), n. [Gantlet is corrupted fr. gantlope; gantlope is for gatelope, Sw. gatlopp, orig., a running down a lane; gata street, lane + lopp course, career, akin to löpa to run. See Gate a way, and Leap.] A military punishment formerly in use, wherein the offender was made to run between two files of men facing one another, who struck him as he passed.
Gantlet Gant"let, n. A glove. See Gauntlet.

gantline.c: Gantline Gant"line` (?), n. A line rigged to a mast; -- used in hoisting rigging; a girtline.

ganza.c: Ganza Gan"za (?), n. [Sp. gansa, ganso, goose; of Gothic origin. See Gannet, Goose.] A kind of wild goose, by a flock of which a virtuoso was fabled to be carried to the lunar world. [Also gansa.] Johnson.

ganz.c: Ganz system Ganz system (?) A haulage system for canal boats, in which an electric locomotive running on a monorail has its adhesion materially increased by the pull of the tow rope on a series of inclined gripping wheels.

gaol.c: Gaol Gaol (jāl), n. [See Jail.] A place of confinement, especially for minor offenses or provisional imprisonment; a jail. [Preferably, and in the United States usually, written jail.]

gaoler.c: Gaoler Gaol"er (jāl"ẽr), n. The keeper of a jail. Same as Jailer.

gap.c: Gap Gap (găp), n. [OE. gap; cf. Icel. gap an empty space, Sw. gap mouth, breach, abyss, Dan. gab mouth, opening, AS. geap expanse; as adj., wide, spacious. See Gape.] 1. An opening in anything made by breaking or parting; as, a gap in a fence; an opening for a passage or entrance; an opening which implies a breach or defect; a vacant space or time; a hiatus; a mountain pass.
Gap Gap, v. t. 1. To notch, as a sword or knife.

gape.c: Gape Gape (gäp; in Eng, commonly gāp; 277), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gaped (gäpt or gāpt); p. pr. & vb. n. Gaping] [OE. gapen, AS. geapan to open; akin to D. gapen to gape, G. gaffen, Icel. & Sw. gapa, Dan. gabe; cf. Skr. jabh to snap at, open the mouth. Cf. Gaby, Gap.] 1. To open the mouth wide; as: (a) Expressing a desire for food; as, young birds gape. Dryden. (b) Indicating sleepiness or indifference; to yawn.
Gape Gape, n. 1. The act of gaping; a yawn. Addison.

gapes.c: gapes gapes (gāps), n. See as the gapes, under gape, n..

gapeseed.c: Gapeseed Gape"seed` (gāp"sēd), n. 1. Any strange sight. Wright.

gapesing.c: Gapesing Gapes"ing (? or?), n. Act of gazing about; sightseeing. [Prov. Eng.]

gapeworm.c: Gapeworm Gape"worm` (? or?), n. (Zool.) The parasitic worm that causes the gapes in birds. See Illustration in Appendix.

gapingstock.c: Gapingstock Gap"ing*stock` (? or?), n. One who is an object of open-mouthed wonder.

gaptoothed.c: Gap-toothed Gap"-toothed` (găp"tōotht`), a. Having conspicuous interstices between the teeth; as, his gap-toothed grin. Dryden.

gar.c: Gar Gar (?), n. [Prob. AS. gār dart, spear, lance. The name is applied to the fish on account of its long and slender body and pointed head. Cf. Goad, Gore, v.] (Zool.) (a) Any slender marine fish of the genera Belone and Tylosurus. See Garfish. (b) The gar pike. See Alligator gar (under Alligator), and Gar pike.
Gar Gar, v. t. [Of Scand. origin. See Gear, n.] To cause; to make. [Obs. or Scot.] Spenser.

garage.c: Garage Ga`rage" (gȧ`räzh" or gȧ`räj" or (Brit.) gȧr"aj), n. [F.] 1. an enclosed structure for housing or parking motor vehicles, especially automobiles.

Garage Ga`rage" (gȧ`räzh" or gȧ`räj" or (Brit.) gȧr"aj), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Garaged (gȧ`räzhd", gȧ`räjd" or gȧr"ajd); p. pr. & vb. n. Garaging (gȧ"räzh"ĭng, gȧ"räj"ĭng or gȧr"a*jĭng).] To keep in a garage. [Colloq.]

garancin.c: Garancin Gar"an*cin (?; 104), n. [F. garance madder, LL. garantia.] (Chem.) An extract of madder by sulphuric acid. It consists essentially of alizarin.

garb.c: Garb Garb (gärb), n. [OF. garbe looks, countenance, grace, ornament, fr. OHG. garawī, garwī, ornament, dress. akin to E. gear. See Gear, n.] 1. (a) Clothing in general. (b) The whole dress or suit of clothes worn by any person, especially when indicating rank or office; as, the garb of a clergyman or a judge. (c) Costume; fashion; as, the garb of a gentleman in the 16th century.
Garb Garb (gärb), n. [F. gerbe, OF. also garbe, OHG. garba, G. garbe; cf. Skr. gṛbh to seize, E. grab.] (Her.) A sheaf of grain (wheat, unless otherwise specified).
Garb Garb, v. t. To clothe; array; deck.

garbage.c: Garbage Gar"bage (?; 48), n. [OE. also garbash, perh. orig., that which is purged or cleansed away; cf. OF. garber to make fine, neat, OHG. garawan to make ready, prepare, akin to E. garb dress; or perh. for garbleage, fr. garble; or cf. OF. garbage tax on sheaves, E. garb sheaf.] Offal, as the bowels of an animal or fish; refuse animal or vegetable matter from a kitchen; hence, anything worthless, disgusting, or loathsome. Grainger.
Garbage Gar"bage, v. t. To strip of the bowels; to clean. “Pilchards... are garbaged.” Holland.

garbel.c: Garbel Gar"bel, n. [Cf. Garble, v. t.] Anything sifted, or from which the coarse parts have been taken. [Obs.]

garble.c: Garble Gar"ble (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Garbled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Garbling.] [Formerly, to pick out, sort, OF. grabeler, for garbeler to examine precisely, garble spices, fr. LL. garbellare to sift; cf. Sp. garbillar to sift, garbillo a coarse sieve, L. cribellum, dim. of cribrum sieve, akin to cernere to separate, sift (cf. E. Discern); or perh. rather from Ar. gharbāl, gharbil, sieve.] 1. To sift or bolt, to separate the fine or valuable parts of from the coarse and useless parts, or from dros or dirt; as, to garble spices. [Obs.]

garboard.c: Garboard Gar"board (?), n. (Naut.) One of the planks next the keel on the outside, which form a garboard strake.

garboil.c: Garboil Gar"boil (?), n. [OF. garbouil; cf. Sp. garbullo, It. garbuglio; of uncertain origin; the last part is perh. fr. L. bullire to boil, E. boil.] Tumult; disturbance; disorder. [Obs.] Shak.

garcinia.c: Garcinia ‖Gar*cin"i*a (?), n. [NL.] (Bot.) A genus of plants, including the mangosteen tree (Garcinia Mangostana), found in the islands of the Indian Archipelago; -- so called in honor of Dr. Garcin.

garcon.c: Garcon ‖Gar`çon" (?), n. [F.] 1. A boy; a young unmarried man.

gard.c: Gard Gard (?), n. [See Garde, Yard] Garden. [Obs.] “Trees of the gard.” F. Beaumont.

gardant.c: Gardant Gar"dant (?), a. [F. See Guardant.] (Her.) Turning the head towards the spectator, but not the body; -- said of a lion or other beast.

garde.c: Garde civique ‖Garde` ci`vique" (?). [F.] See Army organization, above.

garden.c: Garden Gar"den (gär"d'n; 277), n. [OE. gardin, OF. gardin, jardin, F. jardin, of German origin; cf. OHG. garto, G. garten; akin to AS. geard. See Yard an inclosure.] 1. A piece of ground appropriated to the cultivation of herbs, fruits, flowers, or vegetables.
Garden Gar"den, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gardened (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gardening.] To lay out or cultivate a garden; to labor in a garden; to practice horticulture.
Garden Gar"den, v. t. To cultivate as a garden.

gardener.c: Gardener Gar"den*er (?), n. One who makes and tends a garden; a horticulturist.

gardenia.c: Gardenia ‖Garde"ni*a (?), n. [NL.] (Bot.) A genus of plants, some species of which produce beautiful and fragrant flowers; Cape jasmine; -- so called in honor of Dr. Alexander Garden.

gardening.c: Gardening Gar"den*ing (?), n. The art of occupation of laying out and cultivating gardens; horticulture.

gardenless.c: Gardenless Gar"den*less (?), a. Destitute of a garden. Shelley.

gardenly.c: Gardenly Gar"den*ly (?), a. Like a garden. [R.] W. Marshall.

gardon.c: Gardon Gar"don (?), n. [F] (Zool.) A European cyprinoid fish; the id.

gardyloo.c: Gardyloo Gar`dy*loo" (?), n. [F. gare l'eau beware of the water.] An old cry in throwing water, slops, etc., from the windows in Edingburgh. Sir. W. Scott.

gare.c: Gare Gare (?), n. [Cf. Gear.] Coarse wool on the legs of sheep. Blount.

garefowl.c: Garefowl Gare"fowl` (?), n. (Zool.) The great auk; also, the razorbill. See Auk. [Written also gairfowl, and gurfel.]

garfish.c: Garfish Gar"fish` (?), n. [See Gar, n.] (Zool.) (a) A European marine fish (Belone vulgaris); -- called also gar, gerrick, greenback, greenbone, gorebill, hornfish, longnose, mackerel guide, sea needle, and sea pike. (b) One of several species of similar fishes of the genus Tylosurus, of which one species (T. marinus) is common on the Atlantic coast. T. Caribbæus, a very large species, and T. crassus, are more southern; -- called also needlefish. Many of the common names of the European garfish are also applied to the American species.

gargalize.c: Gargalize Gar"ga*lize (?), v. t. [Cf. Gargle, Gargarize.] To gargle; to rinse. [Obs.] Marston.

garganey.c: Garganey Gar"ga*ney (?), n. (Zool.) A small European duck (Anas querquedula); -- called also cricket teal, and summer teal.

gargantuan.c: Gargantuan Gar*gan"tu*an (?; 135), a. [From Gargantua, an allegorical hero of Rabelais.] Characteristic of Gargantua, a gigantic, wonderful personage; enormous; prodigious; inordinate.

gargarism.c: Gargarism Gar"ga*rism (?), n. [F. gargarisme, L. gargarisma. See Gargarize.] (Med.) A gargle.

gargarize.c: Gargarize Gar"ga*rize (?), v. t. [F. gargarizare, fr. Gr.?.] To gargle; to rinse or wash, as the mouth and throat. [Obs.] Bacon.

garget.c: Garget Garget (?), n. [OE. garget, gargate, throat, OF. gargate. Cf. Gorge. The etymol. of senses 2, 3, & 4 is not certain.] 1. The throat. [Obs.] Chaucer.

gargil.c: Gargil Gar"gil (?), n. [Cf. Garget, Gargoyle.] A distemper in geese, affecting the head.

gargle.c: Gargle Gar"gle, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Garggled (?), p. pr. & vb. n. Gargling (?).] [F. gargouiller to dabble, paddle, gargle. Cf. Gargoyle, Gurgle.] 1. To wash or rinse, as the mouth or throat, particular the latter, agitating the liquid (water or a medicinal preparation) by an expulsion of air from the lungs.
Gargle Gar"gle, n. A liquid, as water or some medicated preparation, used to cleanse the mouth and throat, especially for a medical effect.

gargol.c: Gargol Gar"gol (?), n. [Cf. Gargil.] A distemper in swine; garget. Mortimer.

gargoulette.c: Gargoulette ‖Gar`gou*lette" (?), n. [F.] A water cooler or jug with a handle and spout; a gurglet. Mollett.

gargoyle.c: Gargoyle Gar"goyle (?), n. [OE. garguilie, gargouille, cf. Sp. gárgola, prob. fr. the same source as F. gorge throat, influenced by L. gargarizare to gargle. See Gorge and cf. Gargle, Gargarize.] (Arch.) A spout projecting from the roof gutter of a building, often carved grotesquely. [Written also gargle, gargyle, and gurgoyle.]

garibaldi.c: Garibaldi Ga`ri*bal"di (?), n. 1. A jacket worn by women; -- so called from its resemblance in shape to the red shirt worn by the Italians patriot Garibaldi.

garish.c: Garish Gar"ish (gâr"ĭsh), a. [Cf. OE. gauren to stare; of uncertain origin. Cf. gairish.] 1. Showy; dazzling; ostentatious; attracting or exciting attention. “The garish sun.” “A garish flag.” Shak. “In... garish colors.” Asham. “The garish day.” J. H. Newman.

garland.c: Garland Gar"land (?), n. [OE. garland, gerlond, OF. garlande, F. guirlande; of uncertain origin; cf. OHG. wiara, wiera, crown, pure gold, MHG. wieren to adorn.]
Garland Gar"land (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Garlanded; p. pr. & vb. n. Garlanding.] To deck with a garland. B. Jonson.

garlandless.c: Garlandless Gar"land*less, a. Destitute of a garland. Shelley.

garlic.c: Garlic Gar"lic (?), n. [OE. garlek, AS. gārleác; gar spear, lance + leác leek. See Gar, n., and Leek.] 1. (Bot.) A plant of the genus Allium (A. sativum is the cultivated variety), having a bulbous root, a very strong smell, and an acrid, pungent taste. Each root is composed of several lesser bulbs, called cloves of garlic, inclosed in a common membranous coat, and easily separable.

garlicky.c: Garlicky Gar"lick*y (?), a. Like or containing garlic.

garment.c: Garment Gar"ment (?), n. [OE. garnement, OF. garnement, garniment, fr. garnir to garnish. See Garnish.] Any article of clothing, as a coat, a gown, etc.

garmented.c: Garmented Gar"ment*ed, p. a. Having on a garment; attired; enveloped, as with a garment. [Poetic]

garner.c: Garner Gar"ner (?), n. [OE. garner, gerner, greiner, OF. gernier, grenier, F. grenier, fr. L. granarium, fr. granum. See 1st Grain, and cf. Granary.] A granary; a building or place where grain is stored for preservation.
Garner Gar"ner, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Garnered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Garnering.] To gather for preservation; to store, as in a granary; to treasure. Shak.

garnet.c: Garnet Gar"net (?), n. [OE. gernet, grenat, OF. grenet,grenat, F. grenat, LL. granatus, fr. L. granatum pomegranate, granatus having many grains or seeds, fr. granum grain, seed. So called from its resemblance in color and shape to the grains or seeds of the pomegranate. See Grain, and cf. Grenade, Pomegranate.] (Min.) A mineral having many varieties differing in color and in their constituents, but with the same crystallization (isometric), and conforming to the same general chemical formula. The commonest color is red, the luster is vitreous, and the hardness greater than that of quartz. The dodecahedron and trapezohedron are the common forms.
Garnet Gar"net, n. [Etymol. unknown.] (Naut.) A tackle for hoisting cargo in or out.

garnierite.c: Garnierite Gar"ni*er*ite (?), n. [Named after the French geologist Garnier.] (Min.) An amorphous mineral of apple-green color; a hydrous silicate of nickel and magnesia. It is an important ore of nickel.

garnish.c: Garnish Gar"nish (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Garnished (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Garnishing.] [OE. garnischen, garnissen, OF. garnir to provide, strengthen, prepare, garnish, warn, F. garnir to provide, furnish, garnish, -- of German origin; cf. OHG. warnōn to provide, equip; akin to G. wahren to watch, E. aware, ware, wary, and cf. also E. warn. See Wary, -ish, and cf. Garment, Garrison.] 1. To decorate with ornamental appendages; to set off; to adorn; to embellish.
Garnish Gar"nish, n. 1. Something added for embellishment; decoration; ornament; also, dress; garments, especially such as are showy or decorated.

garnishee.c: Garnishee Gar`nish*ee" (?), n. (Law) One who is garnished; a person upon whom garnishment has been served in a suit by a creditor against a debtor, such person holding property belonging to the debtor, or owing him money.

Garnishee Gar`nish*ee", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Garnisheed (-ēd); p. pr. & vb. n. Garnisheeing.] (Law) (a) To make (a person) a garnishee; to warn by garnishment; to garnish. (b) To attach (the fund or property sought to be secured by garnishment); to trustee.

garnisher.c: Garnisher Gar"nish*er (?), n. One who, or that which, garnishes.

garnishment.c: Garnishment Gar"nish*ment (?), n. [Cf. OF. garnissement protection, guarantee, warning.] 1. Ornament; embellishment; decoration. Sir H. Wotton.

garniture.c: Garniture Gar"ni*ture (?), n. [F. garniture. See Garnish, v. t.] That which garnishes; ornamental appendage; embellishment; furniture; dress.

garookuh.c: Garookuh ‖Ga*roo"kuh (?), n. A small fishing vessel met with in the Persian Gulf.

garous.c: Garous Ga"rous (?), a. [From Garum.] Pertaining to, or resembling, garum. Sir T. Browne.

garpike.c: Garpike Gar pike Gar" pike` or Gar"pike`. (Zool.) See under Gar.

garran.c: Garran Gar"ran (?), n. [Gael. garrán, gearrán, gelding, work horse, hack.] (Zool.) See Galloway. [Scot. garron or gerron. Jamieson.]

garret.c: Garret Gar"ret (?), n. [OE. garite, garette, watchtower, place of lookout, OF. garite, also meaning, a place of refuge, F. guérite a place of refuge, donjon, sentinel box, fr. OF. garir to preserve, save, defend, F. guérir to cure; of German origin; cf. OHG. werian to protect, defend, hinder, G. wehren, akin to Goth. warjan to hinder, and akin to E. weir, or perhaps to wary. See Weir, and cf. Guerite.] 1. A turret; a watchtower. [Obs.]

garreted.c: Garreted Gar"ret*ed, a. Protected by turrets. [Obs.] R. Carew.

garreteer.c: Garreteer Gar`ret*eer" (?), n. One who lives in a garret; a poor author; a literary hack. Macaulay.

garreting.c: Garreting Gar"ret*ing (?), n. Small splinters of stone inserted into the joints of coarse masonry. Weale.

garrison.c: Garrison Gar"ri*son (?), n. [OE. garnisoun, F. garnison garrison, in OF. & OE. also, provision, munitions, from garnir to garnish. See Garnish.] (Mil.) (a) A body of troops stationed in a fort or fortified town. (b) A fortified place, in which troops are quartered for its security.

Garrison Gar"ri*son, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Garrisoned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Garrisoning.] (Mil.) (a) To place troops in, as a fortification, for its defense; to furnish with soldiers; as, to garrison a fort or town. (b) To secure or defend by fortresses manned with troops; as, to garrison a conquered territory.

garrot.c: Garrot Gar"rot (?), n. [F. Cf. Garrote.] (Surg.) A stick or small wooden cylinder used for tightening a bandage, in order to compress the arteries of a limb.

garrote.c: Garrote Gar*rote" (?), n. [Sp. garrote, from garra claw, talon, of Celtic origin; cf. Armor. & W. gar leg, ham, shank. Cf. Garrot stick, Garter.] A Spanish mode of execution by strangulation, with an iron collar affixed to a post and tightened by a screw until life become extinct.
Garrote Gar*rote", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Garroted; p. pr. & vb. n. Garroting.] To strangle with the garrote; hence, to seize by the throat, from behind, with a view to strangle and rob.

garroter.c: garroter gar*rot"er (?), n. One who seizes a person by the throat from behind, with a view to strangle and rob him.

garrulity.c: garrulity gar*ru"li*ty (?), n. [L. garrulitas: cf. F. garrulité.] Talkativeness; loquacity.

garrulous.c: Garrulous Gar"ru*lous (?), a. [L. garrulus, fr. garrire to chatter, talk; cf. Gr.? voice,? to speak, sing. Cf. Call.] 1. Talking much, especially about commonplace or trivial things; talkative; loquacious.

garrupa.c: Garrupa Gar*ru"pa (?), n. [Prob. fr. Pg. garupa crupper. Cf. Grouper the fish.] (Zool.) One of several species of California market fishes, of the genus Sebastichthys; -- called also rockfish. See Rockfish.
