geoscopy.c: Geoscopy Ge*os"co*py (?), n. [Gr. ge`a, gh^, the earth + -scopy: cf. F. géoscopie.] Knowledge of the earth, ground, or soil, obtained by inspection. Chambers.

geoselenic.c: Geoselenic Ge`o*se*len"ic (?), a. [Gr. ge`a, gh^, the earth +? moon.] Pertaining to the earth and moon; belonging to the joint action or mutual relations of the earth and moon; as, geoselenic phenomena.

geostatic.c: Geostatic Ge`o*stat"ic (?), a. [Gr. ge`a, gh^, earth + E. static.] (Civil Engin.) Relating to the pressure exerted by earth or similar substance.

geosynclinal.c: Geosynclinal Ge`o*syn*cli"nal (?), n. [Gr. ge`a, gh^, the earth + E. synclinal.] (Geol.) the downward bend or subsidence of the earth's crust, which allows of the gradual accumulation of sediment, and hence forms the first step in the making of a mountain range; -- opposed to geanticlinal.

geothermometer.c: Geothermometer Ge`o*ther*mom"e*ter (?), n. [Gr. ge`a, gh^, the earth + E. thermometer.] (Physics) A thermometer specially constructed for measuring temperetures at a depth below the surface of the ground.

geotic.c: Geotic Ge*ot"ic (?) a. [Gr. ge`a, gh^, the earth.] Belonging to earth; terrestrial. [Obs.] Bailey.

geotropic.c: Geotropic Ge`o*trop"ic (?), a. [See Geotropism.] (Biol.) Relating to, or showing, geotropism.

geotropism.c: Geotropism Ge*ot"ro*pism (?), n. [Gr. ge`a, gh^, the earth +? to turn.] (Biol.) A disposition to turn or incline towards the earth; the influence of gravity in determining the direction of growth of an organ.

gephyrea.c: Gephyrea ‖Ge*phyr"e*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.? a dam, a bridge.] (Zool.) An order of marine Annelida, in which the body is imperfectly, or not at all, annulated externally, and is mostly without setæ.

gephyrean.c: Gephyrean Ge*phyr"e*an (?), a. (Zool.) Belonging to the Gephyrea. -- n. One of the Gerphyrea.

gerah.c: Gerah ‖Ge"rah (?), n. [Heb. g?rah, lit., a bean.] (Jewish Antiq.) A small coin and weight; 1-20th of a shekel.

geraniaceous.c: Geraniaceous Ge*ra`ni*a"ceous (?), a. (Bot.) Of or pertaining to a natural order of pants (Geraniaceæ) which includes the genera Geranium, Pelargonium, and many others.

geranium.c: Geranium Ge*ra"ni*um (je*rā"nĭ*ŭm), n. [L., fr. Gr. gera`nion, from ge`ranos crane: cf. F. géranium. See Crane, n.]

gerant.c: Gerant Ge"rant (?), n. [F. gérant.] The manager or acting partner of a company, joint-stock association, etc.

gerbe.c: Gerbe Gerbe (?), n. [F., prop. a sheaf.] (Pyrotechny) A kind of ornamental firework. Farrow.

gerbille.c: Gerbille Gerbil { Ger"bil (jẽr"bĭl), ‖Ger`bille" (zhar`bel"), } n. [F. gerbille. Cf. Jerboa.] 1. (Zool.) One of several species of small, jumping, murine burrowing rodents, of the genus Gerbillus and related genera of the subfamily Gerbillinae. They have long soft pale fur and hind legs adapted for leaping. In their leaping powers they resemble the jerboa. They inhabit Africa, India, and Southern Europe.

gerent.c: Gerent Ge"rent (?), a. [L. gerens, p. pr. of gerere to bear, manage.] Bearing; carrying. [Obs.] Bailey.

gerful.c: Gerful Ger"ful (?), a. [Cf. OF. girer to twirl, E. gyrate.] Changeable; capricious. [Obs.] Chaucer.

gerlond.c: Gerlond Gerland Ger"land (?), Ger"lond, n. A garland. [Obs.]

gerlind.c: Gerlind Ger"lind (?), n. (Zool.) A salmon returning from the sea the second time. [Prov. Eng.]

germ.c: Germ Germ (jẽrm), n. [F. germe, fr. L. germen, germinis, sprout, but, germ. Cf. Germen, Germane.] 1. (Biol.) That which is to develop a new individual; as, the germ of a fetus, of a plant or flower, and the like; the earliest form under which an organism appears.
Germ Germ (?), v. i. To germinate. [R.] J. Morley.
Germ cell Germ cell. (Biol.) A cell, of either sex, directly concerned in the production of a new organism.
Germ plasm Germ" plasm` (?), (Biol.) See Plasmogen, and Idioplasm.
Germ theory Germ theory. 1. (Biol.) The theory that living organisms can be produced only by the development of living germs. Cf. Biogenesis, Abiogenesis.

german.c: German Ger"man (?), a. [OE. german, germain, F. germain, fr. L. germanus full, own (said of brothers and sisters who have the same parents); akin to germen germ. Cf. Germ, Germane.] Nearly related; closely akin.
German Ger"man, n.; pl. Germans (#) [L. Germanus, prob. of Celtis origin.] 1. A native or one of the people of Germany.
German Ger"man, a. [L. Germanus. See German, n.] Of or pertaining to Germany.

germander.c: Germander Ger*man"der (?), n. [OE. germaunder, F. germandrée, It. calamandrea, L. chamaedrys, fr. Gr.?;? on the earth or ground +? tree. See Humble, and Tree.] (Bot.) A plant of the genus Teucrium (esp. Teucrium Chamædrys or wall germander), mintlike herbs and low shrubs.

germane.c: Germane Ger*mane" (?), a. [See German akin, nearly related.] Literally, near akin; hence, closely allied; appropriate or fitting; relevant.

germanic.c: Germanic Ger*man"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to, or containing, germanium.
Germanic Ger*man"ic, a. [L. Germanicus: cf. F. germanique. See German, n.] 1. Of or pertaining to Germany; as, the Germanic confederacy.

germanism.c: Germanism Ger"man*ism (?), n. [Cf. F. germanisme.] 1. An idiom of the German language.

germanium.c: Germanium Ger*ma"ni*um (?), n. [NL., fr. L. Germania Germany.] (Chem.) A rare element, discovered in 1885 in a silver ore (argyrodite) at Freiberg. It is a brittle, silver-white metal, chemically intermediate between the metals and nonmetals, resembles tin, and is in general identical with the predicted ekasilicon. Symbol Ge. Atomic number 32. Atomic weight 72.59. It has excellent semiconductor properties, and is used in transistors and diodes.

germanization.c: Germanization Ger`man*i*za"tion (?), n. The act of Germanizing. M. Arnold.

germanize.c: Germanize Ger"man*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Germanized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Germanizing (?).] To make German, or like what is distinctively German; as, to Germanize a province, a language, a society.
Germanize Ger"man*ize, v. i. To reason or write after the manner of the Germans.

germarium.c: Germarium ‖Ger*ma"ri*um (?), n. [NL. See Germ.] (Zool.) An organ in which the ova are developed in certain Turbellaria.

germen.c: Germen Ger"men (jẽr"mĕn), n.; pl. E. Germens (#), L. Germina (#). [L.] See Germ.

germicidal.c: germicidal ger"mi*ci`dal (jẽr"mĭ*sī`dail), a. [Germ + L. caedere to kill + -al.] (Biol.) Destructive to germs; -- applied to any agent which has a killing action upon living microorganisms, particularly bacteria or viruses, which are the cause of many infectious diseases.

germicide.c: germicide ger"mi*cide (jẽr"mĭ*sīd), n. A germicidal agent. -- a. Germicidal.

germinal.c: Germinal Ger"mi*nal (?), a. [See Germ.] 1. Pertaining or belonging to a germ; as, the germinal vesicle.
Germinal ‖Ger`mi*nal" (?), n. [F. See Germ.] The seventh month of the French republican calendar [1792 -- 1806]. It began March 21 and ended April 19. See Vendémiaire.

germinant.c: Germinant Ger"mi*nant (?), a. [L. germinans, p. pr.] Sprouting; sending forth germs or buds.

germinate.c: Germinate Ger"mi*nate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Germinated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Germinating.] [L. germinatus, p. p. of germinare to sprout, fr. germen. See Germ.] To sprout; to bud; to shoot; to begin to vegetate, as a plant or its seed; to begin to develop, as a germ. Bacon.
Germinate Ger"mi*nate, v. t. To cause to sprout. Price (1610).

germination.c: Germination Ger`mi*na"tion (?), n. [L. germinatio: cf. F. germination.] The process of germinating; the beginning of vegetation or growth in a seed or plant; the first development of germs, either animal or vegetable.

germinative.c: Germinative Ger"mi*na*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. germinatif.] Pertaining to germination; having power to bud or develop.

germiparity.c: Germiparity Ger`mi*par"i*ty (?), n. [Germ + L. parere to produce.] (Biol.) Reproduction by means of germs.

germogen.c: Germogen Ger"mo*gen (?), n. [Germ + -gen.] (Biol.) (a) A polynuclear mass of protoplasm, not divided into separate cells, from which certain ova are developed. Balfour. (b) The primitive cell in certain embryonic forms. Balfour.

germule.c: Germule Germ"ule (?), n. [Dim. fr. germ.] (Biol.) A small germ.

gern.c: Gern Gern (?), v. t. [See Grin.] To grin or yawn. [Obs.] “[/He] gaped like a gulf when he did gern.” Spenser.

gerocomical.c: Gerocomical Ger`o*com"ic*al (?), a. Pertaining to gerocomy. Dr. John Smith.

gerocomy.c: Gerocomy Ge*roc"o*my (?), n. [F. gérocomie, fr. Gr.? an old man +? to take care of.] That part of medicine which treats of regimen for old people.

gerontes.c: Gerontes ‖Ge*ron"tes (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr.?,?.] (Gr. Antiq.) Magistrates in Sparta, who with the ephori and kings, constituted the supreme civil authority.

gerontocracy.c: Gerontocracy Ger`on*toc"ra*cy (?), n. [Gr.?,?, an old man +? to rule.] Government by old men. [R.] Gladstone.

geropigia.c: Geropigia ‖Ger`o*pig"i*a (?), n. [Pg. geropiga.] A mixture composed of unfermented grape juice, brandy, sugar, etc., for adulteration of wines. [Written also jerupigia.]

gerous.c: -gerous -ger*ous (?). [L. -ger, fr. gerere to bear, carry. See Jest.] A suffix signifying bearing, producing; as, calcigerous; dentigerous.

gerrymander.c: Gerrymander Ger`ry*man"der (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gerrymandered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gerrymandering.] To divide (a State) into districts for the choice of representatives, in an unnatural and unfair way, with a view to give a political party an advantage over its opponent. [Political Cant, U. S.]

gerund.c: Gerund Ger"und (?), n. [L. gerundium, fr. gerere to bear, carry, perform. See Gest a deed, Jest.] (Lat. Gram.)

gerundial.c: Gerundial Ge*run"di*al (?), a. Pertaining to, or resembling, a gerund; as, a gerundial use.

gerundive.c: Gerundive Ge*run"dive (?), a. [L. gerundivus.] Pertaining to, or partaking of, the nature of the gerund; gerundial. -- n. (Lat. Gram.) The future passive participle; as, amandus, i. e., to be loved.

gerundively.c: Gerundively Ge*run"dive*ly, adv. In the manner of a gerund; as, or in place of, a gerund.

gery.c: Gery Ger"y (?), a. [See Gerful.] Changeable; fickle. [Obs.] Chaucer.

gesse.c: Gesse Gesse (?), v. t. & i. To guess. [Obs.] Chaucer.

gesso.c: Gesso ‖Ges"so (?), n. [It., chalk, plaster.] 1. Plaster of Paris, or gypsum, esp. as prepared for use in painting, or in making bas-reliefs and the like; by extension, a plasterlike or pasty material spread upon a surface to fit it for painting or gilding, or a surface so prepared.

Gesso duro ‖Ges"so du"ro (?). [It., hard plaster.] A variety of gesso which when dried becomes hard and durable, often used in making bas-relief casts, which are colored and mounted in elaborate frames.

gest.c: Gest Gest (?), n. [OF. geste exploit. See Jest.]
Gest Gest (?), n. [Cf. Gist a resting place.]

gestant.c: Gestant Ges"tant (?), a. [L. gestans, p. pr. of gestare.] Bearing within; laden; burdened; pregnant. [R.] “Clouds gestant with heat.” Mrs. Browning.

gestation.c: Gestation Ges*ta"tion (?), n. [L. gestatio a bearing, carrying, fr. gestare to bear, carry, intens. fr. gerere, gestum, to bear: cf. F. gestation. See Gest deed, Jest.]

gestatory.c: Gestatory Ges"ta*to*ry (?), a. [L. gestatorius that serves for carrying: cf. F. gestatoire.]

geste.c: Geste Geste (?), v. i. To tell stories or gests. [Obs.]

gestic.c: Gestic Ges"tic (?), a. [See Gest a deed, Gesture.]

gesticulate.c: Gesticulate Ges*tic"u*late (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gesticulated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gesticulating.] [L. gesticulatus, p. p. of gesticulari to gesticulate, fr. gesticulus a mimic gesture, gesticulation, dim. of gestus gesture, fr. gerere, gestum, to bear, carry, peform. See Gestic.] To make gestures or motions, as in speaking; to use postures. Sir T. Herbert.
Gesticulate Ges*tic"u*late, v. t. To represent by gesture; to act. [R.] B. Jonson.

gesticulation.c: Gesticulation Ges*tic`u*la"tion (?), n. [L. gesticulatio: cf. F. gesticulation.] 1. The act of gesticulating, or making gestures to express passion or enforce sentiments.

gesticulatory.c: Gesticulatory Ges*tic"u*la*to*ry (?), a. Representing by, or belonging to, gestures. T. Warton.

gestour.c: Gestour Ges"tour (?), n. [See Gest a deed.] A reciter of gests or legendary tales; a story-teller. [Obs.]

gesture.c: Gesture Ges"ture (?), n. [LL. gestura mode of action, fr. L. gerere, gestum, to bear, behave, perform, act. See Gest a deed.] 1. Manner of carrying the body; position of the body or limbs; posture. [Obs.]
Gesture Ges"ture, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gestured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gesturing.] To accompany or illustrate with gesture or action; to gesticulate.
Gesture Ges"ture, v. i. To make gestures; to gesticulate.

gesturement.c: Gesturement Ges"ture*ment (?), n. Act of making gestures; gesturing. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

get.c: Get Get (jĕt), n. Jet, the mineral. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Get Get (gĕt), n. [OF. get.] 1. Fashion; manner; custom. [Obs.] Chaucer.

Get Get (gĕt), v. t. [imp. Got (gŏt) (Obs. Gat (găt)); p. p. Got (Obsolescent Gotten (gŏt"t'n)); p. pr. & vb. n. Getting.] [OE. geten, AS. gitan, gietan (in comp.); akin to Icel. geta, Goth. bigitan to find, L. prehendere to seize, take, Gr. chanda`nein to hold, contain. Cf. Comprehend, Enterprise, Forget, Impregnable, Prehensile.] 1. To procure; to obtain; to gain possession of; to acquire; to earn; to obtain as a price or reward; to come by; to win, by almost any means; as, to get favor by kindness; to get wealth by industry and economy; to get land by purchase, etc.
Get Get (gĕt), v. i. 1. To make acquisition; to gain; to profit; to receive accessions; to be increased.
Get Get, n. Offspring; progeny; as, the get of a stallion.

geten.c: Geten Get"en (?), obs. p. p. of Get. Chaucer.

geth.c: Geth Geth (?), the original third pers. sing. pres. of Go. [Obs.] Chaucer.

getpenny.c: Get-penny Get"-pen`ny (?), n. Something which gets or gains money; a successful affair. [Colloq.] Chapman.

gettable.c: Gettable Get"ta*ble (?), a. That may be obtained. [R.]

getter.c: Getter Get"ter (?), n. One who gets, gains, obtains, acquires, begets, or procreates.

getterup.c: Getterup Get"ter*up`, n. One who contrives, makes, or arranges for, anything, as a book, a machine, etc. [Colloq.]

getting.c: Getting Get"ting (?), n. 1. The act of obtaining or acquiring; acquisition.

getup.c: get-up getup get"up, get"-up (?), n. 1. General composition or structure; manner in which the parts of a thing are combined; arrangement; format; make-up; style of dress, etc. [Colloq.] H. Kingsley.

geusdism.c: Geusdism Geusd"ism (gĕd"ĭz'm), prop. n. The Marxian socialism and programme of reform through revolution as advocated by the French political leader Jules Basile Guesde (pron. gĕd) (1845-). -- Guesd"ist (#), n. & a.

gewgaw.c: Gewgaw Gew"gaw (?), n. [OE. gigawe, gugawe, gewgaude, prob. the same word as OE. givegove gewgaw, apparently a reduplicated form fr. AS. gifan to give; cf. also F. joujou plaything, and E. gaud, n. See Give, and cf. Giffgaff.] A showy trifle; a toy; a splendid plaything; a pretty but worthless bauble.

geyser.c: Geyser Gey"ser (?), n. [Icel. geysir, fr. geysa to rush furiously, fr. gjōsa to gush. Cf. Gush.] A boiling spring which throws forth at frequent intervals jets of water, mud, etc., driven up by the expansive power of steam.

geyserite.c: Geyserite Gey"ser*ite (gī"zẽr*īt or gī"sẽr*īt; 277), n. [From Geyser.] (Min.) A loose hydrated form of silica, a variety of opal, deposited in concretionary cauliflowerlike masses, around some hot springs and geysers.

gharry.c: Gharry ‖Ghar"ry (?), n. [Hind. gā?i.] Any wheeled cart or carriage. [India]

ghast.c: Ghast Ghast (?), v. t. [OE. gasten. See Ghastly, a.] To strike aghast; to affright. [Obs.]

ghastful.c: Ghastful Ghast"ful (?), a. [See Ghastly, a.] Fit to make one aghast; dismal. [Obs.] -- Ghast"ful*ly, adv.

ghastliness.c: Ghastliness Ghast"li*ness (?), n. The state of being ghastly; a deathlike look.

ghastly.c: Ghastly Ghast"ly (?), a. [Compar. Ghastlier (?); superl. Ghastliest.] [OE. gastlich, gastli, fearful, causing fear, fr. gasten to terrify, AS. gæstan. Cf. Aghast, Gast, Gaze, Ghostly.] 1. Like a ghost in appearance; deathlike; pale; pallid; dismal.
Ghastly Ghast"ly, adv. In a ghastly manner; hideously.

ghawazi.c: Ghawazi ‖Gha*wa"zi (?), n. pl. [Etymol. uncertain.] Egyptian dancing girls, of a lower sort than the almeh.

ghazel.c: Ghazel Ghazal { ‖Ghaz"al (?), ‖Ghaz"el (?) }, n. [Ar. ghazal.] A kind of Oriental lyric, and usually erotic, poetry, written in recurring rhymes.

ghazi.c: Ghazi ‖Gha"zi (?), n. [Ar. ghāzī.] Among Muslims, a warrior champion or veteran, esp. in the destruction of infidels.

ghebre.c: Ghebre Gheber { Ghe"ber, Ghe"bre } (?), n. [Pers. ghebr: cf. F. Guèbre. Cf. Giaour.] A worshiper of fire; a Zoroastrian; a Parsee.

ghee.c: Ghee Ghee (gē), n. [Hind. ghī clarified butter, Skr. ghṛta.] Butter clarified by boiling, and thus converted into a kind of oil. [India] Malcom.

gherkin.c: Gherkin Gher"kin (gẽr"kĭn), n. [D. agurkje, a dim. akin to G. gurke, Dan. agurke; cf. Pol. ogórek, Bohem. okurka, LGr. 'aggoy`rion watermelon, Ar. al-khiyār, Per. khiyār.]

ghess.c: Ghess Ghess (?), v. t. & i. See Guess. [Obs.]

ghetto.c: Ghetto Ghet"to (?), n. [It.] A quarter of a city where Jews live in greatest numbers.

ghibelline.c: Ghibelline Ghib"el*line (?), n. [It. Ghibellino; of German origin.] (It. Hist.) One of a faction in Italy, in the 12th and 13th centuries, which favored the German emperors, and opposed the Guelfs, or adherents of the poses. Brande & C.

ghost.c: Ghost Ghost (gōst), n. [OE. gast, gost, soul, spirit, AS. gāst breath, spirit, soul; akin to OS. gēst spirit, soul, D. geest, G. geist, and prob. to E. gaze, ghastly.]
Ghost Ghost, v. i. To die; to expire. [Obs.] Sir P. Sidney.
Ghost Ghost, v. t. To appear to or haunt in the form of an apparition. [Obs.] Shak.

Ghost dance Ghost dance. A religious dance of the North American Indians, participated in by both sexes, and looked upon as a rite of invocation the purpose of which is, through trance and vision, to bring the dancer into communion with the unseen world and the spirits of departed friends. The dance is the chief rite of the Ghost-dance, or Messiah, religion, which originated about 1890 in the doctrines of the Piute Wovoka, the Indian Messiah, who taught that the time was drawing near when the whole Indian race, the dead with the living, should be reunited to live a life of millennial happiness upon a regenerated earth. The religion inculcates peace, righteousness, and work, and holds that in good time, without warlike intervention, the oppressive white rule will be removed by the higher powers. The religion spread through a majority of the western tribes of the United States, only in the case of the Sioux, owing to local causes, leading to an outbreak.

ghostfish.c: Ghostfish Ghost"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) A pale unspotted variety of the wrymouth.

ghostless.c: Ghostless Ghost"less, a. Without life or spirit. [R.]

ghostlike.c: Ghostlike Ghost"like` (?), a. Like a ghost; ghastly.

ghostliness.c: Ghostliness Ghost"li*ness, n. The quality of being ghostly.

ghostly.c: Ghostly Ghost"ly, a. [OE. gastlich, gostlich, AS. gāstlic. See Ghost.] 1. Relating to the soul; not carnal or secular; spiritual; as, a ghostly confessor.

ghoul.c: Ghoul Ghoul (gōol), n. [Per. ghōl an imaginary sylvan demon, supposed to devour men and animals: cf. Ar. ghūl, F. goule.] An imaginary evil being among Eastern nations, which was supposed to feed upon human bodies. [Written also ghole.] Moore.

ghoulish.c: Ghoulish Ghoul"ish, a. Characteristic of a ghoul; vampirelike; hyenalike.

ghyll.c: Ghyll Ghyll (?), n. A ravine. See Gill a woody glen. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Wordsworth.

giallolino.c: Giallolino ‖Gial`lo*li"no (?), n. [It., from giallo yellow, prob. fr. OHG. gelo, G. gelb; akin to E. yellow.] A term variously employed by early writers on art, though commonly designating the yellow oxide of lead, or massicot. Fairholt.

giambeux.c: Giambeux Giam"beux (zhȧm"bụ), n. pl. [See Jambeux.] Greaves; armor for the legs. [Obs.] Spenser.

giant.c: Giant Gi"ant (?), n. [OE. giant, geant, geaunt, OF. jaiant, geant, F. géant, L. gigas, fr. Gr.?,?, from the root of E. gender, genesis. See Gender, and cf. Gigantic.]
Giant Gi"ant, a. Like a giant; extraordinary in size, strength, or power; as, giant brothers; a giant son.

giantess.c: Giantess Gi"ant*ess, n. A woman of extraordinary size.

giantize.c: Giantize Gi"ant*ize (?), v. i. [Cf. F. géantiser.] To play the giant. [R.] Sherwood.

giantly.c: Giantly Gi"ant*ly, a. Appropriate to a giant. [Obs.] Usher.

giantry.c: Giantry Gi"ant*ry (?), n. The race of giants. [R.] Cotgrave.

giantship.c: Giantship Gi"ant*ship, n. The state, personality, or character, of a giant; -- a compellation for a giant.

giaour.c: Giaour ‖Giaour (?), n. [Turk. giaur an infidel, Per. gawr, another form of ghebr fire worshiper. Cf. Kaffir, Gheber.] An infidel; -- a term applied by Turks to disbelievers in the Muslim religion, especially Christians. Byron.

gib.c: Gib Gib (?), n. [Abbreviated fr. Gilbert, the name of the cat in the old story of “Reynard the Fox”, in the “Romaunt of the Rose”, etc.] A male cat; a tomcat. [Obs.]
Gib Gib, v. i. To act like a cat. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

Gib Gib (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] A piece or slip of metal or wood, notched or otherwise, in a machine or structure, to hold other parts in place or bind them together, or to afford a bearing surface; -- usually held or adjusted by means of a wedge, key, or screw.
Gib Gib, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gibbed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gibbing.] To secure or fasten with a gib, or gibs; to provide with a gib, or gibs.
Gib Gib (?), v. i. To balk. See Jib, v. i. Youatt.
Gib boom Gib" boom` (?). See Jib boom.

gibaro.c: Gibaro Gi"ba*ro (?), n.; pl. Gibaros (#). [Amer. Sp. jíbaro wild.] (Ethnol.) The offspring of a Spaniard and an Indian; a Spanish-Indian mestizo. [Sp. Amer.]

gibbartas.c: Gibbartas Gib*bar"tas (?), n. [Cf. Ar. jebbār giant; or L. gibber humpbacked: cf. F. gibbar.] (Zool.) One of several finback whales of the North Atlantic; -- called also Jupiter whale. [Written also jubartas, gubertas, dubertus.]

gibber.c: Gibber Gib"ber (jĭb"bẽr), n. [From Gib to balk.] A balky horse. Youatt.
gibber gib"ber (gĭb"bẽr), v. i. [imp. & p. p. gibbered (gĭb"bẽrd); p. pr. & vb. n. gibbering.] [Akin to jabber, and gabble.] To speak rapidly and inarticulately. Shak.

gibberish.c: gibberish gib"ber*ish (jĭb"bẽr*ĭsh or gĭb"bẽr*ĭsh), n. [From Gibber, v. i.] 1. Rapid and inarticulate talk; unintelligible language; unmeaning words.
Gibberish Gib"ber*ish, a. Unmeaning; as, gibberish language.

gibbet.c: Gibbet Gib"bet (?), n. [OE. gibet, F. gibet, in OF. also club, fr. LL. gibetum;; cf. OF. gibe sort of sickle or hook, It. giubbetto gibbet, and giubbetta, dim. of giubba mane, also, an under waistcoat, doublet, Prov. It. gibba (cf. Jupon); so that it perhaps originally signified a halter, a rope round the neck of malefactors; or it is, perhaps, derived fr. L. gibbus hunched, humped, E. gibbous; or cf. E. jib a sail.]
Gibbet Gib"bet, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gibbeted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gibbeting.]

gibbier.c: Gibbier Gib"bier (?), n. [F. gibier.] Wild fowl; game. [Obs.] Addison.

gibbon.c: Gibbon Gib"bon (?), n. [Cf. F. gibbon.] (Zool.) Any arboreal ape of the genus Hylobates, of which many species and varieties inhabit the East Indies and Southern Asia. They are tailless and without cheek pouches, and have very long arms, adapted for climbing.

gibbose.c: Gibbose Gib*bose" (?), a. [L. gibbosus, fr. gibbus, gibba, hunch, hump. Cf. Gibbous.] Humped; protuberant; -- said of a surface which presents one or more large elevations. Brande & C.

gibbostity.c: Gibbostity Gib*bost"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. gibbosité.] The state of being gibbous or gibbose; gibbousness.

gibbous.c: Gibbous Gib"bous (?), a. [Cf. F. gibbeux. See Gibbose.]

gibbsite.c: Gibbsite Gibbs"ite (?), n. [Named after George Gibbs.] (Min.) A hydrate of alumina.

gibcat.c: Gib-cat Gib"-cat` (?), n. A male cat, esp. an old one. See 1st Gib. n. [Obs.] Shak.

gibe.c: Gibe Gibe (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gibed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gibing.] [Cf. Prov. F. giber, equiv. to F. jouer to play, Icel. geipa to talk nonsense, E. jabber.] To cast reproaches and sneering expressions; to rail; to utter taunting, sarcastic words; to flout; to fleer; to scoff.
Gibe Gibe, v. i. To reproach with contemptuous words; to deride; to scoff at; to mock.
Gibe Gibe, n. An expression of sarcastic scorn; a sarcastic jest; a scoff; a taunt; a sneer.

gibel.c: Gibel ‖Gib"el (?), n. [G. gibel, giebel.] (Zool.) A kind of carp (Cyprinus gibelio); -- called also Prussian carp.

giber.c: Giber Gib"er (?) n. One who utters gibes. B. Jonson.

gibfish.c: Gibfish Gib"fish` (?), n. The male of the salmon. [Prov. Eng.] Wright.

gibingly.c: Gibingly Gib"ing*ly (?), adv. In a gibing manner; scornfully.

giblet.c: Giblet Gib"let (?), a. Made of giblets; as, a giblet pie.

giblets.c: Giblets Gib"lets (?), n. pl. [OE. gibelet, OF. gibelet game: cf. F. gibelotte stewed rabbit. Cf. Gibbier.] The inmeats, or edible viscera (heart, gizzard, liver, etc.), of poultry.

gibraltar.c: Gibraltar Gi*bral"tar (?), n. 1. A strongly fortified town on the south coast of Spain, held by the British since 1704; hence, an impregnable stronghold.

gibstaff.c: Gibstaff Gib"staff` (?), n. [Prov. E. gib a hooked stick + E. staff.] 1. A staff to guage water, or to push a boat.

gid.c: Gid Gid (?), n. [Cf. Giddy, a.] A disease of sheep, characterized by vertigo; the staggers. It is caused by the presence of the C?nurus, a larval tapeworm, in the brain. See C?nurus.

giddily.c: Giddily Gid"di*ly (?), adv. In a giddy manner.

giddiness.c: Giddiness Gid"di*ness, n. The quality or state of being giddy.

giddy.c: Giddy Gid"dy (?), a. [Compar. Giddier (?); superl. Giddiest.] [OE. gidi mad, silly, AS. gidig, of unknown origin, cf. Norw. gidda to shake, tremble.]
Giddy Gid"dy, v. i. To reel; to whirl. Chapman.
Giddy Gid"dy, v. t. To make dizzy or unsteady. [Obs.]

giddyhead.c: Giddy-head Gid"dy-head` (?), n. A person without thought fulness, prudence, or judgment. [Colloq.] Burton.

giddypaced.c: Giddy-paced Gid"dy-paced` (?), a. Moving irregularly; flighty; fickle. [R.] Shak.

gie.c: Gie Gie (?), v. t. To guide. See Gye. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Gie Gie (?), v. t. To give. [Scot.] Burns.

giereagle.c: Gier-eagle Gier"-ea`gle (?), n. [Cf. D. gier vulture, G. gier, and E. gyrfalcon.] (Zool.) A bird referred to in the Bible (Lev. xi. 18and Deut. xiv. 17) as unclean, probably the Egyptian vulture (Neophron percnopterus).

gierfalcon.c: Gier-falcon Gier"-fal`con (?), n. [Cf. Gier-eagle, Gyrfalcon.] (Zool.) The gyrfalcon.

gieseckite.c: Gieseckite Gie"seck*ite (?), n. [Named after Karl Giesecke.] (Min.) A mineral occurring in greenish gray six-sided prisms, having a greasy luster. It is probably a pseudomorph after elæolite.

giffard.c: Giffard injector Gif"fard in*ject"or (?). (Mach.) See under Injector.

giffgaff.c: Giffgaff Giff"gaff (?), n. [Reduplicated fr. give.] Mutual accommodation; mutual giving. [Scot.]

gift.c: Gift Gift (?), n. [OE. gift, yift, yeft, AS. gift, fr. gifan to give; akin to D. & G. gift, Icel. gift, gipt, Goth. gifts (in comp.). See Give, v. t.] 1. Anything given; anything voluntarily transferred by one person to another without compensation; a present; an offering.
Gift Gift, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gifted; p. pr. & vb. n. Gifting.] To endow with some power or faculty. See gift{4}.

giftedness.c: Giftedness Gift"ed*ness, n. The state of being gifted. Echard.

gig.c: Gig Gig (jĭg or gĭg), n. [Cf. OF. gigue. See Jig, n.] A fiddle. [Obs.]
Gig Gig (gĭg), v. t. [Prob. fr. L. gignere to beget.] To engender. [Obs.] Dryden.
Gig Gig, n. A kind of spear or harpoon. See Fishgig.
Gig Gig, v. t. To fish with a gig.
Gig Gig, n. [OE. gigge. Cf. Giglot.] A playful or wanton girl; a giglot.
Gig Gig, n. [Cf. Icel. gīgja fiddle, MHG. gīge, G. geige, Icel. geiga to take a wrong direction, rove at random, and E. jig.] 1. A top or whirligig; any little thing that is whirled round in play.

gigantean.c: Gigantean Gi`gan*te"an (?), a. [L. giganteus, fr. gigas, antis. See Giant.] Like a giant; mighty; gigantic. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

gigantesque.c: Gigantesque Gi`gan*tesque" (?), a. [F.] Befitting a giant; bombastic; magniloquent.

gigantic.c: Gigantic Gi*gan"tic (?), a. [L. gigas, -antis, giant. See Giant.] 1. Of extraordinary size; like a giant.

gigantical.c: Gigantical Gi*gan"tic*al, a. Bulky, big. [Obs.] Burton. -- Gi*gan"tic*al*ly, adv.

giganticide.c: Giganticide Gi*gan"ti*cide (?), n. [. gigas, -antis, giant + caedere to kill.] The act of killing, or one who kills, a giant. Hallam.

gigantology.c: Gigantology Gi`gan*tol"og*y (?), n. [Gr.?,?, giant + -logy: cf. F. gigantologie.] An account or description of giants.

gigantomachy.c: Gigantomachy Gi`gan*tom"a*chy (?), n. [L. gigantomachia, fr. Gr.?;?,?, giant +? battle: cf. F. gigantomachie.] A war of giants; especially, the fabulous war of the giants against heaven.

guige.c: Guige Gige Gige (gĭj or gēj), Guige, n. [OF. guide, guiche.] (Anc. Armor) The leather strap by which the shield of a knight was slung across the shoulder, or across the neck and shoulder. Meyrick (Ancient Armor).
Guige Guige (gĭj or gēj), n. [Obs.] See Gige.

gigerium.c: Gigerium ‖Gi*ge"ri*um (?), n.; pl. Gigeria (#). [NL., fr. L. gigeria, pl., the cooked entrails of poultry.] (Anat.) The muscular stomach, or gizzard, of birds.

giggle.c: Giggle Gig"gle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Giggled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Giggling (?).] [Akin to gaggle: cf. OD. ghichelen, G. kichern.] To laugh with short catches of the breath or voice; to laugh in a light, affected, or silly manner; to titter with childish levity.
Giggle Gig"gle (?), n. A kind of laugh, with short catches of the voice or breath; a light, silly laugh.

giggler.c: Giggler Gig"gler (?), n. One who giggles or titters.

giggly.c: Giggly Gig"gly (?), a. Prone to giggling. Carlyle.

giggot.c: Giggot Gigot Gig"ot, Gig"got (?), n. [F., fr. OF. gigue fiddle; -- on account of the resemblance in shape. See Jig, n.] 1. A leg of mutton.

giggyng.c: Giggyng Gig"gyng (?), n. [See Gige.] The act of fastending the gige or leather strap to the shield. [Obs.] “Gigging of shields.” Chaucer.

giglet.c: Giglet Giglot { Gig"lot (?), Gig"let (?), } n. [Cf. Icel. gikkr a pert, rude person, Dan. giek a fool, silly man, AS. gagol, gægl, lascivious, wanton, MHG. gogel wanton, giege fool, and E. gig a wanton person.] A wanton; a lascivious or light, giddy girl. [Obs.]

giglot.c: Giglot Gig"lot (?), a. Giddi; light; inconstant; wanton. [Obs.] “O giglot fortune!” Shak.

gigue.c: Gigue ‖Gigue (zheg), n. [F.] A piece of lively dance music, in two strains which are repeated; also, the dance.

gila.c: Gila monster Gi"la mon"ster (?). (Zool.) A large tuberculated lizard (Heloderma suspectum) native of the dry plains of Arizona, New Mexico, etc. It is the only lizard known to have venomous teeth.

gild.c: Gild Gild (gĭld), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gilded or Gilt (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gilding.] [AS. gyldan, from gold gold. √234. See Gold.] 1. To overlay with a thin covering of gold; to cover with a golden color; to cause to look like gold. “Gilded chariots.” Pope.

gildale.c: Gildale Gild"ale` (?), n. [AS. gilgan to pay + E. ale. See Yield, v. t., and Ale.] A drinking bout in which every one pays an equal share. [Obs.]

gilder.c: Gilder Gild"er (?), n. One who gilds; one whose occupation is to overlay with gold.
Gilder Gil"der (?), n. A Dutch coin. See Guilder.

gilding.c: Gilding Gild"ing (gĭld"ĭng), n. 1. The art or practice of overlaying or covering with gold leaf; also, a thin coating or wash of gold, or of that which resembles gold.

gill.c: Gill Gill (gĭl), n. [Dan. giælle, gelle; akin to Sw. gäl, Icel. gjölnar gills; cf. AS. geagl, geahl, jaw.] 1. (Anat.) An organ for aquatic respiration; a branchia.
Gill Gill, n. [Etymol. uncertain.] A two-wheeled frame for transporting timber. [Prov. Eng.]
Gill Gill, n. A leech. [Also gell.] [Scot.] Jameison.
Gill Gill, n. [Icel. gil.] A woody glen; a narrow valley containing a stream. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]
Gill Gill (?), n. [OF. gille, gelle, a sort of measure for wine, LL. gillo, gello., Cf. Gallon.] A measure of capacity, containing one fourth of a pint.
Gill Gill (?), n. [Abbrev. from Gillian.] 1. A young woman; a sweetheart; a flirting or wanton girl. “Each Jack with his Gill.” B. Jonson.

gillflirt.c: Gill-flirt Gill"-flirt` (?), n. A thoughtless, giddy girl; a flirt-gill. Sir W. Scott.

gillhouse.c: Gillhouse Gill"house`, n. A shop where gill is sold.

gillian.c: Gillian Gil"li*an (?), n. [OE. Gillian, a woman's name, for Julian, Juliana. Cf. Gill a girl.] A girl; esp., a wanton; a gill. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

gilly.c: Gilly Gillie { Gil"lie Gil"ly } (?), n. [Gael. gille, giolla, boy, lad.] A boy or young man; a manservant; a young male attendant, in the Scottish Highlands. Sir W. Scott. [wns=1]

gillyflower.c: Gillyflower Gil"ly*flow`er (?), n. [OE. gilofre, gilofer, clove, OF. girofre, girofle, F. girofle: cf. F. giroflée gillyflower, fr. girofle, Gr.? clove tree;? nut +? leaf, akin to E. foliage. Cf. Caryophyllus, July-flower.] [Written also gilliflower.] (Bot.) 1. A name given by old writers to the clove pink (Dianthus Caryophyllus) but now to the common stock (Matthiola incana), a cruciferous plant with showy and fragrant blossoms, usually purplish, but often pink or white.

gilse.c: Gilse Gilse (?), n. [W. gleisiad, fr. glas blue.] (Zool.) See Grilse.

gilt.c: Gilt Gilt (?), n. [See Geld, v. t.] (Zool.) A female pig, when young.
Gilt Gilt, imp. & p. p. of Gild.
Gilt Gilt, p. p. & a. Gilded; covered with gold; of the color of gold; golden yellow. “Gilt hair” Chaucer.
Gilt Gilt, n. 1. Gold, or that which resembles gold, laid on the surface of a thing; gilding. Shak.

giltedged.c: Gilt-edged Gilt-edge { Gilt"-edge` (?), Gilt"-edged` (?), } a. 1. Having a gilt edge; as, gilt-edged paper.

gilthead.c: Gilthead Gilt"head` (?), n. (Zool.) A marine fish. The name is applied to two species: (a) The Pagrus auratus (syn. Chrysophrys auratus), a valuable food fish common in the Mediterranean (so named from its golden-colored head); -- called also giltpoll. (b) The Crenilabrus melops, of the British coasts; -- called also golden maid, conner, sea partridge.

giltif.c: Giltif Gilt"if (?), a. [For gilti, by confusion with -if, -ive, in French forms. See Guilty.] Guilty. [Obs.] Chaucer.

gilttail.c: Gilttail Gilt"tail` (?), n. A yellow-tailed worm or larva.

gim.c: Gim Gim (?), a. [Cf. Gimp, a.] Neat; spruce. [Prov.]

gimbals.c: Gimbals Gimbal Gim"bal (gĭm"bail), or Gim"bals (gĭm"bailz), n. [See Gimmal, n.] A contrivance for permitting a body to incline freely in all directions, or for suspending anything, as a barometer, ship's compass, chronometer, etc., so that it will remain plumb, or level, when its support is tipped, as by the rolling of a ship. It consists of a ring in which the body can turn on an axis through a diameter of the ring, while the ring itself is so pivoted to its support that it can turn about a diameter at right angles to the first.

gimcrack.c: gimcrack gim"crack` (?), n. [OE., a spruce and pert pretender, also, a spruce girl, prob. fr. gim + crack lad, boaster.] A trivial mechanism; a device. Arbuthnot.

gimlet.c: Gimlet Gim"let (?), n. [Also written and pronounced gimbled (?)] [OF. guimbelet, guibelet, F. gibelet, prob. fr. OD. wimpel, weme, a bore, wemelen to bore, to wimble. See Wimble, n.] A small tool for boring holes. It has a leading screw, a grooved body, and a cross handle.
Gimlet Gim"let, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gimleted; p. pr. & vb. n. Gimleting.] 1. To pierce or make with a gimlet.

gimmal.c: Gimmal Gim"mal (?), n. [Prob. the same word as gemel. See Gemel, and cf. Gimbal.] 1. Joined work whose parts move within each other; a pair or series of interlocked rings.
Gimmal Gim"mal, a. Made or consisting of interlocked rings or links; as, gimmal mail.

gimmor.c: Gimmor Gimmer Gim"mer, Gim"mor (?), n. [Cf. Gimmal, n.] A piece of mechanism; mechanical device or contrivance; a gimcrack. [Obs.] Bp. Hall. Shak.

gimp.c: Gimp Gimp (?), a. [W. gwymp fair, neat, comely.] Smart; spruce; trim; nice. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]

Gimp Gimp, n. [OF. guimpe, guimple, a nun's wimple, F. guimpe, OHG. wimpal a veil G. wimpel pennon, pendant. See Wimple, n.] A narrow ornamental fabric of silk, woolen, or cotton, often with a metallic wire, or sometimes a coarse cord, running through it; -- used as trimming for dresses, furniture, etc.
Gimp Gimp, v. t. To notch; to indent; to jag.

gin.c: Gin Gin (?), prep. [AS. geán. See Again.] Against; near by; towards; as, gin night. [Scot.] A. Ross (1778).
Gin Gin, conj. [See Gin, prep.] If. [Scotch] Jamieson.

Gin Gin (gĭn), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gan (găn), Gon (gŏn), or Gun (gŭn); p. pr. & vb. n. Ginning.] [OE. ginnen, AS. ginnan (in comp.), prob. orig., to open, cut open, cf. OHG. inginnan to begin, open, cut open, and prob. akin to AS. gīnan to yawn, and E. yawn. √31. See Yawn, v. i., and cf. Begin.] To begin; -- often followed by an infinitive without to; as, gan tell. See Gan. [Obs. or Archaic] “He gan to pray.” Chaucer.

Gin Gin (jĭn), n. [Contr. from Geneva. See 2d Geneva.] A strong alcoholic liquor, distilled from rye and barley, and flavored with juniper berries; -- also called Hollands and Holland gin, because originally, and still very extensively, manufactured in Holland. Common gin is usually flavored with turpentine.
Gin Gin, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Ginned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Ginning.] 1. To catch in a trap. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

ging.c: Ging Ging (?), n. Same as Gang, n., 2. [Obs.]

ginger.c: Ginger Gin"ger (?), n. [OE. ginger, gingever, gingivere, OF. gengibre, gingimbre, F. gingembre, L. zingiber, zingiberi, fr. Gr.?; of Oriental origin; cf. Ar. & Pers. zenjebīl, fr. Skr. çṛṅgavëra, prop., hornshaped;???ga horn + vëra body.]

gingerbread.c: Gingerbread Gin"ger*bread` (?), n. A kind of plain sweet cake seasoned with ginger, and sometimes made in fanciful shapes. “Gingerbread that was full fine.” Chaucer.

gingerly.c: Gingerly Gin"ger*ly, adv. [Prov. E. ginger brittle, tender; cf. dial. Sw. gingla, gängla, to go gently, totter, akin to E. gang.] Cautiously; timidly; fastidiously; daintily.

gingham.c: Gingham Ging"ham (?), n. [F. guingan; cf. Jav. ginggang; or perh. fr. Guingamp, in France.] A kind of cotton or linen cloth, usually in stripes or checks, the yarn of which is dyed before it is woven; -- distinguished from printed cotton or prints.

ginging.c: Ginging Ging"ing (?), n. (Mining) The lining of a mine shaft with stones or bricks to prevent caving.

gingival.c: Gingival Gin"gi*val (?), a. [L. gingiva the gum.] Of or pertaining to the gums. Holder.

ginglymodi.c: Ginglymodi ‖Gin`gly*mo"di (?), n. [NL.; cf. Gr.? ginglymoid. See Ginglymoid.] (Zool.) An order of ganoid fishes, including the modern gar pikes and many allied fossil forms. They have rhombic, ganoid scales, a heterocercal tail, paired fins without an axis, fulcra on the fins, and a bony skeleton, with the vertebræ convex in front and concave behind, forming a ball and socket joint. See Ganoidel.

ginglymoidal.c: Ginglymoidal Ginglymoid { Gin"gly*moid (?), Gin`gly*moid"al (?), } a. [Gr.?;? ginglymus + e'i^dos form: cf. F. ginglymoide, ginglymoïdal.] (Anat.) Pertaining to, or resembling, a ginglymus, or hinge joint; ginglyform.

ginglymus.c: Ginglymus ‖Gin"gly*mus (?), n.; pl. Ginglymi (#). [NL., fr. Gr.? a hingelike joint, a ball and socket joint.] (Anat.) A hinge joint; an articulation, admitting of flexion and extension, or motion in two directions only, as the elbow and the ankle.

ginhouse.c: Ginhouse Gin"house` (?), n. A building where cotton is ginned.

ginkgo.c: Ginkgo Gink"go (?), n.; pl. Ginkgoes (#). [Chin., silver fruit.] (Bot.) A large ornamental tree (Ginkgo biloba) from China and Japan, belonging to the Yew suborder of Coniferæ. Its leaves are so like those of some maidenhair ferns, that it is also called the maidenhair tree.

ginnee.c: Ginnee Gin"nee (?), n.; pl. Ginn (?). See Jinnee.

ginnet.c: Ginnet Gin"net (?), n. See Genet, a horse.

ginning.c: Ginning Gin"ning (?), n. [See Gin, v. i.] Beginning. [Obs.] Chaucer.

ginnycarriage.c: Ginny-carriage Gin"ny-car`riage (?), n. A small, strong carriage for conveying materials on a railroad. [Eng.]

ginseng.c: Ginseng Gin"seng (?), n. [Chinese.] (Bot.) A plant of the genus Aralia, the root of which is highly valued as a medicine among the Chinese. The Chinese plant (Aralia Schinseng) has become so rare that the American (A. quinquefolia) has largely taken its place, and its root is now an article of export from America to China. The root, when dry, is of a yellowish white color, with a sweetness in the taste somewhat resembling that of licorice, combined with a slight aromatic bitterness.

ginshop.c: Ginshop Gin"shop` (?), n. A shop or barroom where gin is sold as a beverage. [Colloq.]

gip.c: Gip Gip (?), v. t. To take out the entrails of (herrings).
Gip Gip, n. A servant. See Gyp. Sir W. Scott.

gipoun.c: Gipoun Gi*poun" (?), n. [See Jupon.] A short cassock. [Written also gepoun, gypoun, jupon, juppon.] [Obs.]

gipsire.c: Gipsire Gipser { Gip"ser (?), Gip"sire (?), } n. [F. gibecière a game pouch or game pocket. Cf. Gibbier.] A kind of pouch formerly worn at the girdle. Ld. Lytton.

giraffe.c: giraffe gi*raffe" (jĭ*răf"; 277), n. [F. girafe, Sp. girafa, from Ar. zurāfa, zarāfa.] (Zool.) An African ruminant (Giraffa camelopardalis formerly Camelopardalis giraffa) related to the deers and antelopes, but placed in a family (Giraffidae) by itself; the camelopard. It is the tallest of quadriped animals, being sometimes twenty feet from the hoofs to the top of the head. Its neck is very long, and its fore legs are much longer than its hind legs. There are three types, having different patterns of spots on the pelt and different territories: the Reticulated Giraffe, the Masai Giraffe, and the Uganda Giraffe. Intermediate crosses are also observed.

girandole.c: girandole girandola gir"an*do`la, gir"an*dole (jĭr"ain*dōl; 277), n. [F. See Gyrate.] 1. An ornate ornamental branched candlestick, often with a mirror at the back. [wns=1]

girasol.c: Girasol Girasole { Gir"a*sole Gir"a*sol } (?), n. [It. girasole, or F. girasol, fr. L. gyrare to turn around + sol sun.]

gird.c: Gird Gird, v. t. [See Gird, n., and cf. Girde, v.]
Gird Gird, v. i. To gibe; to sneer; to break a scornful jest; to utter severe sarcasms.

Gird Gird (gẽrd), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Girt (?) or Girded; p. pr. & vb. n. Girding.] [OE. girden, gurden, AS. gyrdan; akin to OS. gurdian, D. gorden, OHG. gurten, G. gürten, Icel. gyrða, Sw. gjorda, Dan. giorde, Goth. bigaírdan to begird, and prob. to E. yard an inclosure. Cf. Girth, n. & v., Girt, v. t.] 1. To encircle or bind with any flexible band.

girder.c: Girder Gird"er (?), n. [From Gird to sneer at.] One who girds; a satirist.

girding.c: Girding Gird"ing, n. That with which one is girded; a girdle.

girdle.c: Girdle Gir"dle (?), n. A griddle. [Scot. & Prov. Eng.]
Girdle Gir"dle, n. [OE. gurdel, girdel, AS. gyrdel, fr. gyrdan; akin to D. gordel, G. gürtel, Icel. gyr?ill. See Gird, v. t., to encircle, and cf. Girth, n.]
Girdle Gir"dle, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Girdled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Girdling (?).] 1. To bind with a belt or sash; to gird. Shak.

girl.c: Girl Girl (gẽrl), n. [OE. girle, gerle, gurle, a girl (in sense 1): cf. LG. gör child.]

girlhood.c: Girlhood Girl"hood (?), n. State or time of being a girl.

girlish.c: Girlish Girl"ish, a. Like, or characteristic of, a girl; of or pertaining to girlhood; innocent; artless; immature; weak; as, girlish ways; girlish grief. -- Girl"ish*ly, adv. -- Girl"ish*ness, n.

girlond.c: Girlond Gir"lond (?), n. [See Garland, n.] A garland; a prize. [Obs.] Chapman.

girn.c: Girn Girn (?), v. i. [See Grin, n.] To grin. [Obs.]

girondist.c: Girondist Gi*ron"dist (?), n. [F. Girondiste.] A member of the moderate republican party formed in the French legislative assembly in 1791. The Girondists were so called because their leaders were deputies from the department of La Gironde.
Girondist Gi*ron"dist, a. Of or pertaining to the Girondists. [Written also Girondin.]

girrock.c: Girrock Gir"rock (?), n. [Cf. Prov. F. chicarou.] (Zool.) A garfish. Johnson.

girt.c: Girt Girt (gẽrt), imp. & p. p. of Gird.
Girt Girt, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Girted; p. pr. & vb. n. Girting.] [From Girt, n., cf. Girth, v.] To gird; to encircle; to invest by means of a girdle; to measure the girth of; as, to girt a tree.
Girt Girt, a. (Naut.) Bound by a cable; -- used of a vessel so moored by two anchors that she swings against one of the cables by force of the current or tide.

girth.c: Girth Girth (gẽrth), n. [Icel. gjörð girdle, or gerð girth; akin to Goth. gaírda girdle. See Gird to girt, and cf. Girdle, n.] 1. A band or strap which encircles the body; especially, one by which a saddle is fastened upon the back of a horse.
Girth Girth, v. t. [From Girth, n., cf. Girt, v. t.] To bind as with a girth. [R.] Johnson.

gisarm.c: Gisarm Gis*arm" (jĭs*ärm"), n. [OF. gisarme, guisarme.] (Mediæval Armor) A weapon with a scythe-shaped blade, and a separate long sharp point, mounted on a long staff and carried by foot soldiers.

gise.c: Gise Gise (jīz), v. t. [See Agist.] To feed or pasture. [Obs.]

gisle.c: Gisle Gis"le (gĭz"'l), n. [AS. gīsel; akin to G. geisel, Icel. gīsl.] A pledge. [Obs.] Bp. Gibson.

gismondite.c: Gismondite Gismondine { Gis*mon"dine (jĭs*mŏn"dĭn), Gis*mon"dite (jĭs*mŏn"dīt), } n. [From the name of the discoverer, Gismondi.] (Min.) A native hydrated silicate of alumina, lime, and potash, first noticed near Rome.

gist.c: Gist Gist (jĭst), n. [OF. giste abode, lodgings, F. gîte, fr. gésir to lie, L. jacēre, prop., to be thrown, hence, to lie, fr. jacĕre to throw. In the second sense fr. OF. gist, F. gît, 3d pers. sing. ind. of gésir to lie, used in a proverb, F., c'est là que gît le lièvre, it is there that the hare lies, i. e., that is the point, the difficulty. See Jet a shooting forth, and cf. Agist, Joist, n., Gest a stage in traveling.] 1. A resting place. [Obs.]

gitano.c: Gitano Gitana { ‖Gi*ta"na (?), n. fem.; ‖Gi*ta"no (?), n. masc. } [Sp., fr. (assumed) LL. Aegyptanus, fem. Aegyptana, Egyptian. Cf. Gypsy.] A Spanish gypsy.

gith.c: Gith Gith (gĭth), n. [Prov. E., corn cockle; cf. W. gith corn cockle.] (Bot.) The corn cockle; also anciently applied to the Nigella, or fennel flower.

gittern.c: Gittern Git"tern (gĭt"tẽrn), n. [OE. giterne, OF. guiterne, ultimately from same source as E. guitar. See Guitar, and cf. Cittern.] An instrument like a guitar. “Harps, lutes, and giternes.” Chaucer.
Gittern Git"tern, v. i. To play on gittern. Milton.

gittith.c: Gittith Git"tith (gĭt"tĭth), n. [Heb.] A musical instrument, of unknown character, supposed by some to have been used by the people of Gath, and thence obtained by David. It is mentioned in the title of Psalms viii., lxxxi., and lxxxiv. Dr. W. Smith.

giust.c: Giust Giust (jüst), n. [Obs.] Same as Joust. Spenser.

giusto.c: Giusto ‖Gius"to (jōos"to), a. [It., fr. L. justus. See Just, a.] (Mus.) In just, correct, or suitable time.

give.c: Give Give (gĭv), v. t. [imp. Gave (gāv); p. p. Given (gĭv"'n); p. pr. & vb. n. Giving.] [OE. given, yiven, yeven, AS. gifan, giefan; akin to D. geven, OS. geðan, OHG. geban, G. geben, Icel. gefa, Sw. gifva, Dan. give, Goth. giban. Cf. Gift, n.] 1. To bestow without receiving a return; to confer without compensation; to impart, as a possession; to grant, as authority or permission; to yield up or allow.
Give Give (?), v. i. 1. To give a gift or gifts.

given.c: Given Giv"en (?), p. p. & a. from Give, v.

giver.c: Giver Giv"er (?), n. One who gives; a donor; a bestower; a grantor; one who imparts or distributes.

gives.c: Gives Gives (?), n. pl. [See Give, n.] Fetters.

giving.c: Giving Giv"ing (?), n. 1. The act of bestowing as a gift; a conferring or imparting.

gizzard.c: Gizzard Giz"zard (?), n. [F. gésier, L. gigeria, pl., the cooked entrails of poultry. Cf. Gigerium.]

glabella.c: Glabella ‖Gla*bel"la (?), n.; pl. Glabellæ (#). [NL., fr. L. glabellus hairless, fr. glaber bald.] (Anat.) The space between the eyebrows, also including the corresponding part of the frontal bone; the mesophryon. -- Gla*bel"lar (#), a.

glabellum.c: Glabellum ‖Gla*bel"lum (?), n.; pl. Glabella (#). [NL. See Glabella.] (Zool.) The median, convex lobe of the head of a trilobite. See Trilobite.

glabrate.c: Glabrate Gla"brate (?), a. [L. glabrare, fr. glaber smooth.] (Bot.) Becoming smooth or glabrous from age. Gray.

glabriate.c: Glabriate Glabreate { Gla"bre*ate (?), Gla"bri*ate (?), } v. t. [See Glabrate.] To make smooth, plain, or bare. [Obs.]

glabrous.c: Glabrous Gla"brous (?), a. [L. glaber; cf. Gr.? hollow, smooth,? to hollow.] Smooth; having a surface without hairs or any unevenness.

glace.c: glace Gla`cé" (?), a. [F., p.p. of glacer to freeze, to ice. Cf. Glacier.] Smoothly coated with icing or crystals of sugar; iced; glazed; -- said of fruits, sweetmeats, cake, etc.

glacial.c: Glacial Gla"cial (?), a. [L. glacialis, from glacies ice: cf. F. glacial.] 1. Pertaining to ice or to its action; consisting of ice; frozen; icy; esp., pertaining to glaciers; as, glacial phenomena. Lyell.

glacialist.c: Glacialist Gla"cial*ist, n. One who attributes the phenomena of the drift, in geology, to glaciers.

glaciate.c: Glaciate Gla"ci*ate (?), v. i. [L. glaciatus, p. p. of glaciare to freeze, fr. glacies ice.] To turn to ice.
Glaciate Gla"ci*ate, v. t. 1. To convert into, or cover with, ice.

glacier.c: Glacier Gla"cier (?), n. [F. glacier, fr. glace ice, L. glacies.] An immense field or stream of ice, formed in the region of perpetual snow, and moving slowly down a mountain slope or valley, as in the Alps, or over an extended area, as in Greenland.

glacious.c: Glacious Gla"cious (?), a. Pertaining to, consisting of or resembling, ice; icy. Sir T. Browne.

glacis.c: Glacis Gla"cis (?), n. [F. glacis; -- so named from its smoothness. See Glacier.] A gentle slope, or a smooth, gently sloping bank; especially (Fort.), that slope of earth which inclines from the covered way toward the exterior ground or country (see Illust. of Ravelin).

glad.c: Glad Glad (glăd), a. [Compar. Gladder (?); superl. Gladdest (?).] [AS. glæd bright, glad; akin to D. glad smooth, G. glatt, OHG. glat smooth, shining, Icel. glaðr glad, bright, Dan. & Sw. glad glad, Lith. glodas smooth, and prob. to L. glaber, and E. glide. Cf. Glabrous.]
Glad Glad, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gladded; p. pr. & vb. n. Gladding.] [AS. gladian. See Glad, a., and cf. Gladden, v. t.] To make glad; to cheer; to gladden; to exhilarate. Chaucer.
Glad Glad, v. i. To be glad; to rejoice. [Obs.] Massinger.

gladden.c: Gladden Glad"den (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gladdened (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gladdening (?).] [See Glad, v. t.] To make glad; to cheer; to please; to gratify; to rejoice; to exhilarate.
Gladden Glad"den, v. i. To be or become glad; to rejoice.

gladder.c: Gladder Glad"der (?), n. One who makes glad. Chaucer.

glade.c: Glade Glade (?), n. [Prob. of Scand. origin, and akin to glad, a.; cf. also W. golead, goleuad, a lighting, illumination, fr. goleu light, clear, bright, goleu fwlch glade, lit., a light or clear defile.]

gladen.c: Gladen Gla"den (?), n. [AS. glædene, cf. L. gladius a sword. Cf. Gladiole.] (Bot.) Sword grass; any plant with sword-shaped leaves, especially the European Iris fœtidissima. [Written also gladwyn, gladdon, and glader.]

gladful.c: Gladful Glad"ful (?), a. Full of gladness; joyful; glad. [R.] -- Glad"ful*ness, n. [R.] Spenser.

gladiate.c: Gladiate Glad"i*ate (?), a. [L. gladius sword.] (Bot.) Sword-shaped; resembling a sword in form, as the leaf of the iris, or of the gladiolus.

gladiator.c: Gladiator Glad"i*a`tor (?), n. [L., fr. gladius sword. See Glaive.] 1. Originally, a swordplayer; hence, one who fought with weapons in public, either on the occasion of a funeral ceremony, or in the arena, for public amusement.

gladiatorian.c: Gladiatorian Gladiatorial { Glad`i*a*to"ri*al (?), Glad`i*a*to"ri*an (?), } a. Of or pertaining to gladiators, or to contests or combatants in general.

gladiatorism.c: Gladiatorism Glad"i*a`tor*ism (?), n. The art or practice of a gladiator.

gladiatorship.c: Gladiatorship Glad"i*a`tor*ship, n. Conduct, state, or art, of a gladiator.

gladiature.c: Gladiature Glad"i*a*ture (?), n. [L. gladiatura.] Swordplay; fencing; gladiatorial contest. Gayton.

gladiole.c: Gladiole Glad"i*ole (?), n. [L. gladiolus a small sword, the sword lily, dim. of gladius sword. See Glaive.] (Bot.) A lilylike plant, of the genus Gladiolus; -- called also corn flag.

gladiolus.c: Gladiolus Gla*di"o*lus (?), n.; pl. L. Gladioli (#), E. Gladioluses (#). [L. See Gladiole.]

gladius.c: Gladius ‖Gla"di*us (?), n.; pl. Gladii (#). [L., a sword.] (Zool.) The internal shell, or pen, of cephalopods like the squids.

gladness.c: Gladness Glad"ness (?), n. [AS. glædnes.] State or quality of being glad; pleasure; joyful satisfaction; cheerfulness.

gladship.c: Gladship Glad"ship, n. [AS. glædscipe.] A state of gladness. [Obs.] Gower.

gladstone.c: Gladstone Glad"stone (?), n. [Named after Wm. E. Gladstone.] A four-wheeled pleasure carriage with two inside seats, calash top, and seats for driver and footman.

glair.c: Glair Glair (?), n. [F. glaire, glaire d'?uf, the glair of an egg, prob. fr. L. clarus clear, bright. See Clear, a.]
Glair Glair, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Glaired (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Glairing.] To smear with the white of an egg.

glaireous.c: Glaireous Glair"e*ous (?), a. Glairy; covered with glair.

glairin.c: Glairin Glair"in (?), n. A glairy viscous substance, which forms on the surface of certain mineral waters, or covers the sides of their inclosures; -- called also baregin.

glairy.c: Glairy Glair"y (?), a. Like glair, or partaking of its qualities; covered with glair; viscous and transparent; slimy. Wiseman.

glaive.c: Glaive Glaive (?), n. [F. glaive, L. gladius; prob. akin to E. claymore. Cf. Gladiator.] 1. A weapon formerly used, consisting of a large blade fixed on the end of a pole, whose edge was on the outside curve; also, a light lance with a long sharp-pointed head. Wilhelm.

glama.c: Glama ‖Gla"ma (?), n. [NL.; cf. Gr.?, L. gramiae, Gr.? blear-eyed.] (Med.) A copious gummy secretion of the humor of the eyelids, in consequence of some disorder; blearedness; lippitude.

glamour.c: Glamour Gla"mour (?), n. [Scot. glamour, glamer; cf. Icel. glámeggdr one who is troubled with the glaucoma (?); or Icel. glām-sȳni weakness of sight, glamour; glāmr name of the moon, also of a ghost + sȳni sight, akin to E. see. Perh., however, a corruption of E. gramarye.]

glance.c: Glance Glance (?), n. [Akin to D. glans luster, brightness, G. glanz, Sw. glans, D. glands brightness, glimpse. Cf. Gleen, Glint, Glitter, and Glance a mineral.]
Glance Glance, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Glanced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Glancing (?).] 1. To shoot or emit a flash of light; to shine; to flash.
Glance Glance (?), v. t. 1. To shoot or dart suddenly or obliquely; to cast for a moment; as, to glance the eye.

glancingly.c: Glancingly Glan"cing*ly, adv. In a glancing manner; transiently; incidentally; indirectly. Hakewill.

gland.c: Gland Gland (?), n. [F. glande, L. glans, glandis, acorn; akin to Gr.? for?, and? to cast, throw, the acorn being the dropped fruit. Cf. Parable, n.]

glandage.c: Glandage Glan"dage (?), n. [Cf. OF. glandage. See Gland.] A feeding on nuts or mast. [Obs.] Crabb.

glandered.c: Glandered Glan"dered (?), a. Affected with glanders; as, a glandered horse. Yu?att.

glanderous.c: Glanderous Glan"der*ous (?), a. Of or pertaining to glanders; of the nature of glanders. Youatt.

glanders.c: Glanders Glan"ders (?), n. [From Gland.] (Far.) A highly contagious and very destructive disease of horses, asses, mules, etc., characterized by a constant discharge of sticky matter from the nose, and an enlargement and induration of the glands beneath and within the lower jaw. It may transmitted to dogs, goats, sheep, and to human beings.

glandiferous.c: Glandiferous Glan*dif"er*ous (?), a. [L. glandifer; glans, glandis, acorn + ferre to bear; cf. F. glandifère.] Bearing acorns or other nuts; as, glandiferous trees.

glandiform.c: Glandiform Gland"i*form (?), a. [L. glans, glandis, acorn + -form: cf. F. glandiforme.] Having the form of a gland or nut; resembling a gland.

glandular.c: Glandular Glan"du*lar (?), a. [Cf. F. glandulaire. See Glandule.] Containing or supporting glands; consisting of glands; pertaining to glands.

glandulation.c: Glandulation Glan`du*la"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. glandulation.] (Bot.) The situation and structure of the secretory vessels in plants. Martyn.

glandule.c: Glandule Glan"dule (?), n. [L. glandula, dim. of glans, glandis, acorn: cf. F. glandule. See Gland.] A small gland or secreting vessel.

glanduliferous.c: Glanduliferous Glan`du*lif"er*ous (?), a. [L. glandula gland + -ferous; cf. F. glandulifère.] Bearing glandules.

glandulosity.c: Glandulosity Glan`du*los"i*ty (?), n. Quality of being glandulous; a collection of glands. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

glandulous.c: Glandulous Glan"du*lous (?), a. [L. glandulosus: cf. F. glanduleux.] Containing glands; consisting of glands; pertaining to glands; resembling glands.

glare.c: Glare Glare (glâr), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Glared (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Glaring.] [OE. glaren, gloren; cf. AS. glær amber, LG. glaren to glow or burn like coals, D. gloren to glimmer; prob. akin to E. glass.]
Glare Glare, v. t. To shoot out, or emit, as a dazzling light.
Glare Glare, n. 1. A bright, dazzling light; splendor that dazzles the eyes; a confusing and bewildering light.
Glare Glare, a. [See Glary, and Glare, n.] Smooth and bright or translucent; -- used almost exclusively of ice; as, skating on glare ice. [U. S.]

glareous.c: Glareous Glar"e*ous (glâr"e*ŭs), a. [Cf. F. glaireux. See Glair.] Glairy. John Gregory (1766).

glaringness.c: Glaringness Glariness { Glar"i*ness (?), Glar"ing*ness, } n. A dazzling luster or brilliancy.

glaring.c: Glaring Glar"ing, a. Clear; notorious; open and bold; barefaced; as, a glaring crime. -- Glar"ing*ly, adv.

glary.c: Glary Glar"y (?), a. Of a dazzling luster; glaring; bright; shining; smooth.

glass.c: Glass Glass (glȧs), n. [OE. glas, gles, AS. glæs; akin to D., G., Dan., & Sw. glas, Icel. glas, gler, Dan. glar; cf. AS. glær amber, L. glaesum. Cf. Glare, n., Glaze, v. t.]
Glass Glass, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Glassed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Glassing.] 1. To reflect, as in a mirror; to mirror; -- used reflexively.

glasscrab.c: Glass-crab Glass"-crab` (?), n. (Zool.) The larval state (Phyllosoma) of the genus Palinurus and allied genera. It is remarkable for its strange outlines, thinness, and transparency. See Phyllosoma.

glasseye.c: Glasseye Glass"eye` (?), n. 1. (Zool.) A fish of the great lakes; the wall-eyed pike.

glassfaced.c: Glass-faced Glass"-faced` (?), a. Mirror-faced; reflecting the sentiments of another. [R.] “The glass-faced flatterer.” Shak.

glassful.c: Glassful Glass"ful (?), n.; pl. Glassfuls (?). The contents of a glass; as much of anything as a glass will hold.
Glassful Glass"ful, a. Glassy; shining like glass. [Obs.] “Minerva's glassful shield.” Marston.

glassgazing.c: Glass-gazing Glass"-gaz`ing (?), a. Given to viewing one's self in a glass or mirror; finical. [Poetic] Shak.

glasshouse.c: Glasshouse Glass"house` (?), n. A house where glass is made; a commercial house that deals in glassware.

glassily.c: Glassily Glass"i*ly (?), adv. So as to resemble glass.

glassiness.c: Glassiness Glass"i*ness, n. The quality of being glassy.

glassite.c: Glassite Glass"ite (?), n. A member of a Scottish sect, founded in the 18th century by John Glass, a minister of the Established Church of Scotland, who taught that justifying faith is “no more than a simple assent to the divine testimone passively recived by the understanding.” The English and American adherents of this faith are called Sandemanians, after Robert Sandeman, the son-in-law and disciple of Glass.

glassmaker.c: Glassmaker Glass maker Glass" mak`er (?), or Glass"mak`er, n. One who makes, or manufactures, glass. -- Glass" mak`ing, or Glass"mak`ing, n.

glassrope.c: Glass-rope Glass"-rope` (?), n. (Zool.) A remarkable vitreous sponge, of the genus Hyalonema, first brought from Japan. It has a long stem, consisting of a bundle of long and large, glassy, siliceous fibers, twisted together.

glasssnail.c: Glass-snail Glass"-snail` (?), n. (Zool.) A small, transparent, land snail, of the genus Vitrina.

glasssnake.c: Glass-snake Glass"-snake` (?), n. (Zool.) A long, footless lizard (Ophiosaurus ventralis), of the Southern United States; -- so called from its fragility, the tail easily breaking into small pieces. It grows to the length of three feet. The name is applied also to similar species found in the Old World.

glasssponge.c: Glass-sponge Glass"-sponge` (?), n. (Zool.) A siliceous sponge, of the genus Hyalonema, and allied genera; -- so called from their glassy fibers or spicules; -- called also vitreous sponge. See Glass-rope, and Euplectella.

glassware.c: Glassware Glass"ware (?), n. Ware, or articles collectively, made of glass.

glasswork.c: Glasswork Glass"work` (?), n. Manufacture of glass; articles or ornamentation made of glass.

glasswort.c: Glasswort Glass"wort` (?), n. (Bot.) A seashore plant of the Spinach family (Salicornia herbacea), with succulent jointed stems; also, a prickly plant of the same family (Salsola Kali), both formerly burned for the sake of the ashes, which yield soda for making glass and soap.

glassy.c: Glassy Glass"y (?), a. 1. Made of glass; vitreous; as, a glassy substance. Bacon.

glastonbury.c: Glastonbury thorn Glas"ton*bur*y thorn` (?). (Bot.) A variety of the common hawthorn. Loudon.

glauberite.c: Glauberite Glau"ber*ite (?), n. [From Glauber, a German chemist, died 1668: cf. F. glaubérite, G. glauberit.] (Min.) A mineral, consisting of the sulphates of soda and lime.

glaubers.c: Glauber's salts Glauber's salt Glau"ber's salt` (?) or Glau"ber's salts` (?). [G. glaubersalz, from Glauber, a German chemist who discovered it. See Glauberite.] Sulphate of soda, a well-known cathartic. It is a white crystalline substance, with a cooling, slightly bitter taste, and is commonly called “salts.”

glaucescent.c: Glaucescent Glau*ces"cent (?), a. [See Glaucous.] Having a somewhat glaucous appearance or nature; becoming glaucous.

glaucic.c: Glaucic Glau"cic (?), a. (Chem.) Of or pertaining to the Glaucium flavum or horned poppy; -- formerly applied to an acid derived from it, now known to be fumaric acid.

glaucine.c: Glaucine Glau"cine (?), n. (Chem.) An alkaloid obtained from the plant Glaucium flavum, as a bitter, white, crystalline substance.

glaucodot.c: Glaucodot Glau"co*dot (?), n. [Gr. glayko`s silvery, gray + dido`nai to give.] (Min.) A metallic mineral having a grayish tin-white color, and containing cobalt and iron, with sulphur and arsenic.

glaucoma.c: Glaucoma ‖Glau*co"ma (?), n. [L., fr. Gr. glay`kwma, fr. glayko`s light gray, blue gray.] (Med.) Dimness or abolition of sight, with a diminution of transparency, a bluish or greenish tinge of the refracting media of the eye, and a hard inelastic condition of the eyeball, with marked increase of tension within the eyeball.

glaucomatous.c: Glaucomatous Glau*co"ma*tous (?), a. Having the nature of glaucoma.

glauconite.c: Glauconite Glau"co*nite (?), n. [Cf. F. glauconite, glauconie, fr. L. glaucus. See Glaucous.] (Min.) The green mineral characteristic of the greensand of the chalk and other formations. It is a hydrous silicate of iron and potash. See Greensand.

glaucophane.c: Glaucophane Glau"co*phane (?), n. [Gr. glayko`s silvery, gray + fai`nesqai to appear.] (Min.) A mineral of a dark bluish color, related to amphibole. It is characteristic of certain crystalline rocks.

glaucosis.c: Glaucosis ‖Glau*co"sis (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr. glay`kwsis.] (Med.) Same as Glaucoma.

glaucous.c: Glaucous Glau"cous (glä"kŭs), a. [L. glaucus, Gr. glayko`s.] 1. Of a sea-green color; of a dull green passing into grayish blue. Lindley.

glaucus.c: Glaucus ‖Glau"cus (?), n. [L., sea green.] (Zool.) A genus of nudibranchiate mollusks, found in the warmer latitudes, swimming in the open sea. These mollusks are beautifully colored with blue and silvery white.

glaum.c: Glaum Glaum (?), v. i. [Etymol. uncertain.] To grope with the hands, as in the dark. [Scot.]

glaver.c: Glaver Glav"er (?), v. i. [Of Celtic origin; cf. W. glafr flattery.] 1. To prate; to jabber; to babble. [Obs.]

glaverer.c: Glaverer Glav"er*er (?), n. A flatterer. [Obs.] Mir. for Mag.

glaze.c: Glaze Glaze (glāz), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Glazed (glāzd); p. pr. & vb. n. Glazing.] [OE. glasen, glazen, fr. glas. See Glass.]
Glaze Glaze, v. i. To become glazed of glassy.
Glaze Glaze, n. 1. The vitreous coating of pottery or porcelain; anything used as a coating or color in glazing. See Glaze, v. t., 3. Ure.

glazen.c: Glazen Glaz"en (?), a. [AS. glæsen.] Resembling glass; glasslike; glazed. [Obs.] Wyclif.

glazer.c: Glazer Glaz"er (?), n. 1. One who applies glazing, as in pottery manufacture, etc.; one who gives a glasslike or glossy surface to anything; a calenderer or smoother of cloth, paper, and the like.

glazier.c: Glazier Gla"zier (?), n. [From Glaze.] One whose business is to set glass.

glazing.c: Glazing Glaz"ing (?), n. 1. The act or art of setting glass; the art of covering with a vitreous or glasslike substance, or of polishing or rendering glossy.

glazy.c: Glazy Glaz"y (?), a. Having a glazed appearance; -- said of the fractured surface of some kinds of pin iron.

glead.c: Glead Glead (?), n. A live coal. See Gleed. [Archaic]

gleam.c: Gleam Gleam (?), v. i. [Cf. OE. glem birdlime, glue, phlegm, and E. englaimed.] (Falconry) To disgorge filth, as a hawk.
Gleam Gleam, n. [OE. glem, gleam, AS. glæm, prob. akin to E. glimmer, and perh. to Gr.? warm,? to warm. Cf. Glitter.]
Gleam Gleam, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gleamed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gleaming.] 1. To shoot, or dart, as rays of light; as, at the dawn, light gleams in the east.
Gleam Gleam, v. t. To shoot out (flashes of light, etc.).

gleamy.c: Gleamy Gleam"y, a. Darting beams of light; casting light in rays; flashing; coruscating.

glean.c: Glean Glean (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gleaned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gleaning.] [OE. glenen, OF. glener, glaner, F. glaner, fr. LL. glenare; cf. W. glan clean, glanh?u to clean, purify, or AS. gelm, gilm, a hand?ul.]
Glean Glean, v. i. 1. To gather stalks or ears of grain left by reapers.
Glean Glean, n. A collection made by gleaning.

gleaner.c: Gleaner Glean"er (?), n. 1. One who gathers after reapers.

gleaning.c: Gleaning Glean"ing, n. The act of gathering after reapers; that which is collected by gleaning.

gleba.c: Gleba Gle"ba (?), n.; pl. Glebæ (#). [L., a clod.] (Bot.) The chambered sporogenous tissue forming the central mass of the sporophore in puff balls, stinkhorns, etc.

glebe.c: Glebe Glebe (?), n. [F. glèbe, L. gleba, glaeba, clod, land, soil.] 1. A lump; a clod.

glebosity.c: Glebosity Gle*bos"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being glebous. [R.]

gleby.c: Gleby Glebous { Gleb"ous (?), Gleb"y (?), } a. [Cf. L. glaebosus cloddy.] Pertaining to the glebe; turfy; cloddy; fertile; fruitful. “Gleby land.” Prior.

glede.c: Glede Glede (glēd), n. [AS. glida, akin to Icel. gleða, Sw. glada. Cf. Glide, v. i.] (Zool.) The common European kite (Milvus ictinus). This name is also sometimes applied to the buzzard. [Written also glead, gled, gleed, glade, and glide.]
Glede Glede, n. [See Gleed.] A live coal. [Archaic]

glee.c: Glee Glee (glē), n. [OE. gle, gleo, AS. gleów, gleó, akin to Icel. glȳ: cf. Gr.? joke, jest.]
Glee club Glee club. A club or company organized for singing glees, and (by extension) part songs, ballads, etc.

gleed.c: Gleed Gleed (glēd), n. [AS. glēd, fr. glōwan to glow as a fire; akin to D. gloed, G. glut, Icel. glōð. See Glow, v. i.] A live or glowing coal; a glede. [Archaic] Chaucer. Longfellow.

gleeful.c: Gleeful Glee"ful (?), a. Merry; gay; joyous. Shak.

gleek.c: Gleek Gleek (?), n. [Prob. fr. Icel. leika to play, play a trick on, with the prefix ge-; akin to AS. gelācan, Sw. leka to play, Dan. lege.]
Gleek Gleek, v. i. To make sport; to gibe; to sneer; to spend time idly. [Obs.] Shak.
Gleek Gleek, n. [OF. glic, G. glück, fortune. See Luck.]

gleeman.c: Gleeman Glee"man (?), n.; pl. Gleemen (#). [Glee + man; AS. gleóman.] A name anciently given to an itinerant minstrel or musician.

gleen.c: Gleen Gleen (?), v. i. [Cf. Glance, Glint.] To glisten; to gleam. [Obs.] Prior.

gleet.c: Gleet Gleet (?), n. [OE. glette, glet, glat, mucus, pus, filth, OF. glete.] (Med.) A transparent mucous discharge from the membrane of the urethra, commonly an effect of gonorrhea. Hoblyn.
Gleet Gleet, v. i. 1. To flow in a thin, limpid humor; to ooze, as gleet. Wiseman.

gleety.c: Gleety Gleet"y (?), a. Ichorous; thin; limpid. Wiseman.

gleg.c: Gleg Gleg (?), a. [Icel. glöggr.] Quick of perception; alert; sharp. [Scot.] Jamieson.

gleyre.c: Gleyre Gleire Gleire (?), Gleyre, n. See Glair. [Obs.] Chaucer.

glen.c: Glen Glen (?), n. [Of Celtic origin; cf. W. glyn a deep valley, Ir. & Gael. gleann valley, glen.] A secluded and narrow valley; a dale; a depression between hills.

glengarry.c: Glengarry bonnet Glengarry { Glen*gar"ry (?), n., or Glen*gar"ry bon"net (?) }. [Name of a valley in Scotland.] A kind of Highland Scotch cap for men, with straight sides and a hollow top sloping to the back, where it is parted and held together by ribbons or strings.

glenlivet.c: Glenlivet Glenlivat { Glen*liv"at (?), Glen*liv"et (?), } n. A kind of Scotch whisky, named from the district in which it was first made. W. E. Aytoun.

glenoid.c: Glenoid Gle"noid (?), a. [Gr.?;? socket of a joint + e'i^dos form; cf. F. glénoïde.] (Anat.) Having the form of a smooth and shallow depression; socketlike; -- applied to several articular surfaces of bone; as, the glenoid cavity, or fossa, of the scapula, in which the head of the humerus articulates.

gleucometer.c: Gleucometer Gleu*com"e*ter (?), n. [Gr.? must + -meter: cf. F. gleucomètre.] An instrument for measuring the specific gravity and ascertaining the quantity of sugar contained in must.

gley.c: Gley Gley (?), v. i. [OE. gliȝen, glien, gleien, to shine, to squint; cf. Icel. gljā to glitter.] To squint; to look obliquely; to overlook things. [Scot.] Jamieson.

gliadin.c: Gliadin Gli"a*din (?), n. [Gr.? glue: cf. F. gliadine.] (Chem.) Vegetable glue or gelatin; glutin. It is one of the constituents of wheat gluten, and is a tough, amorphous substance, which resembles animal glue or gelatin.

glib.c: Glib Glib (glĭb), a. [Compar. Glibber (glĭb"bẽr); superl. Glibbest (glĭb"bĕst).] [Prob. fr. D. glibberen, glippen, to slide, glibberig, glipperig, glib, slippery.]
Glib Glib, v. t. To make glib. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
Glib Glib, n. [Ir. & Gael. glib a lock of hair.] A thick lock of hair, hanging over the eyes. [Obs.]
Glib Glib, v. t. [Cf. O. & Prov. E. lib to castrate, geld, Prov. Dan. live, LG. & OD. lubben.] To castrate; to geld; to emasculate. [Obs.] Shak.

glibly.c: Glibly Glib"ly, adv. In a glib manner; as, to speak glibly.

glibness.c: Glibness Glib"ness, n. The quality of being glib.

glicke.c: Glicke Glicke (?), n. [Cf. Gleek, n., 2, and Ir. & Gael. glic wise, cunning, crafty.] An ogling look. [Obs.]

glidden.c: Glidden Glid"den (?), obs. p. p. of Glide. Chaucer.

gliddery.c: Gliddery Glidder { Glid"der (?), Glid"der*y (?), } a. [Cf. Glide.] Giving no sure footing; smooth; slippery. [Prov. Eng.]

glide.c: Glide Glide (?), n. (Zool.) The glede or kite.
Glide Glide, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Glided; p. pr. & vb. n. Gliding.] [AS. glīdan; akin to D. glijden, OHG. glītan, G. gleiten, Sw. glida, Dan. glide, and prob. to E. glad.]
Glide Glide, n. 1. The act or manner of moving smoothly, swiftly, and without labor or obstruction.

gliden.c: Gliden Glid"en (?), obs. p. p. of Glide. Chaucer.

glider.c: Glider Glid"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, glides.

gliding.c: Gliding angle Gliding angle. (Aëronautics) The angle, esp. the least angle, at which a gliding machine or aëroplane will glide to earth by virtue of gravity without applied power.
Gliding machine Gliding machine. (Aëronautics) A construction consisting essentially of one or more aëroplanes for gliding in an inclined path from a height to the ground.

glidingly.c: Glidingly Glid"ing*ly, adv. In a gliding manner.

gliff.c: Gliff Gliff (?), n. [Cf. OE. gliffen, gliften, to look with fear at.] 1. A transient glance; an unexpected view of something that startles one; a sudden fear. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.] Halliwell.

glike.c: Glike Glike (?), n. [See Gleek a jest.] A sneer; a flout. [Obs.]

glimmer.c: Glimmer Glim"mer (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Glimmered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Glimmering.] [Akin to G. glimmer a faint, trembling light, mica, glimmern to glimmer, glimmen to shine faintly, glow, Sw. glimma, Dan. glimre, D. glimmen, glimpen. See Gleam a ray, and cf. Glimpse.] To give feeble or scattered rays of light; to shine faintly; to show a faint, unsteady light; as, the glimmering dawn; a glimmering lamp.
Glimmer Glim"mer, n. 1. A faint, unsteady light; feeble, scattered rays of light; also, a gleam.

glimmering.c: Glimmering Glim"mer*ing, n. 1. Faint, unsteady light; a glimmer. South.

glimpse.c: Glimpse Glimpse (?), n. [For glimse, from the root of glimmer.]
Glimpse Glimpse (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Glimpsed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Glimpsing.] to appear by glimpses; to catch glimpses. Drayton.
Glimpse Glimpse, v. t. To catch a glimpse of; to see by glimpses; to have a short or hurried view of.

glint.c: Glint Glint (glĭnt), n. [OE. glent.] A glimpse, glance, or gleam. [Scot.] “He saw a glint of light.” Ramsay.
Glint Glint, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Glinted; p. pr. & vb. n. Glinting.] [OE. glenten. Cf. Glance, v. i., Glitter, v. i.] To glance; to peep forth, as a flower from the bud; to glitter. Burns.
Glint Glint, v. t. To glance; to turn; as, to glint the eye.

glioma.c: Glioma ‖Gli*o"ma (?), n. [NL., fr. Gr.? glue + -oma.] (Med.) A tumor springing from the neuroglia or connective tissue of the brain, spinal cord, or other portions of the nervous system.

glires.c: Glires ‖Gli"res (?), n. pl. [L., dormice.] (Zool.) An order of mammals; the Rodentia. -- Gli"rine (#), a.

glissade.c: Glissade Glis`sade" (?), n. [F., fr. glisser to slip.] 1. A sliding, as down a snow slope. Tyndall.

glissando.c: Glissando Glis*san"do (?), n. & a. [As if It. = Fr. glissant sliding.] (Mus.) A gliding effect; gliding.

glissette.c: Glissette ‖Glis*sette" (?), n. [F., fr. glisser to slip.] (Math.) The locus described by any point attached to a curve that slips continuously on another fixed curve, the movable curve having no rotation at any instant.

glisten.c: Glisten Glis"ten (glĭs"'n), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Glistened (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Glistening (?).] [OE. glistnian, akin to glisnen, glisien, AS. glisian, glisnian, akin to E. glitter. See Glitter, v. i., and cf. Glister, v. i.] To sparkle or shine; especially, to shine with a mild, subdued, and fitful luster; to emit a soft, scintillating light; to gleam; as, the glistening stars.

glister.c: Glister Glis"ter (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Glistered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Glistering.] [OE. glistren; akin to G. glistern,glinstern, D. glinsteren, and E. glisten. See Glisten.] To be bright; to sparkle; to be brilliant; to shine; to glisten; to glitter.
Glister Glis"ter, n. [Cf. OF. glistere.] Same as Clyster.

glisteringly.c: Glisteringly Glis"ter*ing*ly, adv. In a glistering manner.

glitter.c: Glitter Glit"ter (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Glittered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Glittering.] [OE. gliteren; akin to Sw. glittra, Icel. glitra, glita, AS. glitenian, OS. glītan, OHG. glīzzan, G. gleissen, Goth. glitmunjan, and also to E. glint, glisten, and prob. glance, gleam.]
Glitter Glit"ter, n. A bright, sparkling light; brilliant and showy luster; brilliancy; as, the glitter of arms; the glitter of royal equipage. Milton.

glitteringly.c: Glitteringly Glit"ter*ing*ly, adv. In a glittering manner.

gloam.c: Gloam Gloam, n. The twilight; gloaming. [R.] Keats.

gloaming.c: Gloaming Gloam"ing, n. [See Gloom.] 1. Twilight; dusk; the fall of the evening. [Scot. & North of Eng., and in poetry.] Hogg.

gloar.c: Gloar Gloar (?), v. i. [OD. gloeren, glueren, gluyeren. Cf. Glower.] To squint; to stare. [Obs.]

gloat.c: Gloat Gloat (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gloated; p. pr. & vb. n. Gloating.] [Akin to Icel. glotta to smile scornfully, G. glotzen to gloat.] To look steadfastly; to gaze earnestly; to gaze with passionate desire, lust, or avarice.

globard.c: Globard Glo"bard (?), n. [OE. globerde, from glow.] A glowworm. [Obs.] Holland.

globated.c: Globated Globate { Glo"bate (?), Glo"ba*ted (?), } a. [L. globatus, p. p. of globare to make into a ball, fr. globus ball.] Having the form of a globe; spherical.

globe.c: Globe Globe (glōb), n. [L. globus, perh. akin to L. glomus a ball of yarn, and E. clump, golf: cf. F. globe.] 1. A round or spherical body, solid or hollow; a body whose surface is in every part equidistant from the center; a ball; a sphere.
Globe Globe (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Globed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Globing.] To gather or form into a globe.

globefish.c: Globefish Globe"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) A plectognath fish of the genera Diodon, Tetrodon, and allied genera. The globefishes can suck in water or air and distend the body to a more or less globular form. Called also porcupine fish, and sea hedgehog. See Diodon.

globeflower.c: Globeflower Globe"flow`er (?), n. (Bot.) (a) A plant of the genus Trollius (T. Europæus), found in the mountainous parts of Europe, and producing handsome globe-shaped flowers. (b) The American plant Trollius laxus.

globeshaped.c: Globe-shaped Globe"-shaped` (?), a. Shaped like a globe.

globiferous.c: Globiferous Glo*bif"er*ous (?), a. [Globe + -ferous.] (Zool.) Having a round or globular tip.

globigerina.c: Globigerina ‖Glo*big`e*ri"na (?), n.; pl. Globigerinæ (#). [NL., fr. L. globus a round body + gerere to bear.] (Zool.) A genus of small Foraminifera, which live abundantly at or near the surface of the sea. Their dead shells, falling to the bottom, make up a large part of the soft mud, generally found in depths below 3,000 feet, and called globigerina ooze. See Illust. of Foraminifera.

globose.c: Globose Glo*bose" (?), a. [L. globosus.] Having a rounded form resembling that of a globe; globular, or nearly so; spherical. Milton.

globosely.c: Globosely Glo*bose"ly, adv. In a globular manner; globularly.

globosity.c: Globosity Glo*bos"i*ty (?), n. [L. globositas: cf. F. globosité.] Sphericity. Ray.

globular.c: Globular Glob"u*lar (?), a. [Cf. F. globulaire.] Globe-shaped; having the form of a ball or sphere; spherical, or nearly so; as, globular atoms. Milton.

globularity.c: Globularity Glob`u*lar"i*ty (?), n. The state of being globular; globosity; sphericity.

globule.c: Globule Glob"ule (?), n. [L. globulus, dim. of globus globe: cf. F. globule.] 1. A little globe; a small particle of matter, of a spherical form.

globulet.c: Globulet Glob"u*let (?), n. A little globule. Crabb.

globuliferous.c: Globuliferous Glob`u*lif"er*ous (?), a. [Globule + -ferous.] Bearing globules; in geology, used of rocks, and denoting a variety of concretionary structure, where the concretions are isolated globules and evenly distributed through the texture of the rock.

globulimeter.c: Globulimeter Glob`u*lim"e*ter (?), n. [Globule + -meter.] (Physiol.) An instrument for measuring the number of red blood corpuscles in the blood.
