gump.c: Gump Gump (gŭmp), n. [Cf. Sw. & Dan. gump buttocks, rump, Icel. gumpr.] A dolt; a dunce. [Low.] Holloway.

gumption.c: Gumption Gump"tion (?), n. [OE. gom, gome, attention; akin to AS. geómian, gyman, to regard, observe, gyme care, OS. gomean to heed, Goth. gaumjan to see, notice.]

gun.c: Gun Gun (gŭn), n. [OE. gonne, gunne; of uncertain origin; cf. Ir., Gael., & LL. gunna, W. gum; possibly (like cannon) fr. L. canna reed, tube; or abbreviated fr. OF. mangonnel, E. mangonel, a machine for hurling stones.] 1. A weapon which throws or propels a missile to a distance; any firearm or instrument for throwing projectiles, consisting of a tube or barrel closed at one end, in which the projectile is placed, with an explosive charge (such as guncotton or gunpowder) behind, which is ignited by various means. Pistols, rifles, carbines, muskets, and fowling pieces are smaller guns, for hand use, and are called small arms. Larger guns are called cannon, ordnance, fieldpieces, carronades, howitzers, etc. See these terms in the Vocabulary.
Gun Gun (?), v. i. To practice fowling or hunting small game; -- chiefly in participial form; as, to go gunning.

guna.c: Guna ‖Gu"na (gōo"nȧ), n. [Skr. guna quality.] In Sanskrit grammar, a lengthening of the simple vowels a, i, e, by prefixing an a element. The term is sometimes used to denote the same vowel change in other languages.

gunboat.c: Gunboat Gun"boat` (?), n. 1. (Nav.) A vessel of light draught, carrying one or more guns, used for operations in shallow waters.

gunflint.c: Gunflint Gun"flint` (?), n. A sharpened flint for the lock of a gun, to ignite the charge. It was in common use before the introduction of percussion caps.

gunlock.c: Gunlock Gun"lock` (?), n. The mechanism of a gun for producing the discharge. See Lock.

gunnage.c: Gunnage Gun"nage (?), n. The number of guns carried by a ship of war.

gunner.c: Gunner Gun"ner (?), n. 1. One who works a gun or cannon, whether on land, sea, or in the air; a cannoneer.

gunnery.c: Gunnery Gun"ner*y (?), n. That branch of military science which comprehends the theory of projectiles, and the manner of constructing and using ordnance.

gunnie.c: Gunnie Gun"nie (?), n. (Mining.) Space left by the removal of ore.

gunning.c: Gunning Gun"ning (?), n. The act or practice of hunting or shooting game with a gun.

gunny.c: Gunny cloth Gunny Gun"ny (gŭn"ny̆), n., Gun"ny cloth` (klŏth`; 115). [Hind. goṇ, goṇī, a sack, sacking.] A strong, coarse kind of sacking, made from the fibers (called jute) of two plants of the genus Corchorus (C. olitorius and C. capsularis), of India. The fiber is also used in the manufacture of cordage.

gunpowder.c: Gunpowder Gun"pow`der (gŭn"pou`dẽr), n. (Chem.) A black, granular, explosive substance, consisting of an intimate mechanical mixture of saltpeter, charcoal, and sulphur. It is used in gunnery and blasting.

gunreach.c: Gunreach Gun"reach` (gŭn"rēch`), n. The reach or distance to which a gun will shoot; gunshot.

gunroom.c: Gunroom Gun"room` (gŭn"rōom`), n. (Naut.) An apartment on the after end of the lower gun deck of a ship of war, usually occupied as a messroom by the commissioned officers, except the captain; -- called wardroom in the United States navy.

gunshot.c: Gunshot Gun"shot` (gŭn"shŏt), n. 1. Act of firing a gun; a shot.
gunshot gun"shot`, a. Made by the shot of a gun; as, a gunshot wound.

gunsmith.c: Gunsmith Gun"smith (gŭn"smĭth`), n. One whose occupation is to make or repair small firearms; an armorer.

gunsmithing.c: Gunsmithing Gunsmithery { Gun"smith`er*y (gŭn"smĭth`ẽr*y̆), Gun"smith`ing, } n. The art or business of a gunsmith.

gunstick.c: Gunstick Gun"stick (gŭn"stĭk`), n. A stick to ram down the charge of a musket, etc.; a rammer or ramrod. [R.]

gunstock.c: gunstock gun"stock` (gŭn"stŏk`), n. The stock or wood to which the barrel of a hand gun is fastened.

gunstone.c: gunstone gun"stone` (gŭn"stōn`), n. A cannon ball; -- so called because originally made of stone. [Obs.] Shak.

gunter.c: Gunter rig Gun"ter rig` (?). (Naut.) A topmast arranged with metal bands so that it will readily slide up and down the lower mast.

gunters.c: Gunter's chain Gun"ter's chain` (?). (Surveying) The chain ordinarily used in measuring land. See Chain, n., 4, and Gunter's scale.

Gunter's line Gun"ter's line` (?). A logarithmic line on Gunter's scale, used for performing the multiplication and division of numbers mechanically by the dividers; -- called also line of lines, and line of numbers.

Gunter's quadrant Gun"ter's quad`rant (?). A thin quadrant, made of brass, wood, etc., showing a stereographic projection on the plane of the equator. By it are found the hour of the day, the sun's azimuth, the altitude of objects in degrees, etc. See Gunter's scale.

Gunter's scale Gun"ter's scale` (?). A scale invented by the Rev. Edmund Gunter (1581-1626), a professor of astronomy at Gresham College, London, who invented also Gunter's chain, and Gunter's quadrant.

gunwale.c: Gunwale Gun"wale (?), n. [Gun + wale. So named because the upper guns were pointed from it.] (Naut.) The upper edge of a vessel's or boat's side; the uppermost wale of a ship (not including the bulwarks); or that piece of timber which reaches on either side from the quarter-deck to the forecastle, being the uppermost bend, which finishes the upper works of the hull. [Written also gunnel.]

gurge.c: Gurge Gurge, v. t. [See Gorge.] To swallow up. [Obs.]

gurgle.c: Gurgle Gur"gle (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gurgled (?);p. pr. & vb. n. Gurgling (?).] [Cf. It. gorgogliare to gargle, bubble up, fr. L. gurgulio gullet. Cf. Gargle, Gorge.] To run or flow in a broken, irregular, noisy current, as water from a bottle, or a small stream among pebbles or stones.
Gurgle Gur"gle, n. The act of gurgling; a broken, bubbling noise. “Tinkling gurgles.” W. Thompson.

gurglet.c: Gurglet Gur"glet (?), n. [See Goglet.] A porous earthen jar for cooling water by evaporation.

gurglingly.c: Gurglingly Gur"gling*ly` (?), adv. In a gurgling manner.

gurjun.c: Gurjun Gur"jun (?), n. A thin balsam or wood oil derived from the Diptcrocarpus lævis, an East Indian tree. It is used in medicine, and as a substitute for linseed oil in the coarser kinds of paint.

gurl.c: Gurl Gurl (?), n. A young person of either sex. See Girl. [Obs.] Chaucer.

gurlet.c: Gurlet Gur"let (?), n. (Masonry) A pickax with one sharp point and one cutting edge. Knight.

gurmy.c: Gurmy Gur"my (?), n. (Mining) A level; a working.

gurnet.c: Gurnet Gurnard { Gur"nard (?), Gur"net (?) } n. [OF. gornal, gournal, gornart, perh. akin to F. grogner to grunt; cf. Ir. guirnead gurnard.] (Zool.) One ofseveral European marine fishes, of the genus Trigla and allied genera, having a large and spiny head, with mailed cheeks. Some of the species are highly esteemed for food. The name is sometimes applied to the American sea robins. [Written also gournet.]

gurry.c: Gurry Gur"ry (?), n. An alvine evacuation; also, refuse matter. [Obs. or Local] Holland.
Gurry Gur"ry`, n. [Hind. garhī.] A small fort. [India]

gurt.c: Gurt Gurt (gûrt), n. (Mining) A gutter or channel for water, hewn out of the bottom of a working drift. Page.

gush.c: Gush Gush (gŭsh), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gushed (gŭsht); p. pr. & vb. n. Gushing.] [OE. guschen, cf. Icel. gusa and gjsa, also D. gucsen; perh. akin to AS. geótan to pour, G. giessen, Goth. giutan, E. gut. Cf. Found to cast.]

Gush Gush, v. t. 1. A sudden and violent issue of a fluid from an inclosed plase; an emission of a liquid in a large quantity, and with force; the fluid thus emitted; a rapid outpouring of anything; as, a gush of song from a bird.

gushing.c: Gushing Gush"ing, a. 1. Rushing forth with violence, as a fluid; flowing copiously; as, gushing waters. “Gushing blood.” Milton.

gushingly.c: Gushingly Gush"ing*ly (?), adv. 1. In a gushing manner; copiously. Byron.

gusset.c: Gusset Gus"set (?), n. [F. gousset armpit, fob, gusset, dim. of gousse pod, husk; cf. It. guscio shell, or W. cwysed gore, gusset.] 1. A small piece of cloth inserted in a garment, for the purpose of strengthening some part or giving it a tapering enlargement.

gust.c: Gust Gust (gŭst), n. [Icel. gustr a cool breeze. Cf. Gush.] 1. A sudden squall; a violent blast of wind; a sudden and brief rushing or driving of the wind.
Gust Gust, n. [L. gustus; cf. It. & Sp. gusto. √46.]
Gust Gust, v. t. [Cf. L. gustare, It. gustare, Sp. gustar. See GUST a relish.] To taste; to have a relish for. [Obs.]

gustable.c: Gustable Gust"a*ble (?), a. [See Gust, v.] [Obs.] 1. Capable of being tasted; tastable.
Gustable Gust"a*ble, n. Anything that can be tasted. [Obs.]

gustation.c: Gustation Gus*ta"tion (?), n. [L. gustatio: cf. F. gustation.] The act of tasting. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

gustatory.c: Gustatory Gust"a*to*ry (?), a. Pertaining to, or subservient to, the sense of taste; as, the gustatory nerve which supplies the front of the tongue.

gustful.c: Gustful Gust"ful (?), a. Tasteful; well-tasted. [Obs.] Sir K. Digby. -- Gust"ful*ness, n. [Obs.] Barrow.

gusto.c: Gusto Gus"to (?), n. [It. or Sp., fr. L. gustus; akin to E. choose. Cf. 2d Gust, Goût.] Nice or keen appreciation or enjoyment; relish; taste; fancy; as, he ate it with gusto. Dryden.

gustoso.c: Gustoso ‖Gus*to"so (?), a. & adv. [It.] (Mus.) Tasteful; in a tasteful, agreeable manner.

gusty.c: Gusty Gust"y (?), a. Subject to, or characterized by, gusts or squalls; windy; stormy; tempestuous.

gut.c: Gut Gut (?), n. [OE. gut, got, AS. gut, prob. orig., a channel, and akin to geótan to pour. See FOUND to cast.]
Gut Gut, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gutted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Gutting.] 1. To take out the bowels from; to eviscerate.

gutta.c: gutta guttae ‖Gut"ta (?), n.; pl. Guttae (#). [L.] 1. A drop.

guttapercha.c: Gutta-percha Gut"ta-per`cha (?), n. [Malay gutah gum + pertja the tree from which is it procured.] A concrete juice produced by various trees found in the Malayan archipelago, especially by the Isonandra Gutta, syn. Dichopsis Gutta. It becomes soft, and unpressible at the tamperature of boiling water, and, on cooling, retains its new shape. It dissolves in oils and ethers, but not in water. In many of its properties it resembles caoutchouc, and it is extensively used for many economical purposes. The Mimusops globosa of Guiana also yields this material.

guttate.c: Guttate Gut"tate (?), a. [L. guttatus. Cf. Gutty.] Spotted, as if discolored by drops.

guttated.c: Guttated Gut"ta*ted (?), a. [See Guttate.] Besprinkled with drops, or droplike spots. Bailey.

guttatrap.c: Guttatrap Gut"ta*trap (?), n. The inspissated juice of a tree of the genus Artocarpus (A. incisa, or breadfruit tree), sometimes used in making birdlime, on account of its glutinous quality.

gutter.c: Gutter Gut"ter (?), n. [OE. gotere, OF. goutiere, F. gouttière, fr. OF. gote, goute, drop, F. goutte, fr. L. gutta.]
Gutter Gut*ter, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Guttered (#); p. pr. & vb. n. Guttering.] 1. To cut or form into small longitudinal hollows; to channel. Shak.
Gutter Gut"ter, v. i. To become channeled, as a candle when the flame flares in the wind.

guttersnipe.c: Guttersnipe Gut"ter*snipe" (?), n. (Slang) 1. (a) A small poster, suitable for a curbstone. (b) A curbstone broker. [U. S.]

guttifer.c: Guttifer ‖Gut"ti*fer` (?), n. [NL., fr. L. gutta drop+ ferre to bear.] (Bot.) A plant that exudes gum or resin.

guttiferous.c: Guttiferous Gut*tif"er*ous (?), a. (Bot.) (a) Yielding gum or resinous substances. (b) Pertaining to a natural order of trees and shrubs (Guttiferæ) noted for their abounding in a resinous sap.

guttiform.c: Guttiform Gut"ti*form (?), a. [L. gutta a drop + -form.] Drop-shaped, as a spot of color.

guttle.c: Guttle Gut"tle (?), v. t. & i. [From Gut, n.] To put into the gut; to swallow greedily; to gorge; to gormandize. [Obs.] L'Estrange. Dryden.

guttler.c: Guttler Gut"tler (?), n. A greedy eater; a glutton. [Obs.]

guttulous.c: Guttulous Gut"tu*lous (?), a. [L. guttula a little drop, dim. of gutta drop.] In droplike form. [Obs.]

guttural.c: Guttural Gut"tur*al (?), a. [L. guttur throat: cf. F. gutural.] Of or pertaining to the throat; formed in the throat; relating to, or characteristic of, a sound formed in the throat.
Guttural Gut"tur*al, n. A sound formed in the throat; esp., a sound formed by the aid of the back of the tongue, much retracted, and the soft palate; also, a letter representing such a sound.

gutturalism.c: Gutturalism Gut"tur*al*ism (?), n. The quality of being guttural; as, the gutturalism of A [in the 16th cent.]. Earle.

gutturality.c: Gutturality Gut"tur*al"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being guttural. [R.] “The old gutturality of k.” Earle.

gutturalize.c: Gutturalize Gut"tur*al*ize (?), v. t. To speak gutturally; to give a guttural sound to.

gutturally.c: Gutturally Gut"tur*al*ly, adv. In a guttural manner.

gutturalness.c: Gutturalness Gut"tur*al*ness, n. The quality of being guttural.

gutturine.c: Gutturine Gut"tur*ine (?), a. [L. guttur throat.] Pertaining to the throat. [Obs.] “Gutturine tumor.” Ray.

gutturize.c: Gutturize Gut"tur*ize (?), v. t. [L. guttur throat.] To make in the throat; to gutturalize. [R.]

gutturo.c: Gutturo- Gut"tur*o- (?). A combining form denoting relation to the throat; as, gutturo-nasal, having both a guttural and a nasal character; gutturo-palatal.

gutty.c: Gutty Gut"ty (?), a. [L. gutta drop: cf. F. goutté. Cf. Guttated.] (Her.) Charged or sprinkled with drops.

gutwort.c: Gutwort Gut"wort` (?), n. (Bot.) A plant, Globularia Alypum, a violent purgative, found in Africa.

guy.c: guy guy (gī), n. [Sp. guia guide, a guy or small rope used on board of ships to keep weighty things in their places; of Teutonic origin, and the same word as E. guide. See Guide, and cf. Gye.] A rope, chain, or rod attached to anything to steady it; as: a rope to steady or guide an object which is being hoisted or lowered; a rope which holds in place the end of a boom, spar, or yard in a ship; a chain or wire rope connecting a suspension bridge with the land on either side to prevent lateral swaying; a rod or rope attached to the top of a structure, as of a derrick, and extending obliquely to the ground, where it is fastened.
guy guy, v. t. [imp. & p. p. guyed (gīd); p. pr. & vb. n. guying.] To steady or guide with a guy.
guy guy, n. 1. A grotesque effigy, like that of Guy Fawkes, dressed up in England on the fifth of November, the day of the Gunpowder Plot.
Guy Guy, v. t. To fool; to baffle; to make (a person) an object of ridicule. [Local & Collog U.S.]

guyle.c: Guyle Guyle (?), v. t. To guile. [Obs.] Spenser.

guze.c: Guze Guze (gūz), n. [Cf. Gules.] (Her.) A roundlet of tincture sanguine, which is blazoned without mention of the tincture.

guzzle.c: Guzzle Guz"zle (gŭz"z'l), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Guzzled (gŭz"z'ld), p. pr. & vb. n. Guzzling (gŭz"zlĭng).] [OP. gosillier, prob. orig., to pass through the throat; akin to F. gosier throat; cf. It. gozzo a bird's crop.] To swallow liquor greedily; to drink much or frequently.
Guzzle Guz"zle, v. t. To swallow much or often; to swallow with immoderate gust; to drink greedily or continually; as, one who guzzles beer. Dryden.
Guzzle Guz"zle, n. An insatiable thing or person.

gwiniad.c: Gwiniad Gwin"i*ad (gwĭn"ĭ*ăd), n. [W. gwyniad a whiting, the name of various fishes, fr. gwyn white.] (Zoöl.) A fish (Coregonus ferus) of North Wales and Northern Europe, allied to the lake whitefish; -- called also powan, and schelly. [Written also gwyniad, guiniad, gurniad.]

gybe.c: Gybe Gyb Gyb (jĭb), Gybe (jīb), n. (Naut.) See Jib. [Obs.]

Gybe Gybe, v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Gybed (jībd); p. pr. & vb. n. Gybing.] [See Jibe.] (Naut.) To shift from one side of a vessel to the other; -- said of the boom of a fore-and-aft sail when the vessel is steered off the wind until the sail fills on the opposite side. [Also jibe.]

gye.c: Gye Gye (gī or gē), v. t. [OF. guier; of German origin. See Guide, and cf. Guy.] To guide; to govern. [Obs.]

gyle.c: Gyle Gyle (gīl), n. [F. guiller to ferment. Cf. Guillevat.] Fermented wort used for making vinegar.

gymnal.c: Gymnal Gym"nal (gĭm"nail), a. & n. Same as Gimmal.

gymnasiarch.c: Gymnasiarch Gym*na"si*arch (jĭm*nā"zĭ*ärk), n. [L. gymnasiarchus, Gr. gymnasi`archos; gymna`sion + 'a`rchein to govern: cf. F. gymnasiarque.] (Gr. Antiq.) An Athenian officer who superintended the gymnasia, and provided the oil and other necessaries at his own expense.

gymnasium.c: Gymnasium Gym*na"si*um (jĭm*nā"zĭ*ŭm or jĭm*nā"zhĭ*ŭm; 277) n.; pl. E. Gymnasiums (jĭm*nā"zĭ*ŭmz), L. Gymnasia (jĭm*nā"zĭ*ȧ). [L., fr. Gr. gymna`sion, fr. gymna`zein to exercise (naked), fr. gymo`s naked.] 1. A place or building where athletic exercises are performed; a school for gymnastics.

gymnast.c: Gymnast Gym"nast (jĭm"nȧst), n. [Gr. gymnasth`s a trainer of athletes: cf. F. gymnaste. See Gymnasium.] One who teaches or practices gymnastic exercises; the manager of a gymnasium; an athlete.

gymnastical.c: Gymnastical Gymnastic { Gym*nas"tic (jĭm*năs"tĭk), Gym*nas"tic*al (jĭm*năs"tĭ*kail), } a. [L. gymnasticus, Gr. gymnastiko`s: cf. F. gymnastique. See Gymnasium.] 1. Pertaining to athletic exercises intended for health, defense, or diversion; -- originally said of games or exercises, as running, leaping, wrestling, throwing the discus, the javelin, etc.; in modern times more specifically applied to athletic exercises demonstrating balance and agility, such as tumbling, somersaulting, and bodily maneuvers performed on special equipment such as parallel bars or a balance beam; as, gymnastic exercises, contests, etc.

gymnastically.c: Gymnastically Gym*nas"tic*al*ly, adv. In a gymnastic manner.

gymnastics.c: gymnastics gym*nas"tics (jĭm*năs"tĭks), n. 1. Athletic or disciplinary exercises; the art of performing gymnastic exercises.

gymnical.c: Gymnical Gymnic { Gym"nic (jĭm"nĭk), Gym"nic*al (jĭm"nĭ*kail) } a. [L. gymnicus, Gr. gymniko`s: cf. F. gymnique. See Gymmasium.] Athletic; gymnastic. [Obs.]

gymnite.c: Gymnite Gym"nite (jĭm"nīt), n. [Gr. gymno`s naked. So called as coming from the Bare Hills, Maryland.] (Min.) A hydrous silicate of magnesia.

gymnoblastea.c: Gymnoblastea ‖Gym`no*blas"te*a (jĭm`no*blăs"te*ȧ), n. pl. [NL. fr. Gr. gymno`s naked + blasta`nein to sprout.] (Zool.) The Athecata; -- so called because the medusoid buds are not inclosed in a capsule.

gymnoblastic.c: Gymnoblastic Gym`no*blas"tic (jĭm`no*blăs"tĭk), a. (Zool.) Of or pertaining to the Gymnoblastea.

gymnocarpous.c: Gymnocarpous Gym`no*car"pous (jĭm`no*kär"pŭs), a. [Gr. gymno`s naked + karpo`s fruit.] (Bot.) Naked-fruited, the fruit either smooth or not adherent to the perianth. Gray.

gymnochroa.c: Gymnochroa ‖Gym*noch"ro*a (jĭm*nŏk"ro*ȧ), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. gymno`s naked + chro`a skin, body.] (Zool.) A division of Hydroidea including the hydra. See Hydra.

gymnocladus.c: Gymnocladus ‖Gym*noc"la*dus (jĭm*nŏ"lȧ*dŭs), n. [NL., fr. Gr. gymno`s naked + kla`dos a branch.] (Bot.) A genus of leguminous plants; the Kentucky coffee tree. The leaves are cathartic, and the seeds a substitute for coffee.

gymnocopa.c: Gymnocopa ‖Gym`no*co"pa (jĭm`no*kō"pȧ), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. gymno`s naked + kw`ph an oar.] (Zool.) A group of transparent, free-swimming Annelida, having setæ only in the cephalic appendages.

gymnocyte.c: Gymnocyte Gym"no*cyte (jĭm"no*sīt), n. [Gr. gymno`s naked + ky`tos a hollow vessel.] (Biol.) A cytode without a proper cell wall, but with a nucleus. Haeckel.

gymnocytode.c: Gymnocytode Gym`no*cy"tode (jĭm`no*sī"tōd), n. [Gr. gymno`s naked + E. cytode.] (Biol.) A cytode without either a cell wall or a nucleus. Haeckel.

gymnodont.c: Gymnodont Gym"no*dont (jĭm"no*dŏnt), n. [Gr. gymno`s naked + 'odoy`s, 'odo`ntos, tooth.] (Zoöl.) One of a group of plectognath fishes (Gymnodontes), having the teeth and jaws consolidated into one or two bony plates, on each jaw, as the diodonts and tetradonts. See Bur fish, Globefish, Diodon.

gymnogen.c: Gymnogen Gym"no*gen (jĭm"no*jĕn), n. [Gr. gymno`s naked + -gen.] (Bot.) One of a class of plants, so called by Lindley, because the ovules are fertilized by direct contact of the pollen. Same as Gymnosperm.

gymnoglossa.c: Gymnoglossa ‖Gym`no*glos"sa (jĭm`no*glŏs"sȧ), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. gymno`s naked + glw^ssa tongue.] (Zool.) A division of gastropods in which the odontophore is without teeth.

gymnolaemata.c: Gymnolaemata Gymnolaema { ‖Gym`no*læ"ma (jĭm`no*lē"mȧ), ‖Gym`no*læ"ma*ta (jĭm`no*mȧ*tȧ), } prop. n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. gymno`s naked + laimo`s the throat.] (Zool.) An order of Bryozoa, having no epistome.

gymnonoti.c: Gymnonoti ‖Gym`no*no"ti (jĭm`no*nō"tī), n. pl. [NL. fr. Gr. gymno`s naked + nw^tos the back.] (Zool.) The order of fishes which includes the Gymnotus or electrical eel. The dorsal fin is wanting.

gymnopaedic.c: Gymnopaedic Gym`no*pæd"ic (jĭm`no*pĕd"ĭk or jĭm`no*pē"dĭk), a. [Gr. gymno`s naked + pai^s, paido`s, a child.] (Zool.) Having young that are naked when hatched; psilopædic; -- said of certain birds.

gymnophiona.c: Gymnophiona ‖Gym`no*phi"o*na (jĭm`no*fī"o*nȧ), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. gymno`s naked + 'ofio`neos serpentlike.] (Zool.) An order of Amphibia, having a long, annulated, snakelike body. See Ophiomorpha.

gymnophthalmata.c: Gymnophthalmata ‖Gym`noph*thal"ma*ta (jĭm`nŏf*thăl"mȧ*tȧ), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. gymno`s naked + 'ofqalmo`s the eye.] (Zool.) A group of acalephs, including the naked-eyed medusæ; the hydromedusæ. Most of them are known to be the free-swimming progeny (gonophores) of hydroids.

gymnoplast.c: Gymnoplast Gym"no*plast (jĭm"no*plăst), n. [Gr. gymno`s naked + pla`ssein to shape, mold.] (Biol.) A cell or mass of protoplasm devoid of an envelope, as a white blood corpuscle.

gymnorhinal.c: Gymnorhinal Gym`no*rhi"nal (jĭm"no*rī"nail), a. [Gr. gymno`s naked + "ri`s, "rino`s, the nose.] (Zool.) Having unfeathered nostrils, as certain birds.

gymnosomata.c: Gymnosomata ‖Gym`no*so"ma*ta (jĭm"no*sō"mȧ*tȧ or jĭm"no*sŏm"ȧ*tȧ), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. gymno`s naked + sw^ma, sw`matos, the body.] (Zool.) One of the orders of Pteropoda. They have no shell.

gymnosophist.c: Gymnosophist Gym*nos"o*phist (jĭm*nŏs"o*fĭst), n. [Gr. gymnosofisth`s; gymno`s naked + sofisth`s philosopher; cf. F. gymnosophiste.] One of a sect of philosophers, said to have been found in India by Alexander the Great, who went almost naked, denied themselves the use of flesh, renounced bodily pleasures, and employed themselves in the contemplation of nature.

gymnosophy.c: Gymnosophy Gym*nos"o*phy (jĭm*nŏs"o*fy̆), n. The doctrines of the Gymnosophists. Good.

gymnosperm.c: Gymnosperm Gym"no*sperm (jĭm"no*spẽrm), n. (Bot.) A plant that bears naked seeds (i. e., seeds not inclosed in an ovary), as the common pine and hemlock. Cf. Angiosperm.

gymnospermous.c: Gymnospermous Gym`no*sper"mous (jĭm"no*spẽr"mŭs), a. [Gr. gymno`spermos; gymno`s naked + spe`rma seed: cf. F. gymnosperme.] (Bot.) (a) Having naked seeds, or seeds not inclosed in a capsule or other vessel. (b) Belonging to the class of plants consisting of gymnosperms.

gymnotoka.c: Gymnotoka ‖Gym*not"o*ka (jĭm*nŏt"o*kȧ), n. pl. [NL., fr. Gr. gymno`s naked + to`kos a bringing forth.] (Zool.) The Athecata.

gymnotus.c: Gymnotus ‖Gym*no"tus (jĭm*nō"tŭs), n. [NL., fr. Gr. gymno`s naked + nw^tos the back: cf. F. gymnote.] (Zool.) A genus of South American fresh-water fishes, including the Gymnotus electricus, or electric eel. It has a greenish, eel-like body, and is possessed of electric power.

gyn.c: Gyn Gyn (gĭn), v. i. To begin. See Gin. [Obs.]

gynaecium.c: Gynaecium Gynaeceum { ‖Gyn`æ*ce"um (jĭn`e*sē"ŭm), ‖Gyn`æ*ci"um (jĭn`e*sī"ŭm), } n. [L., fr. Gr. gynaikei^on women's apartments, fr. gynh` a woman.] That part of a large house, among the ancients, exclusively appropriated to women. [Written also gyneceum, gynecium.] Tennyson.

gynaecian.c: Gynaecian Gy*næ"cian (jĭ*nē"shain), a. The same as Gynecian.

gynaecophore.c: Gynaecophore Gy*næ"co*phore (jĭ*nē"ko*fōr), n. [Gr. gynaikei^on the women's apartments + fe`rein to bear.] (Zool.) A ventral canal or groove, in which the males of some diœcious trematodes carry the female. See Illust. of Hæmatozoa.

gynander.c: Gynander Gy*nan"der (jĭ*năn"dẽr), n. [See Gynandrian.] (Bot.) A plant having the stamens inserted in the pistil.

gynandria.c: Gynandria ‖Gy*nan"dri*a (jĭ*năn"drĭ*ȧ), n. pl. [NL. See Gynandrian.] (Bot.) A class of plants in the Linnæan system, whose stamens grow out of, or are united with, the pistil.

gynandrous.c: Gynandrous Gynandrian { Gy*nan"dri*an (jĭ*năn"drĭ*ain), Gy*nan"drous (jĭ*năn"drŭs), } a. [Gr. gy`nandros of doubtful sex; gynh` a woman + 'anh`r, 'andro`s, man: cf. F. gynandre.] (Bot.) Having stamens inserted in the pistil; belonging to the class Gynandria.

gynandromorph.c: Gynandromorph Gy*nan"dro*morph (jĭ*năn"dro*môrf), n. (Zool.) An animal affected with gynandromorphism.

gynandromorphism.c: Gynandromorphism Gy*nan`dro*mor"phism (jĭ*năn`dro*môr"fĭz'm), n. [Gr. gynh` a woman, female + 'anh`r, 'andro`s, a man, male + morfh` form.] (Zool.) An abnormal condition of certain animals, in which one side has the external characters of the male, and the other those of the female.

gynantherous.c: Gynantherous Gy*nan"ther*ous (jĭ*năn"thẽr*ŭs), a. [Gr. gynh` a woman + E. anther.] (Bot.) Pertaining to an abnormal condition of the flower, in which the stamens are converted into pistils. R. Brown.

gynarchy.c: Gynarchy Gyn"ar*chy (jĭn"ȧr*ky̆), n. [Gr. gynh` a woman + -archy.] Government by a woman. Chesterfield.

gynecian.c: Gynecian Gy*ne"cian (jĭ*nē"shain), a. [Gr. gynaikei^os.] Of or relating to women.

gynecocracy.c: Gynecocracy Gyn`e*coc"ra*cy (jĭn`e*kŏk"rȧ*sy̆), n. [Gr. gynaikokrati`a; gynh`, gynaiko`s, a woman + kratei^n to rule: cf. F. gynécocratie. Cf. Gynocracy.] Government by a woman, female power; gyneocracy. Bailey.

gynecological.c: Gynecological Gyn`e*co*log"ic*al (jĭn`e*ko*lŏj"ĭ*kail or gī`ne-), a. Of or pertaining to gynecology.

gynecology.c: Gynecology Gyn`e*col"o*gy (jĭn`e*kŏl"o*jy̆ or gī`ne-), n. [Gr. gynh`, gynaiko`s, a woman + -logy.] The science which treats of the structure and diseases of women. -- Gyn`e*col"o*gist.

gyneolatry.c: Gyneolatry Gyn`e*ol"a*try (jĭn`e*ŏl"ȧ*try̆), n. [Gr. gynh` a woman + latrei`a worship.] The adoration or worship of woman.

gynephobia.c: Gynephobia ‖Gyn`e*pho"bi*a (jĭn`e*fō"bĭ*ȧ), n. [NL., fr. Gr. gynh` a woman + fo`bos fear.] Hatred of women; repugnance to the society of women. Holmes.

gynne.c: Gynne Gyn"ne (gĭn"nei), v. i. To begin. See Gin. [Obs.]

gynobase.c: Gynobase Gyn"o*base (jĭn"o*bās), n. [Gr. gynh` a woman, female + E. base.] (Bot.) A dilated base or receptacle, supporting a multilocular ovary.

gynobasic.c: Gynobasic Gyn`o*ba"sic (jĭn"o*bā"sĭk), a. (Bot.) Pertaining to, or having, a gynobase.

gynocracy.c: Gynocracy Gy*noc"ra*cy (jĭ*nŏk"rȧ*sy̆), n. [See Gynecocracy.] Female government; gynecocracy.

gynodioecious.c: Gynodioecious Gy`no*di*œ"cious (jī`no*di*ē"shŭs), a. [Gr. gynh` a woman + E. diœcious.] (Bot.) Diœcious, but having some hermaphrodite or perfect flowers on an individual plant which bears mostly pistillate flowers.

gynoecium.c: Gynoecium ‖Gy*nœ"ci*um (jĭ*nē"sĭ*ŭm or -shĭ*ŭm), n. [NL., fr. Gr. gynh` a woman + o'i^kos house.] (Bot.) The pistils of a flower, taken collectively. See Illust. of Carpophore.

gynophore.c: Gynophore Gyn"o*phore (jĭn"o*fōr), n. [Gr. gynh` woman, female + fe`rein to bear, produce: cf. F. gynophore.] 1. (Bot.) The pedicel raising the pistil or ovary above the stamens, as in the passion flower. Lindley.

gyp.c: Gyp Gyp (jĭp), n. [Said to be a sportive application of Gr. gy`ps a vulture.] A college servant; -- so called in Cambridge, England; at Oxford called a scout. [Cant]

gypseous.c: Gypseous Gyp"se*ous (jĭp"se*ŭs), a. [L. gypseus. See Gypsum.] Resembling or containing gypsum; partaking of the qualities of gypsum.

gypsey.c: Gypsey Gyp"sey (jĭp"sy̆), n. A gypsy. See Gypsy.

gypsiferous.c: Gypsiferous Gyp*sif"er*ous (jĭp*sĭf"ẽr*ŭs), a. [Gypsum + -ferous: cf. F. gypsifère.] Containing gypsum.

gypsography.c: Gypsography Gyp*sog"ra*phy (jĭp*sŏg"rȧ*fy̆), n. [Gypsum + -graphy.] The act or art of engraving on gypsum.

gypsoplast.c: Gypsoplast Gyp"so*plast (jĭp"so*plăst), n. [Gypsum + Gr. pla`ssein to mold.] A cast taken in plaster of Paris, or in white lime.

gypsum.c: Gypsum Gyp"sum (jĭp"sŭm), n. [L. gypsum, Gr. gy`psos; cf. Ar. jibs plaster, mortar, Per. jabsīn lime.] (Min.) A mineral consisting of the hydrous sulphate of lime (calcium). When calcined, it forms plaster of Paris. Selenite is a transparent, crystalline variety; alabaster, a fine, white, massive variety.

gypsy.c: Gypsy Gyp"sy (jĭp"sy̆), n.; pl. Gypsies (jĭp"sĭz). [OE. Gypcyan, F. égyptien Egyptian, gypsy, L. Aegyptius. See Egyptian.] [Also spelled gipsy and gypsey.] 1. One of a vagabond race, whose tribes, coming originally from India, entered Europe in the 14th or 15th century, and are now scattered over Turkey, Russia, Hungary, Spain, England, etc., living by theft, fortune telling, horsejockeying, tinkering, etc. Cf. Bohemian, Romany.
Gypsy Gyp"sy a. Pertaining to, or suitable for, gypsies.
Gypsy Gyp"sy (jĭp"sy̆), v. i. To play the gypsy; to picnic in the woods. Mostly, Gyp"sy*ing, vb. n.

gypsyism.c: Gypsyism Gyp"sy*ism (jĭp"sĭ*ĭz'm), n. 1. The arts and practices or habits of gypsies; deception; cheating; flattery.

gypsywort.c: Gypsywort Gyp"sy*wort` (jĭp"sĭ*wûrt`), n. (Bot.) A labiate plant (the Lycopus Europæus). Gypsies are said to stain their skin with its juice.

gyracanthus.c: Gyracanthus ‖Gyr`a*can"thus (jĭr`ȧ*kăn"thŭs), n. [NL., fr. Gr. gyro`s round + 'a`kanqa spine.] (Paleon.) A genus of fossil fishes, found in Devonian and carboniferous strata; -- so named from their round, sculptured spines.

gyral.c: Gyral Gy"ral (jī"rail), a. [See Gyre.] 1. Moving in a circular path or way; whirling; gyratory.

gyrate.c: Gyrate Gy"rate (jī"rat), a. [L. gyratus made in a circular form, p. p. of gyrare.] Winding or coiled round; curved into a circle; taking a circular course.

Gyrate Gy"rate (jī"rāt), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Gyrated (jī"ra*tĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Gyrating.] [L. gyratus, p. p. of gyrare to gyrate. See Gyre, n.] To revolve round a central point; to move spirally about an axis, as a tornado; to revolve.

gyration.c: Gyration Gy*ra"tion (ji*rā"shŭn), n. 1. The act of turning or whirling, as around a fixed center; a circular or spiral motion; motion about an axis; rotation; revolution.

gyratory.c: Gyratory Gy"ra*to*ry (jī"rȧ*to*ry̆), a. Moving in a circle, or spirally; revolving; whirling around.

gyre.c: Gyre Gyre (jīr), n. [L. gyrus, Gr. gy^ros, cf. gyro`s round.] A circular motion, or a circle described by a moving body; a turn or revolution; a circuit.
Gyre Gyre, v. t. & i. [Cf. OF. gyrer, girer. See Gyrate.] To turn round; to gyrate. [Obs.] Bp. Hall. Drayton.

gyrencephala.c: Gyrencephala ‖Gyr`en*ceph"a*la (jĭr`ĕn*sĕf"ȧ*lȧ), n. pl. [NL. fr. Gr. gyro`s round + 'egke`falos the brain.] (Zool.) The higher orders of Mammalia, in which the cerebrum is convoluted. -- Gyr`en*ceph"a*lous (jĭr`ĕn*sĕf"ȧ*lŭs), a.

gyrfalcon.c: Gyrfalcon Gyr"fal`con (jẽr"fä`k'n), n. [OE. gerfaucon, OF. gerfaucon, LL. gyrofalco, perh. fr. L. gyrus circle + falco falcon, and named from its circling flight; or cf. E. gier-eagle. See Gyre, n., Falcon.] (Zool.) One of several species and varieties of large Arctic falcons, esp. Falco rusticolus and the white species Falco Islandicus, both of which are circumpolar. The black and the gray are varieties of the former. See Illust. of Accipiter. [Written also gerfalcon, gierfalcon, and jerfalcon.]

gyrland.c: Gyrland Gyr"land (gẽr"laind), v. t. [See Garland.] To garland. [Obs.]

gyrodus.c: Gyrodus ‖Gyr"o*dus (jĭr"o*dŭs), n. [NL., fr. Gr. gyro`s round + 'odoy`s tooth.] (Paleon.) A genus of extinct oölitic fishes, having rounded teeth in several rows adapted for crushing.

gyrogonite.c: Gyrogonite Gy*rog"o*nite (jĭ*rŏg"o*nīt), n. [Gr. gy^ros circle, ring + go`nos fruit.] (Paleon.) The petrified fruit of the Chara hispida, a species of stonewort. See Stonewort. Lyell.

gyroidal.c: Gyroidal Gy*roid"al (ji*roid"ail), a. [Gr. gy^ros circle + -oid + -al.] 1. Spiral in arrangement or action.

gyrolepis.c: Gyrolepis ‖Gy*rol"e*pis (jĭ*rŏl"e*pĭs), n. [NL., fr. Gr. gyro`s round + lepi`s scale.] (Paleon.) A genus of ganoid fishes, found in strata of the new red sandstone, and the lias bone beds. Agassiz.

gyroma.c: Gyroma ‖Gy*ro"ma (ji*rō"mȧ), n. [NL., fr. Gr. gyroy^n to round, bend, fr. gyro`s round.] A turning round. [R.]

gyromancy.c: Gyromancy Gyr"o*man`cy (jĭr"o*măn`sy̆ or jī"ro-), n. [Gr. gy^ros ring, circle + -mancy: cf. F. gyromancie.] A kind of divination performed by drawing a ring or circle, and walking in or around it. Brande & C.

gyron.c: Gyron Gy"ron (jī"rŏn), n. [F. giron; of German origin. See Gore a piece of cloth.] (Her.) A subordinary of triangular form having one of its angles at the fess point and the opposite side at the edge of the escutcheon. When there is only one gyron on the shield it is bounded by two lines drawn from the fess point, one horizontally to the dexter side, and one to the dexter chief corner.

gyronny.c: Gyronny Gy"ron*ny (jī"rŏn*ny̆), a. [F. gironné.] (Her.) Covered with gyrons, or divided so as to form several gyrons; -- said of an escutcheon.

gyropigeon.c: Gyro-pigeon Gy"ro-pi`geon (jī"ro*pĭj`ŭn), n. [L. gyrare to revolve + E. pigeon.] A flying object simulating a pigeon in flight, when projected from a spring trap. It is used as a flying target in shooting matches. Knight.

gyroscope.c: Gyroscope Gy"ro*scope (jī"ro*skōp), n. [Gr. gy^ros ring, circle + -scope.] 1. A rotating wheel, mounted in a ring or rings, for illustrating the dynamics of rotating bodies, the composition of rotations, etc. It was devised by Professor W. R. Johnson, in 1832, by whom it was called the rotascope.

gyroscopic.c: Gyroscopic Gy`ro*scop"ic (jī`ro*skŏp"ĭk), a. Pertaining to the gyroscope; resembling the motion of the gyroscope.

gyrose.c: Gyrose Gy*rose" (ji*rōs" or jī"rōs), a. [See Gyre.] (Bot.) Turned round like a crook, or bent to and fro. Loudon.

gyrostat.c: Gyrostat Gy"ro*stat (jī"ro*stăt), n. [Gr. gy^ros ring, circle + "ista`nai to cause to stand.] (Physics) A modification of the gyroscope, consisting essentially of a fly wheel fixed inside a rigid case to which is attached a thin flange of metal for supporting the instrument. It is used in studying the dynamics of rotating bodies.

gyrostatic.c: Gyrostatic Gy`ro*stat"ic (jī`ro*stăt"ĭk), a. (Physics) Of or pertaining to the gyrostat or to gyrostatics.

gyrostatics.c: Gyrostatics Gy`ro*stat"ics (jī`ro*stăt"ĭks), n. (Physics) The doctrine or theory of the gyrostat, or of the phenomena of rotating bodies.

gyrus.c: Gyrus ‖Gy"rus (jī"rŭs), n.; pl. Gyri (jī"rī). [L. See Gyre, n.] A convoluted ridge between grooves; a convolution; as, the gyri of the brain; the gyri of brain coral. See Brain.

gyte.c: Gyte Gyte (gīt), a. Delirious; senselessly extravagant; as, the man is clean gyte. [Scot.] Sir W. Scott.

gyve.c: Gyve Gyve (jīv), n. [Of Celtic origin; cf. W. gefyn, Ir. geibhionn, Gael. geimheal.] A shackle; especially, one to confine the legs; a fetter. [Written also give.]
Gyve Gyve, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Gyved (jīvd); p. pr. & vb. n. Gyving.] To fetter; to shackle; to chain. Spenser.
